lessons.title: Electronics Warm-up: Voltage, Current and Circuits
lessons.content:
Imagine the water tank on the roof of your building in Dhaka. Water sits up high, and when someone opens a tap downstairs, it rushes down the pipe. The height of the tank gives the water a push. The amount of water flowing through the pipe each second is the flow. A narrow, rusty pipe slows the water down. Electricity works in a surprisingly similar way, and this whole course is about the clever little parts that control that flow: diodes, transistors and the circuits built from them. Before we meet those parts, we need a solid warm-up on the basic words of electricity.

What is electronics? Electricity is the flow of electric charge, usually tiny particles called electrons moving through a wire. Electrical engineering often deals with big power: power stations, transmission lines, fans and motors. Electronics deals with controlling small currents in smart ways, so that a circuit can amplify a weak signal, switch things on and off, store information or compute. Your phone, your laptop, a TV remote and the digital meter on your gas line are all electronics. Every chip inside them is built from the devices you will study in this course.

Charge: Charge is measured in coulombs (C). One electron carries a very tiny negative charge, about 1.6 x 10^-19 coulombs. That means it takes roughly 6.25 x 10^18 electrons to make one coulomb. You never count electrons one by one in practice; you think in coulombs, or more often in current.

Current: Current is how much charge passes a point every second. Its unit is the ampere (A), and one ampere means one coulomb per second. The formula is I = Q / t. If 10 coulombs pass through a wire in 5 seconds, the current is 10 / 5 = 2 A. In electronics we often use smaller units: a milliampere (mA) is one thousandth of an ampere, and a microampere (uA) is one millionth. An LED usually needs around 10 to 20 mA, while a phone charging can draw 1 to 3 A. A funny historical fact: we say current flows from plus to minus (conventional current), but electrons actually move from minus to plus. Scientists picked the direction before electrons were discovered, and the habit stayed. In circuit diagrams we always use conventional current.

Voltage: Voltage is the push that makes charge move, just like the height of the water tank. Its proper name is potential difference, and its unit is the volt (V). Voltage is always measured between two points. A single AA battery gives about 1.5 V, a phone battery about 3.7 V, a USB port gives 5 V, and the wall socket in Bangladesh gives about 220 V AC. Without a voltage difference, charges have no reason to flow, the same way water does not flow between two tanks at the same height.

Resistance: Resistance is how much a material fights against current, like a narrow pipe fighting the water. Its unit is the ohm, written with the Greek letter omega. Copper wire has very low resistance; rubber has a huge resistance. A resistor is a small component made on purpose to have a known resistance, like 220 ohms or 10 kilo-ohms. Resistors are used to limit current, divide voltages and set the working point of transistors, which you will do a lot later.

Ohm's law: The three ideas are tied together by Ohm's law: V = I x R. If you know any two, you can find the third. Example: a 9 V battery is connected across a 450 ohm resistor. The current is I = V / R = 9 / 450 = 0.02 A, which is 20 mA. Another example: a 2 mA current flows through a 1 kilo-ohm resistor, so the voltage across it is 0.002 x 1000 = 2 V. Ohm's law is the single most used formula in this whole course, so make it automatic.

Power: Power is how fast energy is used, measured in watts (W). The formula is P = V x I. Using Ohm's law you can also write P = I^2 x R or P = V^2 / R. A 5 V charger giving 2 A delivers 10 W. A resistor carrying 20 mA with 9 V across it burns 0.18 W as heat. This matters, because small resistors are usually rated for only 0.25 W. Put too much power through one and it gets hot and can burn out. That is why chips need fans and heat sinks: every working transistor turns some energy into heat.

Series circuits: When components are connected one after another in a single path, they are in series. The same current flows through all of them, and their resistances simply add: R total = R1 + R2 + R3. Two resistors of 1 kilo-ohm and 2 kilo-ohm in series make 3 kilo-ohm. Old style decoration lights on a wedding gate in Bangladesh are often wired in long series strings, which is why one broken bulb can make a whole string go dark.

Parallel circuits: When components share the same two connection points, they are in parallel. They all get the same voltage, and the currents split between them. For two resistors, R total = (R1 x R2) / (R1 + R2). Two 1 kilo-ohm resistors in parallel give 500 ohms. The total is always smaller than the smallest one, because you are giving current more paths. The lights and fans in your home are in parallel, so switching off one fan does not turn off the lights.

Kirchhoff's laws: Two simple rules let you solve almost any circuit. Kirchhoff's Current Law (KCL) says the total current flowing into a junction equals the total current flowing out, because charge cannot pile up or vanish. If 5 mA enters a node and 2 mA leaves through one branch, then 3 mA must leave through the other. Kirchhoff's Voltage Law (KVL) says that if you walk around any closed loop, the voltage rises and drops add up to zero. With a 12 V battery and two resistors in series, if one resistor drops 4 V, the other must drop 8 V.

The voltage divider: A very common mini-circuit is two resistors in series across a supply, with the output taken from the middle. The output is Vout = Vin x R2 / (R1 + R2). With Vin = 12 V, R1 = 8 kilo-ohm and R2 = 4 kilo-ohm, Vout = 12 x 4 / 12 = 4 V. You will use exactly this circuit to bias transistors in later lessons, so it is worth practising now.

Capacitors: A capacitor is two metal plates separated by an insulator. It stores charge, a bit like a small bucket that fills with water. Its unit is the farad (F); practical values are microfarads (uF), nanofarads (nF) and picofarads (pF). The rule is Q = C x V. A capacitor blocks steady DC once it is full, but lets changing AC signals pass through. That property is used to smooth power supplies, to couple signals between amplifier stages and to build timers. A charged capacitor can even give you a small shock after the device is unplugged, so be careful with big ones inside old TVs and power supplies.

Inductors: An inductor is a coil of wire. It stores energy in a magnetic field and resists sudden changes in current, a bit like a heavy flywheel that does not like to speed up or slow down quickly. Its unit is the henry (H). Inductors are found in power supplies, radio circuits and the transformers in older chargers. In this course they appear less often than capacitors, but you should recognise them.

AC and DC: Direct current (DC) flows in one direction with a steady value, like the current from a battery. Alternating current (AC) keeps changing direction, rising and falling like a wave. In Bangladesh the mains supply is 220 V at 50 hertz, which means it goes through 50 complete back-and-forth cycles every second. The 220 V is the RMS (effective) value; the actual peak is about 220 x 1.414 = 311 V. Electronic circuits almost always need low-voltage DC, so much of the early part of this course is about turning AC into clean DC.

Analog and digital: An analog signal can take any value in a range, like the smooth voltage from a microphone as you sing. A digital signal uses only a few allowed levels, usually two: low (0) and high (1). Inside a computer, high might be around 1 V or 3.3 V and low near 0 V. The same transistors can work in both worlds: as amplifiers that copy and enlarge analog signals, or as switches that create 0s and 1s. This is why a CSE student studies electronics: the logic gates from your digital logic course are made of real transistors that obey everything in this course.

Real-life example 1, the IPS at home: During load-shedding, many homes in Bangladesh run lights and fans from an IPS. Inside, a 12 V battery is charged from the 220 V AC line using a transformer and diodes, which turn AC into DC. When power goes out, transistors switch the battery current back and forth very fast to recreate AC for your fan. Voltage, current, power, AC and DC are all at work in one box. If the IPS battery is rated 12 V and 100 ampere-hours, it stores roughly 12 x 100 = 1200 watt-hours of energy, enough to run a 60 W load for about 20 hours in theory, though real systems give less because of losses.

Real-life example 2, an LED with a resistor: Suppose you want to light a red LED from a 5 V USB supply. The LED needs about 2 V across it and 15 mA. The resistor must drop the rest: 5 - 2 = 3 V. By Ohm's law, R = 3 / 0.015 = 200 ohms. You would pick the nearest standard value, 220 ohms, which gives about 13.6 mA, still nicely bright. Power in the resistor is 3 x 0.0136, about 0.04 W, well under a 0.25 W rating. This tiny calculation is something engineers do every day.

Common mistakes: Students often mix up voltage and current. Remember: voltage is the push between two points, current is the flow through a component. Another mistake is forgetting units: 2 kilo-ohm is 2000 ohms, and 5 mA is 0.005 A. Mixing kilo and milli correctly makes life easy: volts divided by kilo-ohms gives milliamps directly. Students also forget that parallel resistance is smaller than each branch, and they add parallel resistors like series ones. Finally, many think current gets used up in a resistor. It does not; the same current comes out that goes in. Energy is used up, not charge.

What exams ask: Typical questions include solving a series-parallel resistor network, applying KVL and KCL to find unknown currents, calculating the output of a voltage divider, finding power dissipated in a resistor, and converting between RMS and peak AC values. Short questions may ask you to define current, voltage and resistance or to explain the difference between AC and DC.

Recap: Current is flow of charge in amperes, voltage is the push in volts, resistance fights the flow in ohms, and V = I x R ties them together. Power is P = V x I. Series components share current, parallel components share voltage. KCL and KVL let you solve circuits. Capacitors store charge and pass AC; inductors resist changes in current. With this toolbox ready, the next lesson dives into the material that makes modern electronics possible: semiconductors.
key_points: Current (A) is charge flow per second; voltage (V) is the push between two points; resistance (ohm) opposes flow.
Ohm's law V = I x R and power P = V x I are used in almost every circuit calculation.
Series resistors add; parallel resistors give a smaller total, R1R2/(R1+R2) for two.
KCL: currents into a node equal currents out. KVL: voltages around a loop sum to zero.
A voltage divider gives Vout = Vin x R2/(R1+R2) and is used to bias transistors.
Capacitors store charge (Q = CV) and pass AC; inductors resist changes in current.
Bangladesh mains is 220 V RMS, 50 Hz, with a peak of about 311 V.
Electronics works with both analog signals and digital 0/1 signals using the same devices.
lessons.tip: Always write units next to every number. Volts divided by kilo-ohms gives milliamps directly, which saves you from many silly mistakes.
lessons.task: Find three chargers or adapters at home and read their labels. Write down the input voltage and frequency and the output voltage and current, then calculate each one's output power using P = V x I.

quiz.q: A 12 V battery is connected across a 4 kilo-ohm resistor. What is the current?
quiz.explain: I = V/R = 12 V / 4 kilo-ohm = 3 mA.

quiz.q: Two 6 kilo-ohm resistors are connected in parallel. What is the total resistance?
quiz.explain: For two equal resistors in parallel, the total is half: 6 x 6 / 12 = 3 kilo-ohm.

quiz.q: Which law says the sum of voltages around a closed loop is zero?
quiz.explain: KVL is about voltages around a loop; KCL is about currents at a node.

quiz.q: A voltage divider has Vin = 10 V, R1 = 3 kilo-ohm, R2 = 2 kilo-ohm. What is Vout across R2?
The 220 V written for Bangladesh mains is which value?
quiz.explain: 220 V is the RMS value; the peak is about 311 V.

lessons.title: Semiconductor Materials and Energy Bands
lessons.content:
Think about the roads in Dhaka. Some roads, like a wide empty highway at 3 am, let cars zoom freely. Some, like a blocked lane during a hartal, let nothing through. And some roads are in between: normally jammed, but if a traffic police officer waves the right signal, cars start moving. Materials behave the same way with electric current. Conductors are the free highway, insulators are the blocked lane, and semiconductors are the in-between roads that we can control. All of modern electronics is built on that control.

Conductors: A conductor is a material that lets current flow very easily. Metals such as copper, aluminium, silver and gold are good conductors. The reason is that each metal atom gives up one or more outer electrons into a shared sea of free electrons that can drift through the whole piece of metal. Apply even a small voltage and these free electrons move, giving a current. Copper is used in house wiring and on circuit boards because it conducts well and is fairly cheap. Gold is used on connector pins because it does not rust.

Insulators: An insulator holds on to its electrons very tightly, so almost no free electrons exist to carry current. Rubber, glass, dry wood, plastic and ceramic are insulators. The plastic coating on a wire and the porcelain holders on electric poles are insulators that keep current where it belongs and keep people safe.

Semiconductors: A semiconductor sits between the two. In a perfectly pure form at very low temperature, it behaves almost like an insulator. But at room temperature some electrons break free, and if we add tiny controlled amounts of other elements, its conductivity can be changed by many orders of magnitude. The most important semiconductor is silicon (Si). Germanium (Ge) was used in early transistors. Compound semiconductors such as gallium arsenide (GaAs) and gallium nitride (GaN) are used in LEDs, lasers, fast radio chips and modern fast chargers.

Why silicon? Silicon is the second most common element in the Earth's crust, after oxygen; ordinary sand is mostly silicon dioxide. It forms an excellent natural insulating layer, silicon dioxide, when heated in oxygen, which is extremely useful for making transistors. It can be purified to an amazing level and grown into large, nearly perfect crystals. And it works well at normal temperatures. That combination made silicon the material of the chip industry, which is why California's tech region is nicknamed Silicon Valley.

Atomic structure: An atom has a nucleus of protons and neutrons, surrounded by electrons in shells. The electrons in the outermost shell are called valence electrons, and they decide how the atom bonds and conducts. Silicon has atomic number 14, with electrons arranged 2, 8, 4, so it has 4 valence electrons. Germanium also has 4 valence electrons. Elements with 4 valence electrons are in group 14 (often called group IV) of the periodic table, and they are the classic semiconductors.

Covalent bonds and the crystal: In a silicon crystal, each atom shares its 4 valence electrons with 4 neighbours, and each neighbour shares one back. Each pair of shared electrons is a covalent bond, and every atom ends up with 8 electrons around it, a very stable arrangement. The atoms line up in a regular 3D pattern called a diamond lattice. You can imagine a group of friends standing in a perfect grid, each holding hands with four others. When everyone is holding hands, nobody is free to wander, so pure silicon at very low temperature carries almost no current.

Breaking a bond: At room temperature, atoms vibrate with heat energy. Now and then, a vibration gives a valence electron enough energy to break out of its bond and wander through the crystal. That free electron can carry current. When it leaves, it leaves behind an empty spot in the bond, called a hole. A hole acts like a positive charge, and a neighbouring electron can jump into it, which moves the hole to a new place. So in a semiconductor, current is carried by two kinds of carriers: free electrons and holes. We will study them carefully in the next lesson.

Energy levels: In a single isolated atom, electrons can only have certain fixed energies, called energy levels. You can think of them as fixed steps on a staircase: an electron can stand on a step but not in between. When billions of atoms come close together to form a solid, each level spreads out into a band of very closely spaced levels. This is the band theory of solids, and it explains neatly why materials differ.

Valence band and conduction band: The valence band is the highest band that is normally filled with electrons that are bound in bonds. The conduction band is the next band above it, where electrons are free to move and carry current. Between them there may be a gap of energies that electrons cannot have, called the forbidden gap or band gap. To conduct, an electron must jump from the valence band up to the conduction band, crossing the gap. Think of a two-storey bus: the lower deck is packed tight so nobody can move; the upper deck is empty and roomy. A passenger who climbs the stairs to the upper deck can move around freely.

The electron-volt: Band gaps are measured in electron-volts (eV). One electron-volt is the energy one electron gains when it moves through a potential difference of one volt, about 1.6 x 10^-19 joules. It is a handy tiny unit for atomic-scale energies.

Band gaps compared: In conductors, the valence and conduction bands overlap, so there is no gap and electrons are always free to move. In insulators, the gap is large, roughly more than 4 or 5 eV; diamond, for example, has a gap of about 5.5 eV, so heat at room temperature almost never lifts an electron across. In semiconductors, the gap is small: about 1.1 eV for silicon and about 0.67 eV for germanium at room temperature. Gallium arsenide is about 1.4 eV, and gallium nitride about 3.4 eV. A small gap means some electrons can jump across using heat energy, so the material conducts a little, and we can control how much.

Temperature effects: Here is a big difference between metals and semiconductors. When a metal gets hotter, its atoms vibrate more and get in the way of moving electrons, so its resistance increases. When a semiconductor gets hotter, many more electrons jump the band gap, creating more carriers, so its resistance decreases. We say semiconductors have a negative temperature coefficient of resistance. This is used in thermistors, temperature sensors found in phone batteries, fridges and electric kettles. It is also why chips must be kept cool: as they heat up, currents change and can even run away.

Why germanium lost to silicon: Germanium's smaller band gap means more electrons are freed by heat. This gives larger leakage currents that grow quickly with temperature, so germanium devices misbehave when they get hot. Silicon's larger gap makes devices more stable at normal operating temperatures, and silicon's natural oxide is a huge manufacturing advantage. By the 1960s silicon had become the main material for transistors.

Light and the band gap: The band gap also decides how a semiconductor interacts with light. When an electron falls from the conduction band back to the valence band, it can give off energy as light, and the colour depends on the gap. Silicon is a poor light emitter, which is why LEDs use compounds like gallium arsenide (infrared), gallium arsenide phosphide (red) and indium gallium nitride (blue and green). In reverse, if light with enough energy hits a semiconductor, it can lift electrons across the gap, which is how solar cells and camera sensors work. A useful rule: wavelength in nanometres is roughly 1240 divided by the energy in eV. So a gap of 1.24 eV matches light of about 1000 nm, in the infrared.

Intrinsic carrier numbers: How many carriers does heat create? In pure silicon at room temperature (about 300 K), there are roughly 10^10 free electrons in every cubic centimetre, and the same number of holes. That sounds huge, but a cubic centimetre of silicon has about 5 x 10^22 atoms, so only about one bond in every few trillion is broken. Copper, by comparison, has roughly one free electron per atom. This is why pure silicon is a poor conductor at room temperature, and why the next lesson's trick, doping, is needed to make it useful. The number of thermally created carriers roughly doubles for every 10 degree Celsius rise in silicon around room temperature, which shows how sensitive semiconductors are to heat.

A quick worked check: Suppose an electron in silicon needs at least 1.1 eV to jump the gap. A photon of red light at 650 nm has energy of about 1240 / 650, roughly 1.9 eV, which is more than enough, so red light can create electron-hole pairs in silicon. That is why your phone camera, which uses a silicon sensor, sees red light easily. A photon at 1500 nm, used in fibre-optic internet cables, has about 0.83 eV, which is less than 1.1 eV, so silicon is nearly transparent to it. Fibre receivers therefore use other materials such as indium gallium arsenide, which has a smaller gap.

Real-life example 1, solar panels on rooftops: Bangladesh has millions of solar home systems in rural areas, and many rooftops in cities now carry solar panels. Each panel is made of silicon cells. Sunlight photons with energy above silicon's 1.1 eV gap free electrons and create holes; the cell structure pushes them in opposite directions to create a current. Light with lower energy, deep infrared, passes through without being used, which is one reason cells cannot convert all sunlight into electricity.

Real-life example 2, the hot phone: If you play a heavy game on your phone during a Dhaka summer, the phone gets hot and may slow itself down. Part of the reason is semiconductor physics: as chip temperature rises, leakage currents increase, power use goes up, and heat rises further. The phone's software watches temperature sensors, many of which are themselves semiconductor devices, and reduces the clock speed to protect the chip.

Common mistakes: Students often say semiconductors are half-conductors that conduct half as well as metals. That is wrong; their conductivity can vary over a huge range depending on temperature and doping. Another mistake is thinking that holes are real particles like positrons. A hole is the absence of an electron in a bond; it behaves like a positive carrier, but it is not a separate particle. Students also mix up which bands overlap: in conductors the bands overlap, not in semiconductors. Finally, remember the temperature behaviour is opposite for metals and semiconductors.

What exams ask: Draw and compare energy band diagrams of a conductor, a semiconductor and an insulator. State the band gap of silicon and germanium. Explain why the resistance of a semiconductor falls with temperature. Explain covalent bonding in a silicon crystal with a diagram. Explain why silicon is preferred over germanium. Calculate the wavelength of light that matches a given band gap.

Recap: Materials are conductors, insulators or semiconductors depending on how easily electrons can move. Silicon and germanium have 4 valence electrons and form covalent bonds in a crystal. Band theory says electrons must cross a band gap from the valence band to the conduction band to conduct. Conductors have no gap, insulators a big gap, semiconductors a small one: about 1.1 eV for silicon. Heating a semiconductor lowers its resistance. In the next lesson we will meet electrons and holes properly and learn the magic trick called doping.
key_points: Conductors have overlapping bands, insulators a large gap (over about 4-5 eV), semiconductors a small gap.
Silicon and germanium have 4 valence electrons and form a covalent diamond lattice.
Band gap: about 1.1 eV for silicon, 0.67 eV for germanium at room temperature.
Heat frees electrons in a semiconductor, creating electron-hole pairs.
A semiconductor's resistance falls as temperature rises (negative temperature coefficient); a metal's rises.
Silicon won over germanium because of lower leakage and its useful native oxide.
The band gap sets which light a material emits or absorbs: wavelength (nm) is about 1240 / E (eV).
lessons.tip: Draw the three band diagrams (conductor, semiconductor, insulator) side by side from memory until you can do it in under a minute. Exams love this picture.
lessons.task: Use the rule wavelength = 1240 / E to calculate the light wavelength matching the band gaps of silicon (1.1 eV), GaAs (1.4 eV) and GaN (3.4 eV). Then look up which part of the spectrum each one falls in.

quiz.q: How many valence electrons does a silicon atom have?
quiz.explain: Silicon (2, 8, 4) has 4 valence electrons, like germanium.

quiz.q: What is the approximate band gap of silicon at room temperature?
quiz.explain: Silicon's band gap is about 1.1 eV; germanium's is about 0.67 eV.

quiz.q: What happens to a semiconductor's resistance when it gets hotter?
quiz.explain: Heat frees more electrons across the gap, so there are more carriers and resistance falls.

quiz.q: In which type of material do the valence and conduction bands overlap?
quiz.explain: Metals have overlapping bands, so electrons are always free to move.

quiz.q: What is a hole in a semiconductor?
options: An empty spot where an electron left a bond
quiz.explain: A hole is the absence of an electron in a bond; it acts like a positive carrier.

lessons.title: Intrinsic and Extrinsic Semiconductors: Doping
lessons.content:
Imagine a classroom where every student sits in a fixed seat, with all seats full. Nobody can move. Now the teacher does two clever things. In one class, she brings in a few extra students who have no seats, so they wander around the room. In another class, she removes a few students, leaving empty seats; now the seated students can shuffle into the empty seats one by one, so the empty spots seem to travel across the room. That is doping in a nutshell. Extra wanderers are free electrons; empty seats are holes. With these two tricks, engineers turn almost-useless pure silicon into the material of every chip.

Intrinsic semiconductor: An intrinsic semiconductor is a perfectly pure crystal, such as silicon with no other elements in it. Its only carriers come from heat breaking bonds, as we saw in the last lesson. Every broken bond makes one free electron and one hole, so in an intrinsic semiconductor the number of electrons equals the number of holes. We write n = p = ni, where n is the electron concentration, p is the hole concentration and ni is the intrinsic carrier concentration. For silicon at room temperature, ni is about 10^10 per cubic centimetre. Some textbooks use 1.5 x 10^10; both are acceptable approximations, so use the value your teacher gives.

How holes move: When an electron next to a hole jumps into it, the hole appears where that electron used to be. If this happens again and again in one direction, the hole travels in the opposite direction to the electrons. Since a hole is a missing negative charge, it behaves like a positive charge moving with the electric field. That is why we treat holes as positive carriers. In a picture of a queue at a bus counter, when the first person leaves, everyone steps forward one place, and the empty spot travels backward through the queue.

Generation and recombination: In a semiconductor, electron-hole pairs are created all the time by heat, which is called generation. At the same time, free electrons meet holes and fall back into bonds, which is called recombination. At a steady temperature, these two processes balance, so the numbers stay constant. If you shine light or raise the temperature, generation increases and the numbers rise to a new balance.

Why dope? Pure silicon with 10^10 carriers per cubic centimetre is a poor conductor, and its conductivity changes a lot with temperature, which is bad for reliable circuits. Doping means adding a tiny, carefully controlled amount of an impurity element to the crystal. Even one impurity atom per million silicon atoms gives about 5 x 10^16 extra carriers per cubic centimetre, millions of times more than the intrinsic number. A material doped like this is called an extrinsic semiconductor. The impurity atoms are called dopants.

N-type semiconductor: To make n-type silicon, we add a pentavalent element, one with 5 valence electrons, such as phosphorus, arsenic or antimony. The dopant atom takes the place of a silicon atom in the crystal. Four of its five electrons form covalent bonds with neighbouring silicon atoms. The fifth electron has no bond to join and is only very weakly held; at room temperature it breaks free almost immediately. So every phosphorus atom donates one free electron. That is why these dopants are called donors. The donor atom, having lost an electron, becomes a fixed positive ion locked in the crystal; it cannot move and does not carry current.

P-type semiconductor: To make p-type silicon, we add a trivalent element, one with 3 valence electrons, such as boron, aluminium, gallium or indium. The boron atom can only complete three of the four bonds around it. The fourth bond has a missing electron, a hole. A neighbouring electron easily jumps in to complete the bond, which turns the boron into a fixed negative ion and leaves a mobile hole elsewhere. Since these dopants accept electrons, they are called acceptors. Boron is the most common p-type dopant for silicon.

Majority and minority carriers: In n-type material, electrons greatly outnumber holes, so electrons are the majority carriers and holes are the minority carriers. In p-type, holes are the majority and electrons the minority. Minority carriers never disappear completely, because heat keeps creating electron-hole pairs, but their number is pushed far down by doping. Minority carriers turn out to be very important in diodes and BJTs, where they cause leakage currents and are the key to how a BJT amplifies.

Still neutral: A common confusion is to think n-type silicon is negatively charged. It is not. Each phosphorus atom brings one extra electron but also one extra proton in its nucleus. The free electron wanders, but the positive ion stays behind, and overall the piece of silicon is electrically neutral. The same is true for p-type: it has mobile holes and fixed negative ions, and the total charge is zero.

The mass-action law: In any semiconductor in thermal equilibrium, the product of electron and hole concentrations is a constant at a given temperature: n x p = ni^2. This is called the mass-action law. It means that when doping increases one type of carrier, the other type goes down. Think of a seesaw: push one side up and the other goes down.

Worked example: Silicon at room temperature has ni = 10^10 per cubic centimetre. We dope it with phosphorus at ND = 10^16 per cubic centimetre. Since nearly every donor is ionised, n is about ND = 10^16. Using the mass-action law, p = ni^2 / n = 10^20 / 10^16 = 10^4 per cubic centimetre. So there are 10^16 electrons but only 10,000 holes per cubic centimetre: a trillion to one. Electrons are clearly the majority. If instead we dope with boron at NA = 10^17, then p is about 10^17 and n = 10^20 / 10^17 = 1000 per cubic centimetre.

Energy band picture: Doping also shows up in the band diagram. Donor atoms create an energy level just below the conduction band, about 0.045 eV below it for phosphorus in silicon. Because this gap is tiny compared with the room-temperature thermal energy, donor electrons easily jump into the conduction band. Acceptor atoms create a level just above the valence band, and electrons from the valence band easily jump up into it, leaving holes. The Fermi level, which you can think of as the average energy level where electrons sit, moves up toward the conduction band in n-type material and down toward the valence band in p-type.

Compensation: You can add both donors and acceptors to the same region. They cancel each other: if a region has 10^17 donors and 10^16 acceptors per cubic centimetre, it behaves like n-type with about 9 x 10^16 net donors. Chip makers use this trick all the time, doping a region first one way and then over-doping part of it the other way to build transistors layer by layer.

Temperature and doped material: At room temperature, the carrier number in doped silicon is set mostly by the doping, not by temperature, which makes circuits predictable. At very low temperatures, the donor electrons stay frozen on their atoms. At very high temperatures, intrinsic carriers created by heat become so many that they swamp the doping, and the material behaves like intrinsic silicon again. For silicon devices this usually happens well above 150 degree Celsius, which is one reason chips have maximum operating temperatures.

How doping is done: In factories, dopants are added either by diffusion, where the wafer is heated in a gas containing the dopant so atoms slowly soak into the surface, or by ion implantation, where dopant ions are fired into the silicon with an accelerator, like an extremely precise atomic spray gun. Ion implantation gives very precise control of how many atoms go in and how deep, which is why modern chip factories rely on it.

Light doping and heavy doping: Engineers describe doping levels with simple labels. Light doping might be around 10^14 to 10^16 atoms per cubic centimetre, and heavy doping 10^18 to 10^20 or more. Heavily doped regions are often marked with a plus sign, such as n+ or p+. For example, the source and drain of a MOSFET are usually n+ regions, and the emitter of a BJT is heavily doped compared with its base. Heavy doping makes a region conduct almost like a metal, which is useful where wires connect to the silicon, because it gives a good, low-resistance contact. Light doping is used where we want a wide depletion region or a high breakdown voltage, ideas you will meet in the next two lessons.

A second worked example: A p-type sample has NA = 10^15 boron atoms per cubic centimetre and also ND = 4 x 10^14 phosphorus atoms per cubic centimetre added by mistake. What are the carrier numbers? Net acceptors are 10^15 - 4 x 10^14 = 6 x 10^14, so p is about 6 x 10^14 per cubic centimetre. Then n = ni^2 / p = 10^20 / (6 x 10^14), which is about 1.7 x 10^5 per cubic centimetre. The sample is still p-type, but with fewer holes than intended. This kind of question, combining compensation and the mass-action law, is a favourite in exams.

Real-life example 1, a phone chip: The processor in a phone sold in Bangladesh, made by companies like Qualcomm, MediaTek or Apple, contains billions of transistors. Each transistor is just a pattern of n-type and p-type regions in a silicon wafer, plus thin insulating layers and metal wires. Every one of those regions was created by adding the right dopant in the right place. Without doping, there would be no transistors, no processors and no phones.

Real-life example 2, a solar cell: A typical silicon solar cell, like those on a rural solar home system in Bangladesh, is made of a thin, heavily doped n-type layer on top of a thicker p-type base. Where they meet, a junction forms, and that junction, which we study in lesson 5, separates the electron-hole pairs created by sunlight. So even the humble solar panel on a tin roof is a doping story.

Common mistakes: Thinking n-type is negatively charged and p-type positively charged is the most common mistake; both are neutral. Another mistake is mixing donors and acceptors: remember Donor gives (5 electrons, n-type), Acceptor accepts (3 electrons, p-type). A memory trick: P for Phosphorus is the exception, it makes N-type, while B for Boron makes P-type. Students also forget that minority carriers still exist, and they make arithmetic slips with powers of ten in the mass-action law.

What exams ask: Distinguish intrinsic and extrinsic semiconductors. Explain with bond diagrams how n-type and p-type are formed. Define majority and minority carriers. State the mass-action law and use it to calculate minority carrier concentration. Draw band diagrams showing donor and acceptor levels. Explain why a doped semiconductor is electrically neutral.

Recap: Intrinsic silicon is pure, with equal electrons and holes, about 10^10 each per cubic centimetre. Doping adds donors (5 valence electrons, n-type) or acceptors (3 valence electrons, p-type), increasing carriers by millions of times. Majority carriers dominate; minority carriers remain. The mass-action law n x p = ni^2 links the two. Doped material is still neutral. Next we will see how these carriers actually move to create current: drift and diffusion.
key_points: Intrinsic semiconductor: pure crystal with n = p = ni (about 10^10 per cm^3 for Si at room temperature).
Doping adds tiny amounts of impurity to massively increase carriers, making an extrinsic semiconductor.
N-type: pentavalent donors (P, As, Sb); electrons are majority carriers.
P-type: trivalent acceptors (B, Al, Ga, In); holes are majority carriers.
Mass-action law: n x p = ni^2, so raising one carrier type lowers the other.
Doped semiconductors are electrically neutral; dopant ions are fixed, carriers are mobile.
Donor levels sit just below the conduction band; acceptor levels just above the valence band.
Doping is done in factories by diffusion or ion implantation.
lessons.tip: Keep a tiny table in your notebook: dopant, valence electrons, donor or acceptor, n or p, majority carrier. Fill it with P, As, Sb, B, Al, Ga until you never mix them up.

lessons.title: How Carriers Move: Drift and Diffusion
lessons.content:
Picture two ways people move at Kamalapur railway station. When the announcement says the Chittagong train is on platform 3, everyone walks purposefully toward platform 3. That is movement caused by a push. Now picture a crowded waiting room when the doors open into an empty hall: people naturally spread out into the empty space, even without any announcement, simply because it is less crowded there. Carriers in a semiconductor move in exactly these two ways. The first is called drift, caused by an electric field. The second is called diffusion, caused by crowding. Every diode and transistor works by a mix of these two.

Random thermal motion: Even with no voltage applied, free electrons and holes are not sitting still. At room temperature they zip around randomly at very high speeds, around 10^7 centimetres per second, constantly bumping into vibrating atoms and impurities and changing direction. Because the motion is random, on average they go nowhere, so there is no net current. It is like a swarm of mosquitoes: lots of motion, but the swarm stays in one place.

Drift: When we apply a voltage across a piece of semiconductor, it creates an electric field inside it. The field gives the random motion a small push in one direction. Holes drift along the field direction, and electrons drift against it. The average speed of this push is called the drift velocity. It is far smaller than the random thermal speed, but it is the part that creates current. Both electron and hole drift give current in the same direction, because electrons are negative and move the opposite way.

Mobility: How easily a carrier drifts is measured by its mobility, written with the Greek letter mu. The drift velocity is v = mu x E, where E is the electric field in volts per centimetre. In silicon at room temperature, typical values for lightly doped material are about 1350 square centimetres per volt-second for electrons and about 480 for holes. So electrons are almost three times as mobile as holes. This one fact has big consequences: n-type devices are faster than p-type ones, which is why NPN transistors and nMOS transistors are often preferred, and why pMOS transistors in chips are usually made wider to keep up.

Worked drift example: Suppose an electric field of 100 volts per centimetre acts on electrons in silicon. Their drift velocity is v = 1350 x 100 = 1.35 x 10^5 centimetres per second, that is 1.35 kilometres per second. That is fast, but still about a hundred times slower than their random thermal motion. If you increase the field enormously, the drift velocity stops growing and saturates near 10^7 centimetres per second in silicon. This is called velocity saturation, and it limits how fast very small transistors can switch.

What affects mobility: Mobility falls when carriers bump into things more often. Two main bumps matter. Lattice scattering happens when carriers hit vibrating atoms; it gets worse at higher temperature, so mobility falls as silicon heats up. Impurity scattering happens when carriers are deflected by the charged dopant ions; it gets worse with heavier doping. So heavily doped silicon has lower mobility than lightly doped silicon. Different materials also differ: electrons in gallium arsenide are several times more mobile than in silicon, which is why GaAs is used in some high-frequency radio chips.

Drift current and conductivity: The drift current density, current per unit area, is J = q x (n x mu_n + p x mu_p) x E, where q is the electron charge, 1.6 x 10^-19 coulombs. The part in brackets times q is called the conductivity, sigma = q x (n x mu_n + p x mu_p). Resistivity is just its inverse, rho = 1 / sigma, measured in ohm-centimetres. This formula connects everything from earlier lessons: carriers from doping, mobility from this lesson, and Ohm's law from lesson 1.

Worked conductivity example 1, intrinsic silicon: With n = p = 10^10 per cubic centimetre, sigma = 1.6 x 10^-19 x 10^10 x (1350 + 480), which is about 2.9 x 10^-6 siemens per centimetre. The resistivity is about 3.4 x 10^5 ohm-centimetres. A cube of pure silicon one centimetre on each side would have a resistance of hundreds of thousands of ohms.

Worked conductivity example 2, doped silicon: Now dope with ND = 10^16 donors. Then n is about 10^16, and holes are negligible. Sigma = 1.6 x 10^-19 x 10^16 x 1350, about 2.16 siemens per centimetre, and resistivity about 0.46 ohm-centimetre. Doping with only about one atom in five million changed the resistivity by roughly a factor of 700,000. In practice mobility falls a little at this doping level, so the real number is somewhat different, but the lesson is clear: doping controls conductivity.

From resistivity to a real resistor: Resistance of a bar of material is R = rho x L / A, where L is its length and A its cross-section area. Take the doped silicon above with rho = 0.46 ohm-centimetre, shaped into a bar 0.1 centimetre long with a cross-section of 0.01 by 0.01 centimetre, that is 10^-4 square centimetres. Then R = 0.46 x 0.1 / 10^-4 = 460 ohms. Chip designers build resistors inside integrated circuits in exactly this way, by choosing the doping and the shape of a silicon strip.

Diffusion: Diffusion happens whenever there are more carriers in one place than another. Carriers move randomly, so more of them wander from the crowded region into the empty region than the other way round. The result is a net flow from high concentration to low concentration, with no electric field needed. You see diffusion when a drop of ink spreads in a glass of water, or when the smell of biryani spreads from the kitchen to every room of the house.

Diffusion current: The diffusion current depends on how steeply the concentration changes with distance, called the concentration gradient, written dn/dx. For electrons, J = q x Dn x dn/dx, and for holes J = -q x Dp x dp/dx. Dn and Dp are diffusion coefficients, measured in square centimetres per second. The minus sign for holes appears because holes diffuse down the slope and are positive. You do not need to memorise signs to understand the main idea: carriers flow from crowded to empty, and steeper differences give bigger currents.

Einstein relation: Drift and diffusion are both caused by the same random motion and bumping, so mobility and the diffusion coefficient are linked. The Einstein relation says D / mu = kT / q = VT, where VT is called the thermal voltage. At room temperature, about 300 kelvin, VT is about 26 millivolts (often written 25 or 25.9 mV). So for electrons in silicon, Dn is about 1350 x 0.026, roughly 35 square centimetres per second. The thermal voltage VT will appear again and again in the diode equation and in transistor formulas, so remember: about 26 mV at room temperature.

Carrier lifetime and diffusion length: Extra carriers injected into a region do not live forever. Minority carriers, for example electrons pushed into p-type silicon, eventually recombine with the many holes there. The average time they survive is called the minority carrier lifetime, tau, often in microseconds or less. In that time they diffuse an average distance called the diffusion length, L = square root of (D x tau). For electrons with D = 35 square centimetres per second and tau = 1 microsecond, L = square root of 35 x 10^-6, about 0.006 centimetres or 60 micrometres. This length matters for designing BJTs, where the base must be much thinner than the diffusion length.

Hall effect: How do we know whether a sample is n-type or p-type? One classic test is the Hall effect. Pass a current through a flat sample and put it in a magnetic field at right angles. The magnetic force pushes the moving carriers to one side of the sample, creating a small voltage across it, called the Hall voltage. Because electrons and holes are pushed to the same side but carry opposite charges, the sign of the Hall voltage reveals the carrier type. Its size tells you the carrier concentration. Hall sensors based on this effect are used in phones to detect a flip cover, in laptops to detect a closed lid, and in motors and cars to measure position and speed.

Drift and diffusion together: Inside real devices, both currents usually flow at once. In a PN junction at rest, which we meet in the next lesson, electrons diffuse one way because of crowding, and an electric field builds up that drifts them back the other way. At balance, the two exactly cancel, and no net current flows. When you apply a voltage, you upset the balance and current flows. So understanding both mechanisms is the key to understanding diodes.

Real-life example 1, a Hall sensor in a smartphone cover: Many phone covers sold in Bangladeshi markets have a tiny magnet inside the flap. When you close the flap, the magnet sits over a Hall sensor in the phone. The magnetic field pushes moving carriers in the sensor sideways, a Hall voltage appears, and a circuit detects it and switches the screen off. It is the same physics as in the lab, shrunk to a chip smaller than a grain of rice.

Real-life example 2, a temperature-sensitive circuit: When a semiconductor heats up, two things happen: more intrinsic carriers are generated, and mobility falls because of lattice scattering. In doped silicon resistors inside chips, the falling mobility usually wins near room temperature, so their resistance goes up with temperature, while in pure or lightly doped material the extra carriers dominate. Engineers who design chips for hot environments, like control circuits inside a factory boiler room in Gazipur, must account for both effects.

Common mistakes: Students often think electrons flow at the speed of light in a wire. They do not; drift velocities are small, and what travels fast is the electric signal, not individual electrons. Another mistake is forgetting that diffusion needs no electric field at all. Students also mix up mobility units, and forget that electrons and holes drift in opposite directions but still give current in the same direction. Finally, many forget that VT is about 26 mV only at room temperature; it changes with temperature.

What exams ask: Define drift velocity, mobility and conductivity. Derive or use sigma = q(n mu_n + p mu_p) to calculate the resistivity of intrinsic and doped silicon. Explain diffusion current with a concentration gradient. State the Einstein relation and calculate a diffusion coefficient. Explain the Hall effect and how it identifies carrier type. Define lifetime and diffusion length.

Recap: Carriers move by drift, pushed by an electric field, and by diffusion, spreading from crowded to empty regions. Mobility measures how easily carriers drift; electrons in silicon are about three times as mobile as holes. Conductivity is q(n mu_n + p mu_p), and doping changes it hugely. Diffusion current depends on the concentration gradient. The Einstein relation links D and mu through VT, about 26 mV at room temperature. With these tools, we are ready to join p-type and n-type silicon together and build the most basic device of all: the PN junction.
key_points: Drift is carrier motion caused by an electric field; v = mu x E.
Silicon mobility: electrons about 1350, holes about 480 cm^2/V-s, so electrons are about 3 times faster.
Conductivity sigma = q(n mu_n + p mu_p); resistivity rho = 1/sigma.
Diffusion is flow from high to low concentration, needing no electric field.
Einstein relation: D / mu = VT = kT/q, about 26 mV at room temperature.
Diffusion length L = square root of (D x tau) depends on minority carrier lifetime.
The Hall effect shows whether a sample is n-type or p-type and its carrier concentration.
In a PN junction at rest, drift and diffusion currents cancel each other.
lessons.tip: Memorise three numbers and you will solve most problems here: q = 1.6 x 10^-19 C, mu_n about 1350 and mu_p about 480 cm^2/V-s in silicon, and VT about 26 mV.
lessons.task: Put a drop of food colouring in a still glass of water and watch it for ten minutes without stirring. Then stir another glass. Write two lines on which is like diffusion and which is more like a forced flow, and why.

lessons.title: The PN Junction
lessons.content:
Imagine two neighbourhoods side by side. One is packed with people looking for a seat (free electrons), the other is full of empty seats (holes). Remove the wall between them, and people rush across to grab seats. But as they cross, the border area changes: soon there is a no-man's-land with nobody free and no empty seats, and a kind of invisible fence builds up that stops more people crossing. That invisible fence is the heart of the PN junction, the simplest semiconductor device and the parent of every diode, transistor and solar cell.

What a PN junction is: A PN junction is formed when a p-type region and an n-type region exist side by side in the same single crystal of silicon. It is not made by gluing two pieces together, because the crystal must be continuous for carriers to flow smoothly. In factories, a wafer of one type is doped with the opposite type over part of its surface, creating the junction inside one crystal. A diode is simply a PN junction with metal contacts on each side: the p side is called the anode and the n side is called the cathode.

The first moment: Just as the regions meet, there are many free electrons on the n side and very few on the p side. There are many holes on the p side and very few on the n side. From lesson 4, you know what crowding does: carriers diffuse. Electrons diffuse from n to p, and holes diffuse from p to n. When an electron crosses into the p side, it soon meets a hole and recombines. When a hole crosses into the n side, it recombines with an electron.

The depletion region: As carriers diffuse and recombine near the junction, they leave behind the fixed dopant ions that can no longer be balanced. On the n side, positive donor ions are left uncovered; on the p side, negative acceptor ions are left uncovered. This thin zone around the junction, emptied of mobile carriers, is called the depletion region, also known as the space-charge region or depletion layer. It acts almost like an insulator because it has no free carriers. Its width is typically less than a micrometre, a tiny fraction of the width of a human hair.

The built-in electric field: The exposed positive ions on the n side and negative ions on the p side create an electric field pointing from n to p across the depletion region. This field pushes holes back toward the p side and electrons back toward the n side. In other words, it creates a drift current opposite to the diffusion current. The field grows until drift exactly balances diffusion. At that point, equilibrium is reached and the net current is zero. Nothing visible happens, but inside, two balanced flows are always running in opposite directions.

Barrier potential: The electric field corresponds to a voltage across the depletion region, called the barrier potential, built-in potential or contact potential, written V0 or Vbi. For silicon junctions it is typically about 0.6 to 0.8 volts; for germanium about 0.2 to 0.3 volts. You cannot measure it simply with a voltmeter connected to the two ends, because contact potentials at the metal connections cancel it out, but it controls everything that happens when you apply a voltage.

Calculating the barrier: The built-in potential is V0 = VT x ln(NA x ND / ni^2), where NA and ND are the doping levels on the two sides. Example: NA = 10^17 and ND = 10^16 per cubic centimetre, ni = 10^10, VT = 0.026 V. Then NA x ND / ni^2 = 10^33 / 10^20 = 10^13. The natural log of 10^13 is about 29.9. So V0 = 0.026 x 29.9, about 0.78 V. Heavier doping gives a slightly larger barrier, but because of the logarithm, the change is modest.

Width of the depletion region: The depletion region holds equal amounts of positive and negative charge on its two sides, since the total charge must balance. If one side is lightly doped, it needs a wider zone to uncover the same amount of charge. So the depletion region extends further into the lightly doped side. In a junction with p side 100 times more heavily doped than the n side, almost all of the depletion region is on the n side. Such a junction is called a one-sided or abrupt p+n junction, and it is common in real devices. The width also grows when you apply reverse voltage, roughly in proportion to the square root of (V0 + VR).

Biasing: Applying an external DC voltage to a junction is called biasing. There are two ways to connect a battery: forward bias and reverse bias. The difference between them is the whole reason diodes are useful.

Forward bias: Connect the positive terminal of the battery to the p side (anode) and the negative terminal to the n side (cathode). The applied voltage opposes the built-in barrier, so the barrier becomes lower and the depletion region gets narrower. With a lower barrier, many more majority carriers can diffuse across: holes go from p to n, electrons from n to p. Once across, they become minority carriers and recombine, while the battery supplies new ones. A large current flows. For silicon, the current is tiny below about 0.5 V, then rises steeply; around 0.6 to 0.7 V, real currents of milliamps flow. This is why we say a silicon diode turns on at about 0.7 V.

Reverse bias: Now flip the battery: positive to the n side, negative to the p side. The applied voltage adds to the barrier, so the barrier rises and the depletion region widens. Majority carriers can no longer cross. Only the few minority carriers near the junction get swept across by the field, giving a tiny current called the reverse saturation current, Is. For small silicon diodes it is very small, often in the nanoamp range or below, while germanium diodes have much larger leakage. It is nearly independent of the reverse voltage, but it roughly doubles for every 10 degree Celsius rise in temperature, because heat creates more minority carriers.

A one-way valve: Put these two facts together, and the PN junction is like a one-way valve in a water pipe, or the one-way turnstile at a metro station. Current flows easily from p to n (anode to cathode) under forward bias, and almost no current flows under reverse bias. This property is called rectification, and it is used in every charger and power supply, as you will see in lesson 7.

Junction capacitance: The depletion region is like an insulating layer between two conducting regions, which makes it act like a capacitor. Under reverse bias, as voltage increases, the depletion region widens and the capacitance decreases, just like moving capacitor plates further apart. This is called depletion or transition capacitance. Under forward bias, there is another effect called diffusion capacitance, due to stored minority carriers. Varactor diodes, used for tuning radios, use the voltage-controlled depletion capacitance on purpose.

Breakdown: If you keep increasing the reverse voltage, at some point the reverse current suddenly shoots up. This is called breakdown, and the voltage where it happens is the breakdown voltage, VBR or VZ. Breakdown is not automatically destructive; if the current is limited by a resistor so the diode does not overheat, the diode recovers when the voltage is reduced. Normal rectifier diodes are designed with high breakdown voltages, for example the common 1N4007 is rated at 1000 V, so breakdown never happens in normal use.

Avalanche breakdown: In lightly doped junctions, the depletion region is wide. Minority carriers crossing it are accelerated by the strong field and gain so much energy that when they hit atoms, they knock out new electron-hole pairs. These new carriers are also accelerated and knock out even more, like an avalanche of rocks rolling down a hill in the Chittagong Hill Tracts. This happens at higher voltages, usually above about 6 or 7 V, and can be hundreds or thousands of volts. Avalanche breakdown voltage increases slightly with temperature.

Zener breakdown: In heavily doped junctions, the depletion region is very thin, and even a few volts create a huge electric field. The field is strong enough to pull electrons directly out of their bonds, through a quantum effect called tunnelling. This is Zener breakdown, and it happens at low voltages, typically below about 5 V. Zener breakdown voltage decreases slightly with temperature. Around 5 to 6 V, both mechanisms contribute and the temperature effects nearly cancel, which is why roughly 5.6 V Zener diodes are known for good temperature stability. Diodes designed to work in breakdown are called Zener diodes, whichever mechanism they actually use.

The energy band view: In a band diagram, the bands on the p side sit higher than on the n side at equilibrium, with a smooth slope across the depletion region. The height of the step equals q x V0. Forward bias reduces the step, letting carriers climb over; reverse bias increases it. The Fermi level is flat across the junction at equilibrium, which is the band-diagram way of saying no net current flows.

Real-life example 1, the LED on a charger: Many chargers have a small LED that glows when plugged in. An LED is a PN junction made of a compound semiconductor. Under forward bias, electrons cross into the p side and holes into the n side, and when they recombine, energy is released as light. If you connect an LED backwards, it does not glow, because the junction is reverse biased and only a tiny leakage flows. This is a handy way to check polarity.

Real-life example 2, the solar cell: A solar cell is a large-area PN junction with no external battery. Sunlight creates electron-hole pairs near the junction. The built-in electric field sweeps electrons to the n side and holes to the p side, creating a voltage of around 0.5 to 0.6 V per silicon cell. Panels connect many cells in series to give useful voltages; a common 36-cell panel used with 12 V batteries in rural Bangladesh gives about 18 V with no load.

Common mistakes: Students often say the depletion region contains no charge. Wrong: it contains fixed ion charges; what it lacks is mobile carriers. Another mistake is thinking the barrier potential can be read on a voltmeter across an unbiased diode. Students also mix up which bias widens the depletion region: reverse bias widens it, forward bias narrows it. Finally, they confuse avalanche and Zener: Zener is low voltage, heavy doping, tunnelling; avalanche is high voltage, light doping, impact ionisation.

What exams ask: Explain the formation of the depletion region with diagrams. Derive or use the built-in potential formula. Compare forward and reverse bias with diagrams of the depletion region and band diagram. Explain transition capacitance. Distinguish Zener and avalanche breakdown, including their temperature coefficients. Explain why the depletion region extends more into the lightly doped side.

Recap: Joining p-type and n-type silicon in one crystal creates a PN junction. Diffusion of carriers leaves a depletion region of fixed ions and a built-in field, giving a barrier potential of about 0.7 V in silicon. Forward bias lowers the barrier and lets large current flow; reverse bias raises it and allows only a tiny saturation current. Large reverse voltage causes Zener or avalanche breakdown. Next, we turn this physics into a practical tool: the diode's I-V curve and simple models engineers use to solve circuits.
key_points: A PN junction is p-type and n-type regions in one continuous crystal; a diode has anode (p) and cathode (n).
Diffusion and recombination create a depletion region of fixed ions with no mobile carriers.
The built-in field balances diffusion; barrier potential is about 0.7 V for Si, 0.3 V for Ge.
V0 = VT x ln(NA x ND / ni^2).
Forward bias narrows the depletion region and allows large current; reverse bias widens it, giving tiny saturation current.
The depletion region extends further into the more lightly doped side.
Zener breakdown: heavy doping, low voltage, tunnelling. Avalanche breakdown: light doping, higher voltage, impact ionisation.
Reverse-biased junctions act as voltage-controlled capacitors.
lessons.tip: Draw the junction three times side by side: unbiased, forward biased and reverse biased. Show the depletion width and the battery polarity each time. If you can draw this, you understand the lesson.

options: Fixed dopant ions and almost no mobile carriers

quiz.q: In forward bias, which terminal of the battery connects to the p side?
quiz.explain: Forward bias: positive to p (anode), negative to n (cathode).

quiz.q: What happens to the depletion region under reverse bias?
quiz.explain: Reverse bias adds to the barrier and pushes carriers away, widening the region.

quiz.q: Which breakdown happens at low voltages in heavily doped junctions?
quiz.explain: Zener breakdown uses tunnelling in thin, heavily doped junctions, typically below about 5 V.

quiz.explain: The depletion region extends further into the lightly doped side, here the n side.

lessons.title: Diode Characteristics and Models
lessons.content:
When you learn to ride a bicycle in your neighbourhood lane, you do not think about the physics of friction, balance and torque. You use simple rules: lean a little into the turn, pedal faster to stay up. Engineers treat diodes the same way. Underneath, there is deep physics from the last lesson, but to design circuits quickly, we use a curve that shows how the diode behaves and a few simple models that are good enough for most problems. This lesson is about that curve and those models, and they will be used in every diode circuit for the rest of the course.

The diode symbol: A diode is drawn as a triangle pointing at a bar. The triangle side is the anode (p side), and the bar is the cathode (n side). The triangle points in the direction conventional current can flow easily. On a real diode, the cathode is marked with a stripe or band. On a common black 1N4007 rectifier diode, the grey stripe is the cathode. On an LED, the cathode is usually the shorter leg and has a flat edge on the plastic.

The I-V characteristic: If you slowly change the voltage across a diode and measure the current, then plot current (I) against voltage (V), you get the I-V characteristic curve. It has three regions. The forward region, on the right, where current is tiny until about 0.5 V and then rises extremely steeply. The reverse region, on the left, where only a tiny, almost constant leakage current flows. And the breakdown region, far to the left at the breakdown voltage, where reverse current suddenly increases. The curve is not a straight line, which is why a diode is called a non-linear device. A resistor, by contrast, gives a straight line through the origin.

The Shockley diode equation: The physics of the PN junction gives a formula for the current: I = Is x (e^(V / (n x VT)) - 1). Here Is is the reverse saturation current, VT is the thermal voltage (about 26 mV at room temperature), and n is the ideality factor, a number between 1 and 2 that depends on how the diode is made. For forward voltages more than about 0.1 V, the exponential term is huge and the minus 1 can be ignored, so I is approximately Is x e^(V / (n x VT)). For reverse voltages, the exponential becomes tiny, and I is about minus Is.

The 60 millivolt rule: Because of the exponential, small voltage changes make big current changes. With n = 1, increasing the voltage by VT x ln(10), which is about 60 mV, multiplies the current by 10. So if a diode carries 1 mA at 0.65 V, it carries about 10 mA at 0.71 V and about 100 mA at 0.77 V. This is why we can treat the forward voltage of a silicon diode as roughly 0.7 V over a wide range of currents: the current changes by a hundred times while the voltage moves only about 0.12 V.

Cut-in voltage: The forward voltage at which current becomes noticeable is called the cut-in, threshold, knee or turn-on voltage. For silicon it is around 0.6 to 0.7 V, for germanium around 0.2 to 0.3 V, for Schottky diodes about 0.2 to 0.4 V, and for LEDs anywhere from about 1.8 V (red) to around 3 V (blue and white). These are approximate values; the exact voltage depends on the current.

Temperature effects: For a fixed current, the forward voltage of a silicon diode falls by about 2 mV for every 1 degree Celsius rise in temperature. So a diode at 0.70 V at 25 degree Celsius would show around 0.60 V at 75 degree Celsius for the same current. This property is used to make simple temperature sensors, and it is also a warning: if many diodes share current, the hottest one can grab more current and get even hotter. Reverse saturation current, as we saw, roughly doubles every 10 degree Celsius.

Why we need models: Solving circuits with an exponential equation is hard by hand, because the diode current depends on the diode voltage, which depends on the current through the rest of the circuit. So engineers use simpler models, each a trade-off between accuracy and ease.

Model 1, the ideal diode: The diode is a perfect switch. In forward bias it is a short circuit, zero volts across it, any current allowed. In reverse bias it is an open circuit, zero current. This model is perfect for understanding what a circuit does, and accurate enough when the supply voltages are much larger than 0.7 V, for example in a 220 V rectifier.

Model 2, the constant-voltage-drop model: The diode is off until the voltage reaches about 0.7 V (for silicon). When on, it acts like a 0.7 V battery opposing the current, with no resistance. This is the most commonly used model in exams and quick designs. Example: a 5 V supply, a 1 kilo-ohm resistor and a silicon diode in series, forward biased. Then the current is I = (5 - 0.7) / 1 kilo-ohm = 4.3 mA. With the ideal model, you would get 5 mA, an error of about 16 percent. With a 1.5 V supply, the difference is bigger: 0.8 mA versus 1.5 mA, so the ideal model is useless at low voltages.

Model 3, the piecewise-linear model: The diode is off below a threshold, say 0.6 V, and above it behaves like a battery plus a small resistor, rf, for example 10 or 20 ohms. This captures the fact that the forward voltage rises a little with current. Example: Vth = 0.6 V, rf = 20 ohms, supply 5 V, series resistor 200 ohms. Current I = (5 - 0.6) / (200 + 20) = 4.4 / 220 = 20 mA, and the diode voltage is 0.6 + 0.02 x 20 = 1.0 V.

Model 4, the exponential model and iteration: For the most accuracy by hand, use the Shockley equation with iteration. Guess VD = 0.7 V, find the current from the resistor, then use V2 - V1 = 2.3 x n x VT x log10(I2 / I1) to update the diode voltage, and repeat. Two or three rounds are usually enough. Computers do this automatically in circuit simulators such as SPICE, which use the full exponential model.

The load line: Another way to solve a diode circuit is graphically. In a circuit with supply VDD, resistor R and a diode, KVL gives VDD = ID x R + VD. This is a straight line on the I-V graph, called the load line. It crosses the voltage axis at VD = VDD (when ID = 0) and the current axis at ID = VDD / R (when VD = 0). Where the load line meets the diode's curve is the operating point, also called the quiescent point or Q-point. Example: VDD = 2 V, R = 100 ohms. The line goes from (2 V, 0) to (0, 20 mA). If it meets the diode curve at about 0.72 V, the current is (2 - 0.72) / 100 = 12.8 mA. The load line idea will come back with transistors.

Small-signal resistance: Sometimes a diode carries a steady DC current plus a small AC signal on top. For the small signal, the diode looks like a small resistor, called the dynamic or small-signal resistance: rd = n x VT / ID. At ID = 1 mA and n = 1, rd = 26 ohms. At 10 mA, it is 2.6 ohms. This explains why a diode can be used to make small voltage-controlled resistances, and it prepares you for the transistor's re in lesson 16.

Diode ratings: Every diode has a datasheet listing its limits. The maximum forward current, for example 1 A for the 1N4007 and about 200 mA for the small 1N4148 signal diode. The peak inverse voltage or peak repetitive reverse voltage, for example 1000 V for the 1N4007 and about 100 V for the 1N4148. The maximum power dissipation, which equals forward voltage times current. And the reverse recovery time, how long it takes the diode to stop conducting when switched from forward to reverse; the 1N4148 is fast, a few nanoseconds, while the 1N4007 is much slower, so it is not suitable for high-frequency switching.

Testing a diode: A digital multimeter has a diode-test mode, usually marked with the diode symbol. Put the red probe on the anode and the black probe on the cathode, and a good silicon diode reads about 0.5 to 0.7 V. Reverse the probes, and it shows OL (over limit), meaning no conduction. If it reads near zero both ways, the diode is shorted; if OL both ways, it is open. Repair technicians in Dhaka's Elephant Road and Stadium Market electronics shops check charger and TV boards exactly this way.

Real-life example 1, reverse polarity protection: Cheap battery-powered toys and torches are often damaged when batteries are put in the wrong way round. A simple fix is a diode in series with the supply. If the batteries are correct, the diode is forward biased and passes current, losing about 0.7 V. If reversed, the diode blocks current and saves the circuit. A Schottky diode is often used instead, because its lower forward drop wastes less battery voltage.

Real-life example 2, a diode thermometer: Because a silicon diode's forward voltage drops by about 2 mV per degree Celsius at constant current, you can build a cheap thermometer. Feed a diode with a constant 1 mA and measure its voltage: at 25 degree Celsius it might read 0.650 V; if it reads 0.630 V, the temperature has risen by about 10 degrees. Many chips include temperature sensors that rely on this same diode behaviour.

Common mistakes: Students often forget to subtract the 0.7 V diode drop. Others assume a diode is always on, without first checking whether it is forward or reverse biased; the correct method is to assume a state, solve, and then check that the assumption holds (current positive for an on diode, voltage below cut-in for an off diode). Students also apply the ideal model with small supplies where it gives large errors, and mix up anode and cathode markings.

What exams ask: Sketch and label the diode I-V curve with all three regions. Write the Shockley equation and explain each term. Solve diode circuits with the ideal, constant-voltage-drop and piecewise-linear models and compare the results. Draw a load line and find the Q-point. Calculate dynamic resistance. Explain the effect of temperature on forward voltage and reverse current.

Recap: The diode's I-V curve is exponential in forward bias, nearly flat in reverse bias, and steep at breakdown. The Shockley equation describes it, and every 60 mV multiplies current by about 10. For hand analysis we use the ideal, constant-voltage-drop (0.7 V) or piecewise-linear models, or iterate with the exponential. The load line finds the Q-point graphically, and rd = nVT / ID gives small-signal resistance. Next, we put diodes to work in their most famous job: turning AC into DC with rectifiers.
key_points: The diode I-V curve has forward, reverse and breakdown regions; it is non-linear.
Shockley equation: I = Is(e^(V/nVT) - 1); every ~60 mV multiplies forward current by 10.
Cut-in voltage: Si about 0.7 V, Ge about 0.3 V, Schottky about 0.3 V, LEDs about 1.8-3 V.
Models: ideal (switch), constant-voltage-drop (0.7 V), piecewise-linear (Vth + rf).
Load line VDD = ID x R + VD meets the diode curve at the Q-point.
Small-signal resistance rd = nVT / ID, about 26 ohms at 1 mA.
Silicon forward voltage drops about 2 mV per degree Celsius at constant current.
Assume a diode state, solve, then check the assumption.
lessons.tip: For every diode problem, first decide on or off, then solve, then check. Writing the word 'check' at the end of your answer catches most mistakes.
lessons.task: If you have a multimeter at home or in the lab, use diode mode on any diode or LED and record the forward reading both ways. If not, solve this on paper: 9 V supply, 470 ohm resistor and silicon diode in series; find the current with the ideal and the 0.7 V models and compare.

quiz.q: A 5 V supply drives a silicon diode through a 1 kilo-ohm resistor. Using the 0.7 V model, what is the current?
By roughly how much must forward voltage increase (n = 1) to multiply diode current by 10?
quiz.explain: VT x ln(10) is about 0.026 x 2.3, roughly 60 mV.

quiz.q: What is the small-signal resistance of a diode at 2 mA (n = 1, VT = 26 mV)?
quiz.explain: rd = VT / ID = 26 mV / 2 mA = 13 ohms.

quiz.q: On a multimeter's diode test, a good silicon diode forward biased reads about:
quiz.explain: A forward-biased silicon diode shows its forward drop, about 0.5 to 0.7 V.

quiz.q: How does a silicon diode's forward voltage change with temperature at constant current?
options: Rises about 2 mV per degree Celsius
Falls about 0.7 V per degree Celsius
Falls about 2 mV per degree Celsius
quiz.explain: Forward voltage drops by roughly 2 mV for every degree Celsius rise.

lessons.title: Rectifiers
lessons.content:
Imagine a road where cars drive forward for a while and then reverse for a while, again and again, fifty times every second. That is the electricity coming out of the wall socket in your home in Bangladesh. It is AC, alternating current, and its direction flips back and forth. But your phone, your laptop, your Wi-Fi router and almost every chip inside them want DC, a current that flows in one direction only. So somewhere between the wall and the chip, something has to turn the back-and-forth traffic into a one-way road. That something is a rectifier, and it is built from the diodes you met in the last two lessons.

What a rectifier is: A rectifier is a circuit that converts AC into a current that flows in only one direction. The output is not smooth DC yet. It is a bumpy, one-direction voltage called pulsating DC. Making it smooth is the job of a filter, which is the next lesson. Here we focus only on the one-way part. The key idea is simple: a diode lets current pass in one direction and blocks it in the other, so it acts like a one-way gate. Put diodes in the right places and only the useful direction of current reaches the load.

A quick look at the AC input: The mains supply in Bangladesh is about 220 to 230 V RMS at 50 Hz. RMS is the 'effective' value, the one printed on appliances. The real peak is RMS times the square root of 2, which is about 1.414. So a 230 V RMS supply actually swings up to about 325 V and down to about minus 325 V, fifty times a second. One full cycle takes 1/50 = 20 ms. That is far too much voltage for a phone, so we normally first use a step-down transformer, for example 230 V to 12 V RMS. A 12 V RMS secondary has a peak of 12 x 1.414 = about 17 V. We will call this peak Vm.

Average and RMS values: Two numbers describe any rectified wave. The average or DC value, Vdc, is what a DC voltmeter shows: the area under the wave over one period divided by the period. The RMS value is the square root of the mean of the squared voltage; it tells you how much heating power the wave delivers into a resistor. For a pure sine wave the average over a full cycle is zero, because the positive and negative halves cancel. That is exactly why a rectifier is needed: by removing or flipping the negative half, the average stops being zero and we get some real DC.

The half-wave rectifier: This is the simplest circuit: one diode in series between the transformer secondary and the load resistor. During the positive half cycle the anode is more positive than the cathode, the diode is forward biased, and current flows through the load. During the negative half cycle the diode is reverse biased and blocks, so the load gets zero. The output looks like a row of humps with flat gaps between them. With an ideal diode, Vdc = Vm / pi, which is about 0.318 Vm, and Vrms = Vm / 2. With a silicon diode, replace Vm with Vm minus 0.7 V.

Half-wave worked example: Take the 12 V RMS transformer, so Vm is about 17.0 V. Using the 0.7 V model, the output peak is 17.0 - 0.7 = 16.3 V. The DC value is 16.3 / 3.14 = about 5.2 V. With a 1 kilo-ohm load the average current is about 5.2 mA. Notice how poor that is: a 12 V transformer gives only about 5 V of DC. Half of every cycle is simply thrown away. The ripple frequency, meaning how often a hump repeats, equals the mains frequency, 50 Hz. This matters later because slower ripple is harder to smooth.

Peak inverse voltage: When a diode is blocking, it must survive the reverse voltage across it. The largest reverse voltage it sees is called the peak inverse voltage, PIV, sometimes PRV. In the half-wave rectifier with a resistive load, during the negative peak the whole secondary voltage appears across the diode, so PIV = Vm. Engineers choose a diode whose rated reverse voltage is comfortably above PIV, often with a safety margin of 1.5 to 2 times. The popular 1N4007 is rated 1000 V reverse and 1 A forward, which is why it appears in so many cheap power supplies. A 1N4001 is rated only 50 V.

Efficiency and ripple factor of half-wave: Two classic figures appear in exams. Rectification efficiency is the DC output power divided by the AC input power to the circuit. For an ideal half-wave rectifier it is at most about 40.6 percent. Ripple factor is the RMS value of the AC part left in the output divided by the DC value. For half-wave it is about 1.21, meaning the leftover AC is even bigger than the DC. Both numbers say the same thing in different words: half-wave is simple and cheap but wasteful. It is used only for low-current jobs where a little roughness does not matter.
