The full-wave centre-tap rectifier: To use both halves of the cycle, we can use a transformer whose secondary has a wire taken from its middle, called the centre tap. The centre tap is connected to ground, and each end of the secondary feeds one diode. Each half of the winding gives a peak of Vm. In the positive half cycle, the top end is positive, diode D1 conducts and current flows down through the load. In the negative half cycle, the bottom end becomes positive, D2 conducts, and current again flows down through the load in the same direction. Both halves now produce humps, with no gaps.

Full-wave numbers: Since there are two humps per cycle, the average doubles: Vdc = 2Vm / pi, about 0.636 Vm, and Vrms = Vm / square root of 2, about 0.707 Vm. The ripple frequency is now twice the mains frequency, 100 Hz in Bangladesh, which is easier to filter. Efficiency rises to about 81.2 percent and the ripple factor drops to about 0.48. The catch is PIV. When D1 is conducting, the blocked diode D2 sees the voltage of the whole secondary, both halves together, so PIV = 2Vm for ideal diodes (2Vm - 0.7 if you count the drop of the conducting diode). Also, the centre-tap transformer is bigger and costlier, and each half of the winding works only half the time.

The bridge rectifier: The bridge uses four diodes arranged in a diamond and needs no centre tap. The AC goes into two opposite corners and the DC comes out of the other two. In the positive half cycle, two diagonally opposite diodes, say D1 and D3, conduct and push current through the load from top to bottom. In the negative half cycle, the other pair, D2 and D4, conducts, and the current through the load is again from top to bottom. So the output is full-wave, with Vdc = 2Vm / pi and ripple at 100 Hz, using an ordinary transformer, or even no transformer at all.

Bridge trade-offs: Because current always passes through two diodes in series, the output peak is Vm - 1.4 V for silicon, not Vm - 0.7 V. For a 230 V input this loss is tiny, but for a 5 V supply it hurts, so low-voltage designs sometimes use Schottky diodes with about 0.3 V drop. The good news is PIV: each blocking diode sees only about Vm, half of what the centre-tap circuit demands. Bridges are so common that they are sold as a single four-pin package, marked with two wave symbols for the AC pins and plus and minus for the DC pins, like the small DB107 or the big square metal KBPC types.

Bridge worked example: Use the same 12 V RMS transformer, Vm = 17.0 V. The output peak is 17.0 - 1.4 = 15.6 V. The DC value is 2 x 15.6 / 3.14 = about 9.9 V. Compare this with the 5.2 V we got from half-wave using the same transformer: almost double. With a 1 kilo-ohm load the average current is about 9.9 mA, and each diode carries current for only half the time, so each diode's average current is about 5 mA. Each diode must block about 17 V, so even the cheapest 1N4001 is fine here.

Comparing the three side by side: Half-wave uses one diode, gives 0.318 Vm, ripple at 50 Hz, PIV of Vm. Centre-tap uses two diodes and a special transformer, gives 0.636 Vm, ripple at 100 Hz, PIV of 2Vm. Bridge uses four diodes and an ordinary transformer, gives 0.636 Vm, ripple at 100 Hz, PIV of Vm, but loses two diode drops. In older books you will also see the transformer utilisation factor, which shows how well the transformer's rating is used; it is lowest for half-wave and highest for the bridge. That is why the bridge is the default choice in most real power supplies today.

Precision and controlled rectifiers, just a peek: A plain diode cannot rectify a signal smaller than 0.7 V, because it never turns on. When engineers need to rectify tiny signals, for example from a sensor or an audio meter, they put the diode inside an op-amp feedback loop to make a precision rectifier. You will see op-amps in lessons 23 and 24. In big industrial drives and battery chargers, diodes are sometimes replaced by thyristors (SCRs) whose turn-on moment can be controlled to adjust the output. That belongs to power electronics, so we only name it here.

Real-life example 1, the phone charger in your bag: Open a cheap phone charger (only a broken, unplugged one, and only with an adult's permission) and right near the mains pins you will usually find four tiny diodes or a little black bridge chip. The 230 V AC from the socket goes straight into this bridge, which turns it into pulsating DC with peaks of about 325 V. A big capacitor next to it smooths that into roughly 300 V DC, and then a switching circuit steps it down to a safe 5 V for USB. So every time you charge your phone at night, a bridge rectifier is working a hundred humps per second for you.

Real-life example 2, the IPS and the car battery: In many Bangladeshi homes an IPS keeps fans and lights running during load shedding. When the mains power is present, the IPS charges its 12 V lead-acid battery. Inside, a transformer brings the mains down, and a rectifier, usually a bridge built from strong diodes or controlled switches, turns it into DC to push current into the battery. The same idea charges a car battery at a garage in Dhaka or an e-rickshaw battery overnight at a charging station. Battery charging is one place where the bumps of pulsating DC are not a big problem, because the battery itself smooths things out.

Common mistakes: Students often forget the second diode drop in a bridge and write Vm - 0.7. Another mistake is using the RMS value of the transformer as if it were the peak; always multiply by 1.414 first. Many mix up the PIV of centre-tap (2Vm) and bridge (Vm). Some think the ripple frequency of a full-wave rectifier is still 50 Hz; it is 100 Hz because there are two humps per input cycle. Finally, remember that for the centre-tap circuit, Vm means the peak of half the secondary, not the whole secondary.

What exams ask: Typical questions are: draw the circuit and the input and output waveforms of a half-wave, centre-tap or bridge rectifier and explain operation for each half cycle; derive Vdc = Vm / pi or 2Vm / pi; find Vdc, Idc and PIV for a given transformer and load; compare the three rectifiers in a table; and calculate efficiency or ripple factor. A good habit is to always write the three steps: find Vm from the RMS value, subtract the diode drops, then use the formula. Label the diodes in your diagrams and show the current path with arrows for each half cycle.

Quick recap: AC flips direction, DC does not. A rectifier uses diodes as one-way gates to make pulsating DC. Half-wave keeps only one half and gives about 0.318 Vm. Full-wave circuits, centre-tap and bridge, keep both halves and give about 0.636 Vm with ripple at twice the mains frequency. Centre-tap needs a special transformer and diodes rated for 2Vm. The bridge needs four diodes and loses about 1.4 V, but it is the everyday winner. The output is still bumpy, so in the next lesson we add a capacitor and build a complete DC power supply.
key_points: A rectifier converts AC into pulsating DC using diodes as one-way gates.
Bangladesh mains is about 230 V RMS, 50 Hz; peak = RMS x 1.414 (about 325 V).
Half-wave: Vdc = Vm/pi (0.318 Vm), Vrms = Vm/2, ripple 50 Hz, PIV = Vm, efficiency max 40.6%.
Full-wave: Vdc = 2Vm/pi (0.636 Vm), Vrms = 0.707 Vm, ripple 100 Hz, efficiency max 81.2%.
Centre-tap needs a centre-tapped transformer and diodes with PIV = 2Vm.
Bridge uses four diodes, PIV = Vm, but loses two diode drops (about 1.4 V).
Ripple factor: about 1.21 for half-wave and 0.48 for full-wave.
lessons.tip: For every rectifier question, write three steps in order: peak from RMS, subtract the diode drops, then apply the formula. Draw the current path for each half cycle with a different colour pen.
lessons.task: On paper, take a 9 V RMS transformer and a 470 ohm load. Find Vm, then Vdc, Idc and PIV for half-wave, centre-tap (9 V each half) and bridge rectifiers using the 0.7 V diode model, and put the answers in a small table.

quiz.q: What is the DC (average) output of an ideal half-wave rectifier with peak Vm?
quiz.explain: Half-wave keeps one hump per cycle, so Vdc = Vm/pi, about 0.318 Vm.

quiz.q: In Bangladesh (50 Hz mains), what is the ripple frequency of a bridge rectifier output?
quiz.explain: Full-wave rectifiers give two humps per input cycle, so ripple is 2 x 50 = 100 Hz.

quiz.q: What PIV must each diode withstand in an ideal full-wave centre-tap rectifier?
quiz.explain: The blocking diode sees the whole secondary, both halves together, which is 2Vm.

quiz.q: A 12 V RMS transformer feeds a silicon bridge rectifier. About what is the output peak?
quiz.explain: Vm = 12 x 1.414 = 17.0 V; two diodes conduct, so 17.0 - 1.4 = 15.6 V.

quiz.q: Why is the bridge rectifier more popular than the centre-tap type?
options: It needs no centre-tapped transformer and diode PIV is only Vm
quiz.explain: The bridge works with an ordinary transformer and each diode only blocks about Vm.

lessons.title: Filters and the DC Power Supply
lessons.content:
Think about a water tank on the roof of a building in Dhaka. The pump below does not run smoothly; it pushes water up in bursts. Yet when you open the tap in the kitchen, water flows steadily. Why? Because the tank stores water during each burst and lets it out evenly in between. A rectifier is like that bursting pump: it gives a bumpy, pulsating DC. To get a steady DC that a phone or a microcontroller can trust, we need a tank for electric charge. That tank is the capacitor, and a circuit that smooths the bumps is called a filter.

Where we are: In the last lesson we turned AC into pulsating DC with half-wave and full-wave rectifiers. In this lesson we finish the job. We will see how a capacitor filter works, how to calculate the ripple that is left over, what other filters exist, and how all the pieces join to form a complete DC power supply. At the end we will open up the block diagram of a phone charger and a laptop adapter. Detailed voltage regulation with a Zener diode is lesson 10, so here we only mention regulators briefly.

Why pulsating DC is not enough: A DC voltmeter on a bridge rectifier output would show a steady number, about 0.636 times the peak, but that is only the average. The real voltage keeps falling to zero 100 times a second. A digital chip that needs 5 V would reset every time the voltage dips. An audio amplifier fed with it would produce a loud 100 Hz hum in the speaker. A motor would shake. So we want the output to stay close to its peak all the time, with only a small wobble. That small wobble is called ripple.

The capacitor filter idea: Put a large capacitor in parallel with the load, right after the rectifier. As the rectified voltage rises toward its peak, the diodes conduct and charge the capacitor up to nearly the peak, Vp. After the peak, the input voltage starts to fall faster than the capacitor can discharge. Now the diodes become reverse biased, because the capacitor voltage is higher than the input, and they switch off. The capacitor alone feeds the load, and its voltage slowly drops. When the next hump of the input rises above the capacitor voltage, the diodes turn on again and top it up. The result is a sawtooth-like wave that stays close to the peak.

How fast the capacitor discharges: While it alone feeds the load, the capacitor loses charge at a rate set by the load current. Charge Q = C x V, so a change in voltage is the change in charge divided by C. If the load draws current I for a time t, the voltage drops by about I x t / C. For a big capacitor the drop is small. Another way to see it is the time constant R x C. If R x C is much longer than the time between humps, the voltage barely sags. A rule of thumb is to make RC at least about ten times the ripple period.

The ripple formula: For a full-wave rectifier the humps come every 1 / (2f) seconds, where f is the mains frequency. If we assume the capacitor discharges for almost that whole time, the peak-to-peak ripple is Vr(pp) = I / (2 f C). For half-wave, humps come every 1 / f, so Vr(pp) = I / (f C), twice as large. The DC output is then about Vdc = Vp - Vr(pp) / 2. These formulas are approximations, slightly pessimistic, but they are what textbooks and exams use, and they are good enough to choose a capacitor.

Worked example: A 12 V RMS transformer feeds a bridge, so the peak after two diode drops is about 15.6 V (from lesson 7). The load draws 0.5 A. We use a 2200 microfarad capacitor and mains of 50 Hz. Ripple: Vr(pp) = 0.5 / (2 x 50 x 0.0022) = 0.5 / 0.22 = about 2.3 V. The DC output is about 15.6 - 2.3 / 2 = about 14.5 V. If we want only 1 V of ripple, we need C = 0.5 / (2 x 50 x 1) = 0.005 F, that is 5000 microfarads, so we might pick a standard 4700 or 6800 microfarad part.

Ripple factor with a filter: The ripple factor r is the RMS value of the ripple divided by the DC output. The capacitor ripple looks roughly like a triangle wave, and for a triangle the RMS value is the peak-to-peak value divided by 2 times the square root of 3, about 3.46. In our example Vr(rms) = 2.3 / 3.46 = about 0.66 V, so r = 0.66 / 14.5 = about 0.046, or 4.6 percent. Compare that with 0.48 for an unfiltered full-wave output. One capacitor made the output roughly ten times smoother. A bigger capacitor or a lighter load makes it even smoother.

The hidden cost, surge and peak currents: The capacitor filter is not free. Because the diodes only conduct for a short moment near each peak, they must deliver all the charge for the whole cycle in that short burst. So the diode current comes in tall, narrow spikes, often several times the average load current. Also, when you first switch on, the capacitor is empty and behaves almost like a short circuit, so a large inrush current flows. Designers choose diodes with a good surge rating, and sometimes add a small resistor or a thermistor to limit inrush. The transformer also runs warmer because of these spiky currents.

Capacitor details that matter: Big filter capacitors are usually electrolytic. They have a plus and a minus leg, and connecting them backwards can make them swell or even burst, so polarity matters. The voltage rating printed on the can must be higher than the peak voltage, with margin; for a 15.6 V peak you would choose at least a 25 V capacitor. Electrolytics also have a ripple current rating and age faster when hot. Many dead adapters and old TV boards have bulging capacitor tops, a sign the capacitor dried out and the filter stopped working. Large capacitors in high-voltage supplies can keep their charge after unplugging, so a bleeder resistor is often added to empty them safely.

Other filters: The capacitor filter is the most common, but there are others. An inductor (choke) in series with the load resists changes in current, so it smooths current, and it works better at heavy loads. An LC filter puts a series inductor followed by a shunt capacitor, combining both actions. A pi filter, also written C-L-C, uses a capacitor, then an inductor, then another capacitor, and gives very low ripple. An RC filter replaces the costly inductor with a resistor, which is cheap but wastes some voltage, so it suits light loads. Inductors are heavy and bulky at 100 Hz, which is why modern designs prefer capacitors plus a regulator.

Adding a regulator: Even after filtering, the output still has some ripple, and it changes when the mains voltage changes or when the load current changes. Sensitive circuits need a fixed voltage. So the last block of a power supply is a voltage regulator. A simple Zener shunt regulator is covered in lesson 10. Integrated regulators such as the 7805 give a fixed 5 V, and the LM317 gives an adjustable voltage. A linear regulator like the 7805 needs its input to stay about 2 V or more above its output at all times, even at the bottom of the ripple, and it burns the extra voltage as heat. That is why the ripple must be kept within limits before the regulator.

The block diagram of a linear DC power supply: Put everything together and you get five blocks. One: a step-down transformer that brings 230 V AC to a safe lower AC voltage and isolates you from the mains. Two: a rectifier, usually a bridge, that makes pulsating DC. Three: a filter, usually a capacitor, that smooths it into DC with small ripple. Four: a regulator that holds the output steady. Five: the load, such as an amplifier or a microcontroller board. This is the classic block diagram drawn in every exam, and it is how many older radios, TV sets and lab bench supplies work.

Measuring a supply: Two numbers describe how good a supply is. Ripple, measured in volts peak-to-peak or as ripple factor, tells you how much AC is left. Regulation tells you how much the output changes from no load to full load. Load regulation in percent is (V no load minus V full load) divided by V full load, times 100. For example, if the output is 12.6 V with nothing connected and 12.0 V at full load, the load regulation is 0.6 / 12.0 x 100 = 5 percent. A good regulated supply has a fraction of a percent. Lesson 10 goes deeper into line and load regulation.

Linear vs switching supplies: The transformer in a linear supply works at 50 Hz, so it needs a heavy iron core, which is why old adapters were big and heavy. A switch-mode power supply, SMPS, is smarter. It rectifies the mains directly, then switches that DC on and off very fast, tens or hundreds of kilohertz, using a transistor. At such high frequency, the transformer can be tiny. Then the output is rectified and filtered again, and a feedback loop adjusts the switching to hold the voltage steady. SMPS designs are much lighter and more efficient, often above 80 or 90 percent, while a linear supply wastes the extra voltage as heat.

Real-life example 1, inside a phone charger: Here is what happens in a typical 5 V USB charger, step by step. The 230 V AC enters and passes through a fuse or fusible resistor for safety. A small bridge rectifier turns it into pulsating DC with peaks near 325 V. A high-voltage electrolytic capacitor, often rated 400 V, smooths it to about 300 V DC. A switching transistor chops this DC at high frequency into a tiny ferrite transformer, which steps it down and keeps you isolated from the mains. A fast diode, often a Schottky, rectifies the output, and low-voltage capacitors filter it to about 5 V. An optocoupler sends feedback from the output side back to the controller so the 5 V stays steady. Fast chargers simply ask the controller for higher voltages, such as 9 V or 12 V, through protocols like USB Power Delivery.

Real-life example 2, a router supply during load shedding: Many families in Bangladesh run their Wi-Fi router from a small 12 V DC UPS or a battery during load shedding. The router's own adapter is a small SMPS giving 12 V DC. Inside the router, the 12 V goes through further filter capacitors and regulators to produce 5 V, 3.3 V and even lower voltages like 1.2 V for its processor. If the adapter's filter capacitor dries out, ripple rises, and the router keeps restarting or the Wi-Fi drops randomly. Technicians at Elephant Road or Multiplan computer markets often fix such adapters just by replacing a bulging capacitor.

Common mistakes: Many students use the RMS transformer voltage as the capacitor voltage; the capacitor charges to the peak, so always multiply by 1.414 and subtract diode drops. Some forget that full-wave ripple uses 2f, so they get a ripple twice too large. Others think a bigger capacitor is always free; it raises surge current and cost. Another confusion is between ripple voltage and ripple factor: one is in volts, the other is a ratio. Finally, remember that in a filtered supply the diodes conduct only for a small part of each cycle, not the whole half cycle as in an unfiltered rectifier.

What exams ask: Expect questions such as: explain with waveforms how a capacitor filter reduces ripple; derive Vr(pp) = I / (2fC); calculate the ripple, DC output and ripple factor for given values; find the capacitor needed for a target ripple; compare capacitor, LC and pi filters; and draw and explain the block diagram of a regulated DC power supply. A newer favourite is to compare linear and switching power supplies. Draw neat waveforms showing the diode conduction intervals and the discharge slope, because many marks come from the diagram.

Quick recap: A rectifier gives pulsating DC; a capacitor filter stores charge at each peak and feeds the load in between, leaving a small ripple. Ripple is about I / (2fC) for full-wave and I / (fC) for half-wave, and the DC output is the peak minus half the ripple. Bigger capacitors mean smaller ripple but bigger diode surge currents. LC, pi and RC filters are alternatives. A complete supply has a transformer, rectifier, filter, regulator and load, while modern chargers use the switch-mode trick to stay small and efficient. Next, we will use diodes to shape waveforms: clippers and clampers.
key_points: A capacitor filter charges to the peak and feeds the load between peaks, leaving a small ripple.
Ripple (peak-to-peak): about I/(2fC) for full-wave and I/(fC) for half-wave.
DC output is about Vp - Vr(pp)/2; ripple factor = Vr(rms)/Vdc, with Vr(rms) about Vr(pp)/3.46.
Bigger C gives less ripple but larger diode surge and peak currents.
Other filters: choke, LC, pi (C-L-C) and RC filters.
Linear supply blocks: transformer, rectifier, filter, regulator, load.
Phone chargers are switch-mode supplies: rectify mains, switch at high frequency, small transformer, rectify, filter, feedback.
lessons.tip: Always find the peak first and keep units in farads and amperes when using the ripple formula. Writing 2200 microfarads as 0.0022 F saves you from the most common calculation slip.
lessons.task: Look at the label of any phone charger or laptop adapter at home. Write down its input range (for example 100-240 V, 50/60 Hz) and output (for example 5 V 2 A). Then, on paper, find the capacitor needed for a full-wave linear supply giving 1 A with 1.5 V ripple at 50 Hz.

quiz.q: In a capacitor-filtered rectifier, when do the diodes conduct?
options: During the whole positive half cycle
Only for a short time near each peak of the input
Only when the input is negative
quiz.explain: The diodes conduct only when the input rises above the capacitor voltage, which happens briefly near each peak.

quiz.q: A full-wave supply at 50 Hz delivers 1 A with a 1000 microfarad capacitor. About what is the peak-to-peak ripple?
Which change reduces the ripple of a capacitor filter?
quiz.explain: Ripple is I/(2fC), so a larger C gives smaller ripple.

quiz.q: Which is the correct order of blocks in a linear regulated DC supply?
quiz.explain: The mains is first stepped down, then rectified, filtered and finally regulated.

quiz.q: Why can a phone charger use a tiny transformer?
options: It switches at tens to hundreds of kilohertz, so a small core is enough
It has no transformer at all
quiz.explain: Higher operating frequency allows a much smaller transformer core in a switch-mode supply.

lessons.title: Wave-Shaping with Diodes: Clippers, Clampers and Multipliers
lessons.content:
Picture a bus with a low roof driving through a gate. Anything taller than the gate gets cut off, and everything below passes untouched. Now picture a lift that takes the whole bus and raises it two floors without changing its shape. Diodes can do both of these tricks to a voltage wave. The first trick, cutting off the part of a wave above or below a level, is called clipping. The second trick, sliding the whole wave up or down without changing its shape, is called clamping. Put clampers together cleverly and you can even build voltage multipliers that make more voltage than you put in.

Why wave-shaping matters: Real signals are messy. A sensor might send a spike that could kill the delicate input pin of a microcontroller. A radio might receive a sudden loud burst. A video signal might lose its reference level as it passes through capacitors. Wave-shaping circuits fix these problems with just a few cheap parts: diodes, resistors, capacitors and sometimes a small DC source. They are also great exam material, because they test whether you truly understand when a diode is on and when it is off. The core skill of this whole lesson is: find the input voltage at which the diode changes state, then sketch.

Clippers in one sentence: A clipper, also called a limiter, removes the part of a signal above or below a chosen level and leaves the rest alone. There are two main families. In a series clipper, the diode is in series with the load. In a shunt clipper, also called a parallel clipper, the diode is across the output, in parallel with the load, with a series resistor before it. Each family can clip the positive side or the negative side, and each can be 'biased' with a battery to move the clipping level. We will use the 0.7 V silicon model from lesson 6 throughout.

Series clipper: Put a diode in series with a resistor load and feed a sine wave with a 10 V peak. If the diode points toward the load, it conducts only when the input is above 0.7 V. So during the positive half the output follows the input minus 0.7, reaching 9.3 V at the peak, and during the negative half the diode is off and the output is zero. You may notice this is exactly a half-wave rectifier, and you are right: a half-wave rectifier is a series clipper that removes the negative half. Flip the diode and it removes the positive half instead.

Biased series clipper: Now add a 3 V battery in series with the diode, so the diode needs the input to beat the battery plus 0.7 V before it conducts. With the battery opposing the input, the diode turns on only when the input exceeds 3.7 V. Above that, the output follows the input minus 3.7 V, so the peak output is 10 - 3.7 = 6.3 V. Below 3.7 V the diode is off and the output is zero. The general method stays the same: write the condition for the diode to be on, find the transition voltage, and then describe the output on each side of that voltage.

Shunt clipper: Now put a resistor in series and the diode across the output to ground, with the anode at the output and the cathode at ground. When the input is below 0.7 V, the diode is off, almost no current flows through the resistor into the light load, and the output follows the input. When the input tries to rise above 0.7 V, the diode turns on and holds the output at 0.7 V; the extra voltage drops across the series resistor. So a 10 V peak sine comes out with its positive half flattened at 0.7 V and its negative half untouched, reaching minus 10 V. Flip the diode and the negative side is clipped at minus 0.7 V.

Biased shunt clipper: Put a battery VB in series with the shunt diode. Now the diode turns on only when the output reaches VB + 0.7. Example: input 10 V peak, VB = 4 V, diode anode at the output. The output follows the input until it reaches 4.7 V, then stays flat at 4.7 V while the input goes higher, and follows the input again on the way down. The negative half passes untouched to minus 10 V. By choosing VB you can place the clipping level wherever you want. The series resistor is important: it limits the current through the diode when it clamps. Without it the diode and the source would fight and something would burn.

Double-ended clippers: Use two shunt branches, one facing each way, each with its own battery. One branch clips the top at, say, +4.7 V and the other clips the bottom at, say, minus 6.7 V. Now a large sine wave becomes almost a square wave, flat on top and bottom. A neat way to build a symmetrical double clipper is with two Zener diodes back to back. With two 5.1 V Zeners in series facing opposite ways, one is in breakdown and the other is forward biased, so the output is limited to about plus or minus (5.1 + 0.7) = 5.8 V. Zeners are covered in detail in lesson 10.

The transfer characteristic: Besides sketching the output wave in time, exams often ask for the transfer characteristic: a graph of output voltage against input voltage. For a shunt clipper with a 4.7 V limit, the graph is a straight 45-degree line through the origin (output equals input) until 4.7 V, then a flat horizontal line at 4.7 V. Each bend on this graph is a point where a diode changes state. The transfer graph is a powerful shortcut: once you have it, you can find the output for any input, sine, triangle or square, without redoing the analysis.

Clampers: A clamper, also called a DC restorer or level shifter, adds a DC level to a signal so that its positive or negative peak sits at a chosen level, while keeping the shape and the peak-to-peak value the same. A basic clamper has a capacitor in series, then a diode from the output to ground, and the load resistor across the output. The trick is that the capacitor charges through the diode quickly, but discharges through the large load resistor very slowly. So once charged, the capacitor acts like a battery in series with the input, shifting the whole wave up or down.

Clamper worked example: Feed a square wave that swings between +10 V and minus 10 V. Put the diode with its cathode at the output and anode at ground. During the first negative half, the input is minus 10 V; the diode turns on and the capacitor charges to 10 V, with its output-side plate positive relative to the input side, and the output is held at about 0 V (minus 0.7 V with a real diode). When the input jumps to +10 V, the capacitor's 10 V adds to it, so the output becomes about 20 V, and the diode is now reverse biased. The output now swings between 0 and +20 V (or minus 0.7 and +19.3 V). The peak-to-peak value, 20 V, did not change; the wave was simply lifted. This is a positive clamper. Flip the diode for a negative clamper, which pushes the wave down to sit between 0 and minus 20 V.

Clamper design rule and biased clampers: For good clamping, the capacitor must not lose much charge during the time the diode is off. That means the time constant R times C must be much larger than the period of the signal; a common textbook rule is that 5RC should be much larger than half the period. For a 1 kHz square wave, half the period is 0.5 ms, so with R = 100 kilo-ohms, a 1 microfarad capacitor gives RC = 100 ms, far more than enough. Adding a battery in series with the diode gives a biased clamper, which clamps the peak to that battery voltage instead of zero, for example placing the bottom of the wave at +2 V.

Voltage multipliers, the half-wave doubler: Combine a clamper and a peak detector and you get more voltage than the input peak. In the half-wave voltage doubler, capacitor C1 and diode D1 form a positive clamper, lifting a sine of peak Vm so it swings from 0 to 2Vm. Then diode D2 and capacitor C2 form a peak rectifier that charges C2 to the peak of that shifted wave, which is 2Vm. So a 10 V peak input gives about 20 V DC across C2 (minus diode drops). Each diode must block 2Vm, and C2 must be rated for at least 2Vm. The output ripple is at the mains frequency, like any half-wave circuit.

Full-wave doubler and higher multipliers: In a full-wave voltage doubler, two diodes charge two capacitors on alternate half cycles, each to Vm. The capacitors are in series, so the output across both is 2Vm, and the ripple is at twice the input frequency. By adding more diode and capacitor stages in a ladder, you can make a tripler (3Vm) or a quadrupler (4Vm). This ladder is the Cockcroft-Walton multiplier, famous for powering early particle accelerators. Multipliers are great for high voltage at tiny current. Under heavy load the capacitors discharge between peaks and the output drops a lot, so they are not used for big power.

Real-life example 1, protecting a microcontroller pin: Suppose you build a project with an Arduino or an ESP32 for your school science fair, maybe a soil moisture alarm for the rooftop garden. The input pins can survive only a little above their supply voltage. Inside the chip, and often outside too, there are two diodes on each pin: one to the supply rail and one to ground. If a long wire picks up a spike of +20 V, the upper diode conducts and clips the pin near the supply plus a diode drop; for a negative spike the lower diode clips near minus 0.7 V. A series resistor limits the current. That is a double-ended clipper doing silent bodyguard duty in almost every electronic gadget.

Real-life example 2, the mosquito bat: The electric mosquito racket sold everywhere in Bangladesh, from Gulistan footpaths to village haats, runs on a small rechargeable battery of a few volts. Yet the mesh gives a strong zap. Inside, a tiny transistor oscillator turns the battery DC into AC, a small step-up transformer raises it to a few hundred volts, and then a diode-capacitor voltage multiplier builds that up further to the high voltage on the grid. When a mosquito bridges the wires, the stored charge discharges through it with a crack. Microwave ovens use a similar idea on a bigger scale: a high-voltage transformer and a half-wave doubler produce a few thousand volts for the magnetron.

A third quick example, video and audio: In old analog TV receivers, the video signal passed through coupling capacitors that removed its DC level, so black would not always look black. A clamper, called a DC restorer, put the sync tips back at a fixed level so the picture brightness stayed correct. In radios and walkie-talkies, a clipper limits very loud audio so the transmitter does not overload. Guitar 'distortion' pedals deliberately clip the signal with diodes to make that rough, crunchy rock sound. So clipping can be a protection, a correction, or even an art.

Common mistakes: The biggest mistake is guessing the diode state instead of checking it. Always assume a state, solve, and check the condition. Many students forget the series resistor in shunt clippers and do not realise it carries the extra voltage. In biased circuits, students add the battery with the wrong sign; always trace from the output through the diode and battery to ground. With clampers, a very common error is to change the peak-to-peak value; it must stay the same. And in doublers, people forget that the diodes and the output capacitor must be rated for 2Vm, not Vm.

What exams ask: Expect: sketch the output of a given clipper for a 10 V or 20 V peak sine or square input; find the clipping levels of a biased or double-ended clipper; draw the transfer characteristic; analyse a clamper for a square wave input and state the output levels; explain why RC must be large in a clamper; draw and explain a half-wave voltage doubler and find the PIV of its diodes; and give applications of clippers and clampers. Draw the input and output waves one above the other with the same time axis, and label every voltage level clearly.

Quick recap: Clippers cut off part of a wave above or below a level. Series clippers have the diode in series; shunt clippers have it across the output with a series resistor. A battery in series with the diode moves the clipping level to VB + 0.7, and two branches or back-to-back Zeners clip both sides. Clampers shift a whole wave up or down using a capacitor that charges through a diode and discharges slowly, keeping the peak-to-peak value. Voltage multipliers stack clampers and peak detectors to make 2Vm, 3Vm and more. Next lesson: the Zener diode and how it holds a voltage steady.
key_points: Clippers (limiters) remove the part of a wave above or below a level; clampers shift the whole wave.
Series clipper: diode in series with load; a half-wave rectifier is a series clipper.
Shunt clipper: series resistor plus diode across the output; clips at 0.7 V, or VB + 0.7 V when biased.
Two biased branches or back-to-back Zeners give a double-ended clipper.
A clamper (C, diode, R) keeps shape and peak-to-peak value; needs RC much larger than the period.
Half-wave doubler: clamper plus peak detector gives 2Vm; diodes and C2 rated for 2Vm.
Method: find the input voltage where the diode changes state, then sketch output or transfer curve.
lessons.tip: Before sketching any diode wave-shaping circuit, write one line: 'Diode is ON when ...'. Find that transition voltage first; the drawing then becomes almost automatic.
lessons.task: On graph paper, draw a 10 V peak sine wave. Below it, sketch the output of (a) a shunt clipper with a 3 V bias battery, and (b) a positive clamper, using the 0.7 V diode model. Mark every voltage level, then draw the transfer characteristic of circuit (a).

quiz.q: A shunt clipper has a silicon diode in series with a 4 V battery. At about what voltage is the output clipped?
quiz.explain: The diode turns on when the output reaches VB + 0.7 = 4.7 V.

quiz.q: What does a clamper change about a signal?
options: Its DC level only, not its shape
quiz.explain: A clamper shifts the DC level; shape and peak-to-peak value stay the same.

quiz.q: A square wave of +10 V / -10 V enters an ideal positive clamper. What are the output levels?
quiz.explain: The positive clamper lifts the wave so its bottom sits at 0 V; peak-to-peak stays 20 V.

quiz.q: In a half-wave voltage doubler with input peak Vm, what voltage must the diodes block?
quiz.explain: Each diode sees a reverse voltage of 2Vm in the half-wave doubler.

quiz.q: Why must RC be large in a clamper?
options: So the capacitor barely discharges while the diode is off
To make the diode conduct all the time
quiz.explain: A large time constant keeps the capacitor voltage nearly constant, so the wave is shifted without distortion.

lessons.title: Zener Diode and Voltage Regulation
lessons.content:
Think of the overflow pipe on a rooftop water tank. However hard the pump pushes, the water level in the tank never rises above the overflow pipe, because the extra water simply spills out. The level stays fixed. A Zener diode does the same thing for voltage. Push more voltage at it in the reverse direction, and it lets the extra current spill through while the voltage across it stays almost constant. That simple behaviour makes the Zener the cheapest voltage regulator and voltage reference in electronics, and it is the star of this lesson.

What a Zener diode is: A Zener diode is a silicon PN junction diode that is heavily doped and specially designed to work safely in reverse breakdown. An ordinary rectifier diode like the 1N4007 is never meant to break down; if it does, it may be destroyed. A Zener is built to sit in breakdown all day long, as long as its current and power stay within limits. Its symbol looks like a normal diode, but the bar at the cathode has small bent ends, like a flattened letter Z. In use, it is connected in reverse: cathode toward the positive side.

The Zener characteristic: In the forward direction, a Zener behaves like any silicon diode, conducting at about 0.7 V. In the reverse direction, it blocks with only a tiny leakage current until the reverse voltage reaches the Zener voltage, VZ. At that point the current rises sharply, and the curve becomes almost vertical. Along that vertical part, the current can change a lot while the voltage hardly changes. Zeners are sold with VZ values from about 2.4 V to over 100 V, in standard steps such as 3.3, 4.7, 5.1, 6.2, 9.1 and 12 V. For example, the 1N4733A is a 5.1 V, 1 W Zener.

Key ratings: Three current values matter. The knee current IZK is the minimum reverse current needed to keep the Zener firmly in breakdown; below it, the voltage starts to drop and regulation fails. The test current IZT is where VZ is measured by the maker. The maximum current IZM is set by the power rating: IZM = PZ / VZ. For a 5.1 V, 1 W Zener, IZM = 1 / 5.1 = about 196 mA. A designer keeps the Zener current between a safe minimum and IZM. The small slope of the breakdown curve is described by the Zener resistance rZ, often just a few ohms, so a change of current dI changes the voltage by about rZ x dI.

Zener effect and avalanche effect: Lesson 5 introduced two breakdown mechanisms, and they matter here. In very heavily doped junctions, the depletion layer is extremely thin, so the electric field is strong enough to pull electrons straight out of their bonds. This is the Zener effect, and it dominates in diodes below about 5 V. In less heavily doped junctions, carriers gain enough speed to knock out more carriers in a chain reaction; this is avalanche breakdown, and it dominates above about 6 V. Both kinds are sold as 'Zener diodes'. The two effects change with temperature in opposite directions, which is why Zeners near 5 to 6 V have very small temperature drift.

Zener models: For circuit work, we model a Zener in breakdown as a battery of value VZ, sometimes with a small series resistance rZ. If the reverse voltage across it is less than VZ, the Zener is off and acts like an open circuit, just like the off state of a normal diode. So the first step in every Zener problem is to decide whether it is on, meaning in breakdown, or off. The standard trick: remove the Zener, find the voltage that would appear across its terminals, and compare it with VZ. If that voltage is bigger than VZ, the Zener is on and holds VZ; if not, it is off.

The simple shunt regulator: The basic Zener regulator has just two parts. A series resistor R goes from the unregulated input Vin to the output node, and the Zener goes from the output node to ground, in reverse, in parallel with the load RL. While the Zener is in breakdown, the output is held at VZ. The current through R is IR = (Vin - VZ) / R. That current splits: the load takes IL = VZ / RL and the Zener takes the rest, IZ = IR - IL. It is called a shunt regulator because the regulating element, the Zener, is in parallel with the load and diverts extra current away from it.

How the shunt regulator regulates: Imagine Vin rises a little. More current flows through R, but the output voltage cannot rise much, because the Zener simply takes the extra current. Now imagine the load draws more current. The current through R stays about the same, because Vin and VZ have not changed, so the Zener gives up some of its current to the load. Either way, the Zener acts as a current sponge, soaking up or releasing current so the voltage stays near VZ. The limits are clear: the Zener current must never fall below its minimum, and must never exceed IZM.

Analysis example: Let Vin = 12 V, R = 220 ohms, VZ = 5.1 V, and RL = 510 ohms. First check if the Zener is on: without it, the load would get 12 x 510 / (220 + 510) = about 8.4 V, which is more than 5.1 V, so it is on. Then IR = (12 - 5.1) / 220 = 31.4 mA. IL = 5.1 / 510 = 10 mA. IZ = 31.4 - 10 = 21.4 mA. Zener power PZ = 5.1 x 0.0214 = about 0.11 W, well within a 0.5 W or 1 W rating. The resistor power is 6.9 x 0.0314 = about 0.22 W, so a quarter-watt resistor is too close; choose 0.5 W.

Designing a regulator, step 1: Now the design direction. Suppose the input from a small unregulated adapter varies between 10 V and 14 V, and the load needs 5.1 V at any current from 0 to 50 mA. We pick a 5.1 V Zener and decide the Zener must keep at least 5 mA flowing to stay in breakdown. The worst case for keeping the Zener alive is the lowest input with the highest load: Vin = 10 V and IL = 50 mA. The resistor must still pass IL + IZmin = 55 mA. So R(max) = (10 - 5.1) / 0.055 = 89 ohms. We choose the nearest smaller standard value, 82 ohms.

Designing a regulator, step 2: Next check the worst case for burning the Zener: the highest input with no load, Vin = 14 V and IL = 0. Then IR = (14 - 5.1) / 82 = 108.5 mA, and all of it flows through the Zener. Zener power = 5.1 x 0.1085 = 0.55 W. A 0.5 W Zener would be overloaded, so we choose a 1 W Zener like the 1N4733A, whose IZM is about 196 mA, giving a comfortable margin. Finally, the resistor's worst power is (14 - 5.1) squared / 82 = 79.2 / 82 = about 0.97 W, so we pick a 2 W resistor. That is a complete, safe design in a few lines of arithmetic.

Line regulation: Line regulation tells you how much the output changes when the input (the 'line') changes. It is often written as the change in output voltage divided by the change in input voltage, sometimes as a percentage. With the Zener model including rZ, the output change is roughly dVin x rZ / (R + rZ), because R and rZ form a voltage divider for changes. For example, if R = 82 ohms and rZ = 7 ohms, a 4 V input change causes about 4 x 7 / 89 = 0.31 V output change, a line regulation of about 0.31 / 4 = 7.9 percent of the input change. A lower rZ or a larger R improves it.

Load regulation: Load regulation tells you how much the output drops when the load current goes from zero to full. The usual formula is load regulation = (VNL - VFL) / VFL x 100 percent, where VNL is the no-load output voltage and VFL is the full-load voltage. If the output is 5.20 V with no load and 5.10 V at full load, the load regulation is 0.10 / 5.10 x 100 = about 2 percent. In a Zener regulator the drop comes from the Zener current changing by the full load current, multiplied by rZ. Good IC regulators manage well under 1 percent; an ideal regulator would have zero.

Limits of the Zener shunt regulator: The simple Zener regulator is wasteful. Current flows through R and the Zener even when the load needs nothing, so energy is burned constantly. It also cannot supply large load currents unless the Zener and resistor are huge. So for bigger currents, we add a transistor. In the series pass regulator, the Zener sets a reference voltage at the base of an emitter follower, and the transistor carries the load current. The output is VZ minus about 0.7 V, and the Zener only needs to supply the small base current. You will meet the transistor in lesson 12, and this circuit will make even more sense then.

IC regulators and references: Today most products use integrated regulators that contain a stable reference, an error amplifier and a pass transistor in one package. The 78xx series gives fixed outputs: 7805 for 5 V, 7812 for 12 V, and the 79xx series gives negative voltages. They need about 2 V or more of headroom between input and output. The LM317 is adjustable: its output is Vout = 1.25 x (1 + R2 / R1), ignoring a small adjust-pin current. For example, R1 = 240 ohms and R2 = 720 ohms gives 1.25 x 4 = 5 V. Chips such as the TL431 act like a programmable, very precise Zener, and are found in almost every phone charger's feedback loop.

Other Zener jobs: Besides regulation, Zeners protect circuits. A Zener across a power input will conduct and clamp the voltage if a spike comes in, often together with a fuse that blows if the fault lasts. Back-to-back Zeners make a double-ended clipper, as you saw in lesson 9. A Zener in series with a meter can make a voltmeter that only starts reading above a certain voltage. In measuring instruments, a temperature-compensated Zener or a band-gap reference provides an accurate known voltage, so that an ADC can compare against it.

Real-life example 1, a 5 V supply for a hobby project: Suppose you have an old 12 V adapter from a broken router and want to power a small 5 V sensor that draws 20 mA. You could use a 5.1 V Zener with a series resistor. Assume the adapter gives 11 to 13 V. With 5 mA minimum Zener current, R(max) = (11 - 5.1) / 0.025 = 236 ohms, so choose 220 ohms. Worst no-load Zener current = (13 - 5.1) / 220 = 36 mA, so PZ = 0.18 W, fine for a 0.5 W Zener. It works, but if the load later needs 300 mA, you would switch to a 7805 or a small buck converter.

Real-life example 2, protecting a solar charge circuit: In rural Bangladesh many homes use solar home systems with small panels and 12 V batteries. A solar panel's open-circuit voltage can climb above 20 V on a bright, cool morning, which can stress small electronics connected to it. Simple chargers and indicator circuits often use a Zener, sometimes driving a transistor, as an overvoltage sensor: when the voltage rises above VZ plus a little, the Zener conducts, the transistor turns on, and the controller cuts off or diverts the charging. The same idea protects the input of many cheap LED drivers and USB devices from spikes.

Common mistakes: Many students connect the Zener forward in diagrams; in a regulator, the cathode must face the positive side. Others forget to check whether the Zener is actually in breakdown before using VZ. In design, a classic error is checking only one worst case: you must check both minimum Zener current (lowest input, highest load) and maximum Zener power (highest input, lowest load). People also forget the resistor's power rating. Another confusion is mixing up line and load regulation: line is about input change, load is about load current change.

What exams ask: Expect: draw and explain the Zener I-V characteristic and label VZ, IZK and IZM; explain Zener and avalanche breakdown; analyse a given shunt regulator to find IR, IL, IZ and PZ; find the range of RL or Vin over which the Zener stays in regulation; design R for a given input range and load range; define and calculate line and load regulation; and draw a series pass regulator. When solving, always write the on or off check first, then the three currents in a neat column. It earns marks and keeps you honest.

Quick recap: A Zener diode is built to work in reverse breakdown, holding a nearly fixed voltage VZ while its current changes. Its safe range is between the knee current and IZM = PZ / VZ. Below about 5 V the Zener effect dominates, above about 6 V avalanche dominates. In a shunt regulator, IR = (Vin - VZ) / R splits into the load and the Zener; design R for the lowest input and highest load, then check Zener power at the highest input and no load. Line and load regulation measure quality. For bigger currents, add a pass transistor or use an IC like the 7805 or LM317. Next: special diodes like LEDs and solar cells.
key_points: A Zener is a heavily doped diode designed to operate in reverse breakdown at a nearly constant VZ.
Keep Zener current between the knee current IZK and IZM = PZ / VZ.
Zener effect dominates below about 5 V, avalanche above about 6 V; near 5-6 V temperature drift is small.
Shunt regulator: IR = (Vin - VZ)/R, IL = VZ/RL, IZ = IR - IL.
Design R for lowest Vin and highest load; check Zener power at highest Vin and no load.
Load regulation = (VNL - VFL)/VFL x 100%; line regulation compares output change to input change.
For larger currents use a series pass transistor or IC regulators such as the 7805 and LM317.
lessons.tip: In every Zener problem, first remove the Zener and find the open-circuit voltage at its terminals. If it is greater than VZ the Zener is on; if not, it is off. This one check prevents most wrong answers.
lessons.task: Design on paper a Zener regulator giving 9.1 V to a load drawing 0 to 30 mA from an input that varies from 15 V to 18 V. Choose R, then find the worst-case Zener power and resistor power, and pick suitable ratings.

quiz.q: What is the maximum current of a 12 V, 1 W Zener diode?
quiz.explain: IZM = PZ / VZ = 1 / 12 = about 83 mA.

quiz.q: In a shunt regulator, Vin = 15 V, VZ = 10 V, R = 100 ohms and IL = 30 mA. What is the Zener current?
When choosing the series resistor of a Zener regulator, which worst case sets its maximum value?
options: Lowest input and highest load current
quiz.explain: The Zener must stay in breakdown when the input is lowest and the load takes the most current.

quiz.q: An output is 9.3 V at no load and 9.0 V at full load. What is the load regulation?
Which breakdown mechanism dominates in a 3.3 V Zener diode?
quiz.explain: Below about 5 V the junction is very thin and the strong field pulls electrons directly out of bonds: the Zener effect.

lessons.title: Special Diodes: LED, Photodiode, Solar Cell and Friends
lessons.content:
Think about a family where all the cousins share the same grandparents but each one chose a different job. One became a doctor, one a cricketer, one a singer. They still look alike, but they do very different things. Special diodes are like that. Every one of them is built around the same PN junction you met in lesson 5, but the makers changed the material, the doping or the shape so that the junction does a special job: give light, catch light, make power from sunlight, switch super fast, or act like a tiny capacitor whose value you can tune with voltage.

Why care about these? Because they are everywhere around you. The tiny light on your phone charger, the screen backlight of your TV, the IR receiver that hears your TV remote, the solar panel on a village rooftop in Kurigram, the fast diode inside a laptop adapter, the tuner in an old FM radio, and the laser in a supermarket barcode scanner are all special diodes. As a CSE student you will also meet them in embedded systems, sensors, optical fibre networking and computer hardware labs.

What this lesson covers: We will look at seven members of the family: the LED, the photodiode, the solar cell, the Schottky diode, the varactor diode, the laser diode and the optocoupler. For each one we will ask three questions. What is different inside it? How is it biased, forward or reverse? And where do we use it? The Zener diode is also a special diode, but it gets its own lesson (lesson 10), so we only mention it here.

Light and energy, a tiny recap: In lesson 2 you saw that electrons in a semiconductor live in energy bands with a band gap in between. When an electron falls from the conduction band down into a hole in the valence band, it loses energy equal to roughly the band gap. That energy has to go somewhere. In silicon, it mostly turns into heat, shaking the crystal. In some other materials, like gallium arsenide (GaAs) and gallium nitride (GaN), it comes out as a packet of light called a photon. Materials where this happens easily are called direct band gap materials. Silicon has an indirect band gap, which is why ordinary silicon diodes do not glow.

Colour comes from the band gap: The energy of a photon decides its colour. A handy formula is wavelength in nanometres is about 1240 divided by the band gap in electron-volts. If the band gap is 1.9 eV, the wavelength is about 1240 / 1.9 = 650 nm, which is red. If it is about 2.7 eV, you get about 460 nm, which is blue. Infrared LEDs, like the one in your TV remote, use smaller band gaps, around 1.4 eV, giving about 900 nm, which your eyes cannot see. So chemists choose the material mix to pick the colour.

The LED: LED stands for Light Emitting Diode. It is a PN junction made from a direct band gap material, and it is used in forward bias. When forward current flows, electrons from the n side and holes from the p side meet near the junction and recombine, and each recombination can release a photon. More current means more recombinations per second, so more light. The light output is roughly proportional to the current, which is why we control LEDs by current, not by voltage.

LED forward voltage: Because the band gap is bigger than silicon's, the LED needs more forward voltage to turn on. Typical values: red about 1.8 to 2.2 V, green about 2 to 3 V, blue and white about 2.8 to 3.4 V. A white LED is usually a blue LED coated with a yellow phosphor; blue plus yellow looks white to our eyes. LEDs also have a low reverse breakdown, often only about 5 V, so you should not put a big reverse voltage on them.

Designing an LED circuit: An LED must always have something to limit its current, usually a series resistor. The rule is R = (Vsupply - VLED) / ILED. Example: a 5 V USB supply, a red LED with VLED = 2 V, and you want 10 mA. R = (5 - 2) / 0.010 = 300 ohms. The nearest standard value is 330 ohms, which gives about 9 mA. Power in the resistor is (3 V) x (9 mA) = about 27 mW, so a tiny quarter-watt resistor is fine. If you skip the resistor, the current shoots up because of the steep diode curve and the LED burns out, often in a second.

The photodiode: A photodiode does the opposite job of an LED. Light goes in, current comes out. It is a PN (or PIN, with an extra undoped layer in the middle) junction with a window so light can reach the depletion region. When a photon with enough energy hits the depletion region, it creates an electron-hole pair. The electric field already sitting in the depletion region sweeps the electron to the n side and the hole to the p side. That flow is a current, called the photocurrent.

How a photodiode is biased: For sensing, a photodiode is normally used in reverse bias. In the dark, only a tiny leakage current flows, called the dark current, often a few nanoamps. When light falls on it, the reverse current grows almost in proportion to the light intensity, for example 0 lux gives 2 nA and bright room light might give 10 microamps. Reverse bias also makes the depletion region wider, which catches more photons and makes the diode faster because its capacitance drops. This is called photoconductive mode. Fast photodiodes are what receive the light pulses in optical fibre internet cables.

The solar cell: A solar cell is basically a big photodiode used with no external bias at all. Light makes electron-hole pairs, the junction field separates them, and the cell itself pushes current out into a load, like a little battery powered by sunlight. This is called photovoltaic mode. A single silicon cell gives an open-circuit voltage of about 0.5 to 0.6 V and a short-circuit current that depends on its area and the sunlight. To get useful voltage, cells are connected in series; about 36 cells in series make a panel suitable for charging a 12 V battery.

Solar cell numbers: Two key points describe a solar cell. Open-circuit voltage, Voc, is the voltage when no current is drawn. Short-circuit current, Isc, is the current when the terminals are shorted. In between there is a sweet spot called the maximum power point, where volts times amps is largest. Example: a small panel with Voc = 21 V and Isc = 1.2 A might deliver its maximum power at about 17 V and 1.1 A, giving about 19 W. Good chargers track this point automatically, which is called MPPT, maximum power point tracking. Commercial silicon panels convert roughly 18 to 22 percent of sunlight into electricity.

The Schottky diode: A Schottky diode is not a PN junction. It is a junction between a metal and an n-type semiconductor. Current is carried mainly by majority carriers (electrons), so there is almost no stored minority charge to clear out when it switches off. Two results follow. First, its forward voltage is low, about 0.2 to 0.4 V instead of 0.7 V, which wastes less power. Second, it switches off very fast, which is great in high-frequency circuits. The cost: higher reverse leakage current and usually a lower reverse voltage rating. You find Schottky diodes in switching power supplies, phone chargers and solar panel bypass protection.

Schottky example: Suppose a diode carries 2 A in a charger. A normal silicon diode at 0.7 V wastes 0.7 x 2 = 1.4 W as heat. A Schottky at 0.35 V wastes 0.35 x 2 = 0.7 W. That is half the heat, so the charger can be smaller and cooler. This is exactly why designers love them in low-voltage, high-current supplies.

The varactor diode: Every reverse-biased PN junction has a depletion region with charge on each side, like the two plates of a capacitor with an insulating gap between them. A wider gap means less capacitance. When you increase the reverse voltage, the depletion region gets wider, so the capacitance gets smaller. A varactor (also called a varicap) is a diode specially made to use this effect. For example, a varactor might be 30 pF at 1 V reverse and 10 pF at 8 V reverse. Put it in an LC circuit and you can tune the resonant frequency with a voltage instead of a mechanical knob. That is how electronic tuners in radios and TVs, and voltage-controlled oscillators in phones, work.

The laser diode: A laser diode is a cousin of the LED but more disciplined. It also works in forward bias, but the chip is built with mirror-like ends forming an optical cavity. Above a certain current, called the threshold current, light bouncing between the mirrors triggers stimulated emission: one photon causes another identical photon with the same colour, direction and phase. The result is a narrow, strong, single-colour beam. Below threshold it behaves like a dim LED; above threshold the light output rises sharply with current. Laser diodes are in barcode scanners, laser pointers, optical mice, DVD drives and, very importantly, fibre-optic transmitters for the internet.

The optocoupler: An optocoupler (or opto-isolator) is an LED and a light sensor, often a phototransistor, sealed together in one small package with no electrical connection between them. When current flows in the LED, its light turns the sensor on. The signal crosses the gap as light, so the two sides can be at completely different voltages. This is called galvanic isolation. A microcontroller running at 3.3 V can safely control a circuit connected to 220 V mains through an optocoupler. Chargers use one to send a feedback signal from the safe low-voltage side back to the dangerous high-voltage side.

Real-life example 1, a solar home system in a village: Bangladesh has installed millions of solar home systems in rural areas. Picture a house in a char area. On the tin roof there is a panel of silicon solar cells in photovoltaic mode. A charge controller, often with Schottky diodes to stop the battery from discharging back into the panel at night, feeds a 12 V battery. At night the battery powers white LED bulbs, maybe 5 W each, which give as much light as an old 40 W filament bulb. During the day, four special diodes are working together: solar cells making power, Schottky diodes blocking reverse current, and later LEDs turning that power back into light.

Real-life example 2, your TV remote: When you press the volume button, a microcontroller in the remote blinks an infrared LED at about 38 kHz in a coded pattern. You cannot see it, but your phone camera can; try it and you will see the LED flash purple-white. Inside the TV, a photodiode inside an IR receiver module catches these flashes and turns them into tiny currents. A small amplifier and filter tuned to 38 kHz clean up the signal so that lamps and sunlight do not confuse it. The TV processor reads the code and turns the volume up. LED out, photodiode in, a full optical link in your living room.

Common mistakes: Students often say a photodiode works in forward bias like an LED. No, for sensing it is used in reverse bias, while a solar cell runs with no external bias and delivers power. Another mistake is connecting an LED directly to a battery without a resistor. A third is thinking Schottky diodes are PN junctions; they are metal-semiconductor junctions. And many forget that a varactor's capacitance goes down when reverse voltage goes up, not up.

What exams ask: Expect questions like these. Explain why silicon is not used for LEDs. Calculate the series resistor for an LED. Compare photodiode and solar cell. List two advantages and one disadvantage of a Schottky diode. Explain how a varactor tunes a circuit. Draw the symbol of each special diode: the LED has arrows pointing out, the photodiode has arrows pointing in, the Schottky has an S-shaped bar, and the varactor has a capacitor plate drawn next to the bar.

Recap: Same PN junction family, different jobs. LED and laser diode: forward bias, electricity into light, laser needs threshold current. Photodiode: reverse bias, light into current. Solar cell: no bias, light into power. Schottky: metal-semiconductor, low drop and fast. Varactor: reverse bias, voltage-controlled capacitor. Optocoupler: LED plus sensor for isolation. Next, we meet the transistor, the device that changed the world.
key_points: Special diodes are PN (or metal-semiconductor) junctions tuned for one job.
LEDs use direct band gap materials in forward bias; colour depends on band gap (wavelength in nm is about 1240 / Eg in eV).
Always limit LED current: R = (Vs - VLED) / I, e.g. (5 - 2) / 10 mA = 300 ohms.
Photodiode: reverse biased; photocurrent grows with light; dark current is tiny.
Solar cell: no external bias, about 0.5-0.6 V per silicon cell; maximum power point matters.
Schottky: metal-semiconductor junction, about 0.2-0.4 V drop, very fast, more leakage.
Varactor: capacitance drops as reverse voltage rises; used for electronic tuning.
Laser diode needs threshold current; optocoupler gives electrical isolation using light.
lessons.tip: Make a small table with three columns: bias (forward, reverse or none), energy direction (electric to light or light to electric) and one use. Fill it for every special diode. Most exam questions are answered by that one table.
lessons.task: Point your TV remote at your phone camera and press a button. Watch the IR LED flash on screen. Then calculate the resistor needed for a blue LED (3.2 V) at 15 mA from a 9 V battery and pick the nearest standard value.

quiz.q: Why does an ordinary silicon diode not glow like an LED?
options: Silicon has an indirect band gap, so recombination energy mostly becomes heat
Silicon diodes are only used in reverse bias
quiz.explain: In indirect band gap materials like silicon, recombination mostly makes heat, not photons.

quiz.q: A red LED (2 V) runs from 5 V at 10 mA. What series resistor is needed?
For light sensing, a photodiode is normally used in which way?
quiz.explain: Reverse bias gives a tiny dark current and a photocurrent that grows with light.

quiz.q: What is the main advantage of a Schottky diode?
options: Low forward drop and fast switching
quiz.explain: Metal-semiconductor junction: about 0.2-0.4 V drop and almost no stored charge, so fast.

quiz.q: When reverse voltage on a varactor increases, its capacitance...
quiz.explain: Higher reverse voltage widens the depletion region, like moving capacitor plates apart, so capacitance drops.

lessons.title: The Bipolar Junction Transistor (BJT)
lessons.content:
Imagine a big water tank on the roof of a building in Dhaka, with a pipe going down to the taps. In the pipe there is a valve, and the valve is controlled by a tiny side pipe. A trickle of water in the tiny pipe opens the big valve, and a huge flow rushes through the main pipe. A small flow controls a big flow. That is the whole idea of a transistor. A tiny current into one terminal controls a much bigger current between the other two. With that one trick, humans built amplifiers, radios, computers and phones.

Why the BJT matters: The bipolar junction transistor was invented at Bell Labs in 1947 to 1948 by John Bardeen, Walter Brattain and William Shockley (the very first one was a point-contact transistor, the junction version came soon after). It replaced big, hot vacuum tubes. Today most digital chips use MOSFETs (lessons 18 to 20), but BJTs are still everywhere: in audio amplifiers, radio circuits, sensor interfaces, motor drivers, voltage regulators and in the inputs of many op-amps. More importantly, the BJT teaches you how to think about amplification and switching, which you will use in every later electronics and computer hardware course.

What this lesson covers: We will look at the structure of npn and pnp transistors, the names of the three terminals, the symbols, how current flows inside, the key equation IE = IC + IB, the current gains alpha and beta and how they are related, a few worked numbers, and how to check a transistor with a multimeter. Biasing, configurations, switching and amplifier design come in the next four lessons, so here we build the foundation.

Structure: A BJT is a sandwich of three doped semiconductor layers, so it has two PN junctions. In an npn transistor, a thin p-type layer sits between two n-type layers. In a pnp transistor, a thin n-type layer sits between two p-type layers. The three layers are called the emitter, the base and the collector. The word bipolar means both kinds of carriers, electrons and holes, take part in the current, unlike FETs that use only one kind.

The three layers are not equal: The emitter is heavily doped, because its job is to emit (inject) lots of carriers. The base is very thin, often only around a micrometre or less, and lightly doped, so that carriers pass through it without getting lost. The collector is moderately doped and physically the largest, because it collects the carriers and has to get rid of heat. This is why you cannot simply swap the emitter and collector and expect the transistor to work equally well, even though both are n-type in an npn.

Two junctions, two diodes: Between emitter and base there is the base-emitter junction (BE junction). Between base and collector there is the collector-base junction (CB junction). If you measure an npn transistor with a multimeter in diode mode, you see two diodes pointing out from the base: base to emitter reads about 0.6 to 0.7 V, and base to collector reads about 0.6 to 0.7 V, while collector to emitter reads open both ways. But two separate diodes glued together do not make a transistor. The magic only happens because the base is so thin that the two junctions interact.

The symbols: In the circuit symbol, the emitter has an arrow. The arrow shows the direction of conventional current through the emitter. For npn, the arrow points out of the transistor (memory trick: Not Pointing iN). For pnp, the arrow points in (Points iN Proudly). The base is the line in the middle, and the collector is the other slanted line without an arrow.

How an npn works, step by step: For normal amplifying use, called the active region, we forward bias the base-emitter junction and reverse bias the collector-base junction. Step one: the forward biased BE junction lets the heavily doped emitter push a big flood of electrons into the base. Step two: the base is thin and lightly doped, so only a few of these electrons find a hole and recombine; these few make the small base current. Step three: most electrons, often more than 99 percent, diffuse across the thin base and reach the edge of the collector-base depletion region. Step four: the strong electric field of the reverse biased CB junction sweeps them into the collector. That big flow is the collector current.

Why the small base current controls the big one: The number of electrons the emitter injects depends exponentially on the base-emitter voltage, just like a diode. A small change in VBE, and so a small change in base current, changes the electron flood a lot, and nearly all of that flood ends up at the collector. So the base acts like the tap handle and the collector current is the main water flow. For a pnp, everything is the same but with holes instead of electrons and all voltages and currents reversed.

The current equation: By Kirchhoff's current law, the current going in must equal the current coming out. In an npn, current enters at the collector and the base and leaves at the emitter. So IE = IC + IB. Example: if IC = 5 mA and IB = 0.05 mA, then IE = 5.05 mA. Since IB is tiny, we often say IE is approximately IC.

Alpha, the common-base current gain: Alpha (written as the Greek letter alpha, often αdc) is the fraction of emitter current that reaches the collector: alpha = IC / IE. Because a few carriers are lost in the base, alpha is just a bit less than 1, typically 0.98 to 0.998. Example: IC = 4.95 mA and IE = 5 mA gives alpha = 0.99.

Beta, the common-emitter current gain: Beta (also called hFE on datasheets) is how many times bigger the collector current is than the base current: beta = IC / IB. Typical small transistors have beta from about 50 to 400. Example: IB = 20 microamps and IC = 2 mA gives beta = 2 mA / 0.02 mA = 100. This is the number students use most, because in most circuits we control the base and watch the collector.

Linking alpha and beta: Since IE = IC + IB, you can show that beta = alpha / (1 - alpha) and alpha = beta / (beta + 1). Try it: alpha = 0.99 gives beta = 0.99 / 0.01 = 99. Alpha = 0.995 gives beta = 199. Notice how a tiny change in alpha makes a big change in beta. That is why beta varies a lot from one transistor to another, even of the same part number, and also changes with temperature and current. A good circuit should not depend on the exact value of beta, an idea that drives the biasing methods of lesson 14.

A worked problem: An npn transistor has beta = 150, and the base current is 30 microamps. Find IC, IE and alpha. IC = beta x IB = 150 x 30 microamps = 4.5 mA. IE = IC + IB = 4.5 mA + 0.03 mA = 4.53 mA. Alpha = beta / (beta + 1) = 150 / 151, which is about 0.993. Check: IC / IE = 4.5 / 4.53, also about 0.993. Always do a check like this; it catches slips.

Leakage current: Even when the base is open, a small current flows from collector to emitter because the reverse biased CB junction leaks a little, and the transistor then amplifies that leakage. The CB leakage is called ICBO and the collector-emitter leakage with open base is ICEO, roughly (beta + 1) x ICBO. For silicon at room temperature these are tiny, nanoamps, but they roughly double for every 10 degrees Celsius rise. In hot places like a closed metal box in Bangladeshi summer, this can matter.

The four modes in one look: The two junctions can each be forward or reverse biased, giving four modes. BE forward, CB reverse: active, used for amplifiers. Both forward: saturation, the transistor acts like a closed switch. Both reverse: cut-off, like an open switch. BE reverse, CB forward: reverse active, rarely used because the gain is poor. Lessons 13 and 15 explore these in detail.

Ratings to respect: Every transistor has limits written on its datasheet: maximum collector current (for example 100 mA for the small BC547, 600 mA for 2N2222), maximum collector-emitter voltage (45 V for BC547, 40 V for 2N2222), and maximum power dissipation, roughly VCE x IC. Exceed these and the transistor gets hot and dies. Power transistors like TIP31 or 2N3055 come in bigger metal packages and are screwed to heat sinks.

Real-life example 1, the mobile phone repair shop: Walk into a phone repair shop at Bashundhara City or a small market in your town. Repair technicians often test transistors on a board using a multimeter's diode mode. For an npn, red probe on the base and black on the emitter should read around 0.6 V; red on base and black on collector also around 0.6 V; reversed, they should read open. If collector to emitter reads close to zero both ways, the transistor is shorted, often the reason a charging circuit or backlight stopped working. That simple two-diode picture of a BJT is a real repair tool.

Real-life example 2, a doorbell that sings: Cheap musical doorbells and toys use a melody chip that can only give a tiny current, maybe 1 mA, but the speaker needs 100 mA or more to be loud. A single transistor fixes it: the chip drives the base with about 1 mA, and with beta around 100 the collector can pass about 100 mA through the speaker. The tiny side pipe opens the big valve, exactly like the water tank on the roof.

Common mistakes: Students mix up which terminal has the arrow (it is always the emitter). Many think the collector current is caused by the collector voltage; actually, in the active region IC is set by the base-emitter side and hardly depends on VCE. Others forget that beta is not a fixed constant. And some swap emitter and collector in the lab; it may work weakly in reverse active mode with a much smaller beta, which is confusing.

What exams ask: Draw the structure and symbol of npn and pnp transistors. Explain the working of an npn transistor in the active region with a diagram of electron flow. Why is the base thin and lightly doped? Derive beta = alpha / (1 - alpha). Numericals: given alpha and IE, find IC and IB; given beta and IB, find IC and IE. Explain ICBO and ICEO.

Recap: A BJT is three layers, emitter, base and collector, with two junctions. Forward bias BE and reverse bias CB, and a small base current controls a large collector current. IE = IC + IB, alpha = IC / IE is close to 1, beta = IC / IB is often 50 to 400, and beta = alpha / (1 - alpha). Next lesson, we connect the transistor in three different ways and read its characteristic curves.
key_points: A BJT has three layers (emitter, base, collector) and two junctions; npn and pnp types.
Emitter heavily doped, base thin and lightly doped, collector largest.
Active region: BE junction forward biased, CB junction reverse biased.
IE = IC + IB; the arrow in the symbol is on the emitter and shows conventional current.
Alpha = IC / IE (about 0.98-0.998); beta = IC / IB (about 50-400).
beta = alpha / (1 - alpha) and alpha = beta / (beta + 1).
Beta varies with device, temperature and current, so good designs do not depend on it exactly.
Leakage ICEO is about (beta + 1) x ICBO and roughly doubles every 10 degrees C.
lessons.tip: Memorise only two things: IE = IC + IB and beta = IC / IB. Every other formula in this lesson can be derived in two lines from these, which is safer in an exam than remembering five formulas.
lessons.task: Solve on paper: a transistor has alpha = 0.98 and IE = 10 mA. Find IC, IB and beta. Then draw an npn and a pnp symbol from memory and mark E, B and C.

quiz.q: In the active region of a BJT, how are the junctions biased?
quiz.explain: Active region: base-emitter forward biased, collector-base reverse biased.

quiz.q: A BJT has IB = 20 microamps and IC = 3 mA. What is beta?
quiz.explain: beta = 3 mA / 0.02 mA = 150.

quiz.q: If alpha = 0.99, beta is about...
quiz.explain: beta = alpha / (1 - alpha) = 0.99 / 0.01 = 99.

quiz.q: Why is the base of a BJT made thin and lightly doped?
options: To make it the strongest emitter
So most injected carriers cross it to the collector instead of recombining
quiz.explain: Few holes and a short path mean very few injected electrons recombine in the base.

quiz.q: In the npn symbol, the arrow on the emitter...
quiz.explain: npn: Not Pointing iN, the emitter arrow points out.

lessons.title: BJT Configurations and Characteristics
lessons.content:
A cricket team has the same eleven players every match, but the captain can arrange them differently. Put the best batter at the top and you score fast. Put him in the middle and the innings is steady. The players do not change, only the arrangement. A transistor has three terminals, and in most circuits one of them is shared between the input and the output. Which terminal you share changes how the transistor behaves: big current gain, big voltage gain, or neither but a great buffer. These arrangements are called configurations.

Why this matters: When you read a circuit or design one, the first question is: which configuration is this transistor in? The answer tells you roughly how much gain to expect, what the input and output impedances are, and whether the output is inverted. And the characteristic curves, the graphs of current against voltage, are the transistor's personality sheet. Datasheets are full of them, lab experiments in your course ask you to plot them, and the load-line method of lesson 14 is drawn right on top of them.

What this lesson covers: The three configurations, common base (CB), common emitter (CE) and common collector (CC); the input and output characteristic curves for CB and CE; the three regions of operation, cut-off, active and saturation, and how to spot each on the curves; the Early effect; and a comparison table you can memorise. Detailed biasing, switching and small-signal gain formulas come in the next three lessons.

The idea of a common terminal: A transistor is a three-terminal device, but an input needs two wires and an output needs two wires. So one terminal must be shared by both, and it is usually tied to ground for signals. If the base is shared, it is common base. If the emitter is shared, it is common emitter.
