If the collector is shared, it is common collector. A quick way to identify a configuration: find where the input goes in and where the output comes out; the leftover terminal is the common one.

Common base (CB): Input goes into the emitter, output comes from the collector, the base is common. The input current is IE and the output current is IC, so the current gain is alpha, slightly less than 1. But the voltage gain can be large because the output resistance is high and the input resistance is very low, often tens of ohms. The output is in phase with the input. CB is used in high-frequency amplifiers, like RF stages, because it behaves well at high frequencies.

CB input characteristics: Plot IE against VBE while keeping VCB fixed. It looks just like a forward-biased diode curve: almost nothing until about 0.5 V, then IE rises steeply near 0.7 V. Increasing VCB shifts the curve slightly to the left, meaning a little more emitter current for the same VBE, because the wider collector depletion region makes the effective base narrower.

CB output characteristics: Plot IC against VCB for several fixed values of IE, say 1 mA, 2 mA and 3 mA. In the active region the lines are almost flat and horizontal, with IC very close to IE, about alpha x IE. Even at VCB = 0, collector current still flows, because the CB junction field is already there to collect carriers. To stop IC completely, you need to slightly forward bias the CB junction, roughly -0.5 V, which is the saturation region. Below the line IE = 0 is the cut-off region, where only the tiny leakage ICBO flows.

Common emitter (CE): Input goes into the base, output comes from the collector, and the emitter is common. This is the most popular configuration, by far. The current gain is beta, often around 100. The voltage gain is also large. So the power gain, current gain times voltage gain, is the highest of the three. The input resistance is medium, about a kilo-ohm or a few, and the output resistance is medium-high. One special feature: the output is inverted, 180 degrees out of phase with the input. When the base voltage goes up, IC goes up, the drop across the collector resistor grows, and the collector voltage goes down.

CE input characteristics: Plot IB against VBE for fixed VCE. Again, a diode-like curve, but now the current is in microamps, because IB is small. Turn-on is around 0.6 to 0.7 V for silicon. Increasing VCE shifts the curve slightly to the right: with a larger VCE, the base gets slightly narrower, fewer carriers recombine there, so a bit less base current flows for the same VBE.

CE output characteristics: This is the most famous graph in transistor theory. Plot IC on the vertical axis against VCE on the horizontal axis, drawing a separate curve for each base current: IB = 0, 10, 20, 30, 40 microamps. With beta = 100, the curves sit at about IC = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 mA. Each curve rises steeply at very small VCE, then bends and runs nearly flat. The flat part is the active region. The spacing between curves shows beta: if IB goes from 20 to 30 microamps and IC goes from 2 to 3 mA, then beta = 1 mA / 10 microamps = 100.

Reading the three regions on the CE curves: Cut-off is the area below the IB = 0 curve, along the horizontal axis; here IC is only the tiny leakage ICEO and the transistor is off, like an open switch. Saturation is the steep part on the far left, where VCE is very small, about 0.1 to 0.3 V; here both junctions are forward biased and IC is no longer beta x IB, it is less, set by the outside circuit. The transistor is fully on, like a closed switch. The active region is the wide flat middle area, where IC is about beta x IB, and this is where amplifiers live.

The Early effect: In real transistors, the flat lines of the active region are not perfectly flat; they slope up slightly. As VCE grows, the collector-base depletion region widens and eats into the base, making it thinner. A thinner base means fewer carriers are lost, so IC goes up a little. This is called base-width modulation or the Early effect, after James Early. If you extend all the sloped lines to the left, they meet at one point on the negative VCE axis, at -VA, where VA is the Early voltage, typically 50 to 200 V. It gives the transistor a finite output resistance, ro = VA / IC. For example, VA = 100 V and IC = 1 mA gives ro = 100 kilo-ohms.

Common collector (CC), the emitter follower: Input goes into the base, output comes from the emitter, and the collector is common (tied to the supply, which is ground for signals). The output voltage simply follows the input voltage, about 0.7 V lower. So the voltage gain is just under 1, like 0.98. Why use it? Because the current gain is beta + 1, which is high, the input resistance is very high and the output resistance is very low. It is a buffer: it can take a weak signal that cannot supply much current and drive a heavy load, such as a speaker or a long cable. Output is in phase with input.

A tiny emitter follower example: Base at 5 V, emitter connected to ground through a 1 kilo-ohm resistor, beta = 100. VE = 5 - 0.7 = 4.3 V. IE = 4.3 V / 1 kilo-ohm = 4.3 mA. IB = IE / (beta + 1) = 4.3 / 101, about 0.043 mA = 43 microamps. So the source only supplies 43 microamps but the load gets 4.3 mA. Seen from the base, the 1 kilo-ohm resistor looks like about (beta + 1) x 1 kilo-ohm, roughly 101 kilo-ohms. That is the impedance-lifting magic of the CC.

Comparison you can memorise: CB: low input resistance, high output resistance, current gain alpha (below 1), high voltage gain, no phase inversion, good for high frequency. CE: medium input, medium-high output, current gain beta (high), high voltage gain, highest power gain, 180 degree phase inversion, the general-purpose amplifier. CC: high input, low output, current gain beta + 1, voltage gain about 1, no inversion, used as a buffer or impedance matcher.

The pnp version: Everything above works for pnp too, but with polarities flipped. VBE is about -0.7 V, VCE is negative in the active region, and currents flow out of the collector instead of in. Many textbooks plot pnp curves with magnitudes so they look the same as npn curves. Do not panic about the signs; just remember pnp is the mirror image.

Real-life example 1, a lab in your university: In an EDC lab at BUET, DU or any private university, a classic experiment is plotting CE characteristics. You set up a BC547 with two variable supplies. You fix IB at 10 microamps using the base supply and a resistor, then vary VCE from 0 to 10 V and note IC at each step. Then you repeat for IB = 20, 30 and 40 microamps. On graph paper you get the family of curves. You mark the saturation region near the left, measure beta from the spacing, and extend the slopes to estimate the Early voltage. This one experiment turns all the theory above into something you can see with your own hands.

Real-life example 2, an old cassette player and a microphone: In an old cassette player or a simple microphone preamp, the first stage is often a CE amplifier because it gives lots of voltage and power gain to the tiny signal from the tape head or microphone. The last stage, driving the headphones or the cable to the next box, is often an emitter follower, because it can supply current without its output voltage sagging. CE for gain, CC for drive: this pairing appears again and again in real circuits.

Common mistakes: Students often think saturation means maximum gain. It is the opposite; in saturation the transistor is fully on and IC no longer increases with IB, so there is no amplification. Another mistake is identifying the configuration by where the supply is connected instead of by which terminal is shared between input and output for the signal. Many forget the 180 degree phase shift of CE. And some think the CC has no use because its voltage gain is below 1, ignoring its current gain and buffering.

What exams ask: Draw the circuit to obtain CE input and output characteristics and explain the curves. Mark cut-off, active and saturation regions. Compare CB, CE and CC in a table. Explain why CE gives phase inversion. Explain the Early effect with a sketch. Find beta from given curve readings. Find VE, IE and IB in a simple emitter follower.

Recap: Three configurations, named by the shared terminal. CE gives the most power gain and inverts; CB gives voltage gain with low input resistance and suits high frequency; CC gives current gain and acts as a buffer with voltage gain near 1. The CE output curves show three regions: cut-off at the bottom, saturation on the left, active in the flat middle. The slight upward slope is the Early effect. Next lesson, we learn how to set the transistor's operating point reliably using biasing circuits.
key_points: Configuration is named by the terminal shared between input and output: CB, CE, CC.
CE: current gain beta, high voltage and highest power gain, output inverted 180 degrees.
CB: current gain alpha (below 1), very low input resistance, good at high frequency.
CC (emitter follower): voltage gain about 1, high input and low output resistance, a buffer.
CE output curves: IC vs VCE for steps of IB; spacing gives beta.
Regions: cut-off (IB = 0, off), active (IC = beta x IB), saturation (VCE about 0.2 V, fully on).
Early effect: active-region lines slope up; ro = VA / IC.
lessons.tip: Draw the CE output curve family at least five times from memory, labelling the axes and the three regions. Once it lives in your fingers, half the questions in lessons 13 to 16 become easy.
lessons.task: Using beta = 120, sketch the CE output curves for IB = 0, 10, 20 and 30 microamps (IC values 0, 1.2, 2.4 and 3.6 mA) on graph paper. Shade the cut-off, saturation and active regions in three colours.

quiz.q: Which configuration gives the highest power gain?
quiz.explain: CE has both high current gain (beta) and high voltage gain, so the highest power gain.

quiz.q: In saturation, VCE is typically about...
quiz.explain: Saturated BJT: both junctions forward biased, VCE(sat) about 0.1-0.3 V.

quiz.q: The voltage gain of an emitter follower is...
quiz.explain: The emitter follows the base about 0.7 V lower: gain just under 1, in phase.

quiz.q: On CE curves, IB rises from 20 to 40 microamps and IC rises from 3 to 6 mA. Beta is...
quiz.explain: beta = 3 mA / 20 microamps = 150.

quiz.q: What causes the slight upward slope of CE output curves in the active region?
options: Ohm's law in the base resistor
quiz.explain: Higher VCE widens the CB depletion region, narrowing the base, so IC rises a little.

lessons.title: BJT DC Biasing
lessons.content:
Before a singer goes on stage, the sound engineer sets the microphone stand at the right height. Too low and the singer has to bend; too high and they stretch. Only at the right height can the singer move freely in both directions. A transistor amplifier is the same. Before any signal arrives, we must park the transistor at a good resting point, so the signal can swing up and down freely without hitting the floor (cut-off) or the ceiling (saturation). Setting this resting point with DC voltages and resistors is called biasing.

Why biasing matters: An amplifier with bad biasing clips the signal, distorts music and wastes power. Worse, a badly biased transistor may drift with temperature or with the natural spread of beta between devices, so a circuit that works on your bench fails in a customer's hot room. Every analog circuit, from the audio stage of a radio to the sensor interface on a microcontroller board, starts with correct DC biasing. Exams love biasing numericals because they test Ohm's law, KVL and transistor rules together.

What this lesson covers: The operating point or Q-point, the DC load line, the three classic bias circuits, fixed bias, emitter-stabilised bias and voltage-divider bias, worked numericals for each, what happens when beta or temperature changes, the idea of a stability factor, thermal runaway, and a quick look at collector-feedback bias. We use silicon transistors with VBE = 0.7 V throughout.

The Q-point: Q stands for quiescent, which means quiet. The Q-point is the DC collector current ICQ and collector-emitter voltage VCEQ when no signal is applied. On the CE output curves of lesson 13 it is one dot. For a linear amplifier we usually want it in the middle of the active region, so the signal has equal room to swing both ways. For a switch we want the transistor to jump between cut-off and saturation instead, which is lesson 15.

The DC load line: In a CE circuit with supply VCC and collector resistor RC, KVL around the output gives VCE = VCC - IC x RC. This is a straight line on the IC vs VCE graph. Two easy points: when IC = 0, VCE = VCC (cut-off end); when VCE = 0, IC = VCC / RC (saturation end). Example: VCC = 12 V, RC = 2.2 kilo-ohms gives the points (12 V, 0) and (0, 5.45 mA). The transistor must sit somewhere on this line, and the base current decides where: the Q-point is where the line crosses the curve for the actual IB.

Fixed bias: The simplest circuit. A resistor RB goes from VCC to the base, RC goes from VCC to the collector, and the emitter goes straight to ground. KVL around the base loop: VCC = IB x RB + VBE, so IB = (VCC - 0.7) / RB. Then IC = beta x IB and VCE = VCC - IC x RC. It is called fixed bias because IB is fixed by RB and VCC alone.

Fixed bias worked example: VCC = 12 V, RB = 470 kilo-ohms, RC = 2.2 kilo-ohms, beta = 100. IB = (12 - 0.7) / 470k = 24.0 microamps. IC = 100 x 24.0 microamps = 2.40 mA. VCE = 12 - 2.40 x 2.2 = 12 - 5.29 = 6.71 V. That is a nice Q-point near the middle of the 0 to 12 V range. Always check: is VCE more than about 0.2 V? Yes, so the transistor really is in the active region.

The problem with fixed bias: Now replace the transistor with another of the same part number but beta = 200, which is very common. IB is still 24.0 microamps, so IC = 4.81 mA and VCE = 12 - 4.81 x 2.2 = 1.42 V. The Q-point has slid almost into saturation. Any decent signal will now clip. The circuit is completely at the mercy of beta. Temperature makes it worse: beta rises with temperature, and so does leakage current. Fixed bias is easy to analyse but is rarely used in serious amplifiers.

Emitter-stabilised bias: Add a resistor RE between the emitter and ground. Now the base loop is VCC = IB x RB + VBE + IE x RE, and with IE = (beta + 1) x IB we get IB = (VCC - 0.7) / (RB + (beta + 1) x RE). Notice the trick: RE appears to the base as (beta + 1) times bigger. If beta increases, this term grows, which holds IB down, which partly cancels the increase in IC. That is negative feedback in action: if IC tries to rise, VE rises, VBE across the junction shrinks, and IB falls.

Emitter-stabilised worked example: VCC = 12 V, RB = 430 kilo-ohms, RC = 2 kilo-ohms, RE = 1 kilo-ohm. With beta = 100: IB = 11.3 / (430k + 101k) = 21.3 microamps, IC = 2.13 mA, VCE is about 12 - 2.13 x (2 + 1) = 5.61 V. With beta = 200: IB = 11.3 / (430k + 201k) = 17.9 microamps, IC = 3.58 mA. Doubling beta raised IC by about 68 percent, better than the 100 percent of fixed bias but still not great. To do better we need RE much larger compared to RB / beta, which leads to the next circuit.

Voltage-divider bias: This is the workhorse of discrete amplifiers. Two resistors R1 (top, from VCC) and R2 (bottom, to ground) form a voltage divider that sets the base voltage, plus RC and RE as before. If the divider current is much bigger than the base current, the base voltage is almost fixed by the divider and does not care about beta. Approximate method: VB = VCC x R2 / (R1 + R2), VE = VB - 0.7, IE = VE / RE, IC is about IE, VCE = VCC - IC x (RC + RE). The rule for the approximation to hold: beta x RE should be at least 10 x R2.

Voltage-divider worked example: VCC = 12 V, R1 = 22 kilo-ohms, R2 = 4.7 kilo-ohms, RC = 2.2 kilo-ohms, RE = 1 kilo-ohm, beta = 100. Check the rule: beta x RE = 100 kilo-ohms, 10 x R2 = 47 kilo-ohms, so it is fine. VB = 12 x 4.7 / 26.7 = 2.11 V. VE = 1.41 V. IE = 1.41 mA, so IC is about 1.41 mA. VCE = 12 - 1.41 x 3.2 = 7.49 V. Beta never appeared in the calculation at all.

The exact method and beta change: For more accuracy, replace the divider with its Thevenin equivalent: VTH = 2.11 V and RTH = R1 parallel R2 = 22 x 4.7 / 26.7 = 3.87 kilo-ohms. Then IB = (VTH - 0.7) / (RTH + (beta + 1) x RE). With beta = 100: IB = 1.41 / (3.87k + 101k) = 13.5 microamps, IC = 1.35 mA. With beta = 200: IB = 1.41 / (3.87k + 201k) = 6.9 microamps, IC = 1.38 mA. Doubling beta changed IC by only about 2 percent. That is why voltage-divider bias is the favourite.

Stability factor: Engineers measure how sensitive a bias circuit is using stability factors. The best known is S = change in IC / change in ICO (the leakage current). For fixed bias, S = beta + 1, which might be 101, very bad. For voltage-divider bias, S is approximately 1 + RTH / RE when beta is large, for our example 1 + 3.87 / 1 = 4.9, much better. A smaller S means a more stable Q-point. Similar factors exist for changes in VBE and beta. You do not need to derive all of them in a first course, but you should know smaller is better and that RE is the hero.

Thermal runaway: Here is the danger loop. A transistor heats up because of power VCE x IC. Heat increases leakage and beta and lowers VBE, so IC rises. More IC means more heat. If nothing stops it, IC keeps climbing until the transistor burns. This is thermal runaway, and it mainly threatens power transistors. The cure is the same negative feedback: an emitter resistor, a good bias design, and a heat sink to carry heat away. VBE drops about 2 mV for every 1 degree Celsius rise, a number worth remembering.

Collector-feedback bias: Another neat circuit connects RB from the collector to the base instead of from VCC. If IC rises, the collector voltage falls, so less current flows through RB into the base, which pulls IC back down. It is self-correcting and uses few parts. The equation is IB = (VCC - 0.7) / (RB + beta x RC) approximately, so beta x RC acts like the beta x RE term in emitter bias.

Real-life example 1, a phone charger's status LED driver and a radio stage: Inside an old transistor radio, the kind still sold in village haats, each amplifier stage uses voltage-divider bias. Repair technicians measure the DC voltages at base, emitter and collector with a multimeter and compare them with the expected ones. If VB is about 2 V, VE about 1.4 V, and VC around 7 V, the stage is healthy. If VE is 0 V, the transistor or RE path is open. If VC is almost equal to VE, the transistor is saturated or shorted. Biasing knowledge is literally a fault-finding tool.

Real-life example 2, the summer test: Imagine a small amplifier designed in an air-conditioned lab in Dhaka at 25 degrees C, then installed in a tin-roofed shop in Rajshahi where the box reaches 50 degrees C in May. With fixed bias, beta and leakage rise, the Q-point slides toward saturation and the music becomes harsh, or the output transistor overheats. With voltage-divider bias and an emitter resistor, IC barely changes and the shopkeeper keeps listening to the cricket commentary. This is why product designers test circuits at high temperature.

Common mistakes: Forgetting to check that the transistor is actually in the active region after finding IC. If your VCE comes out negative or below 0.2 V, the transistor is saturated and IC = beta x IB is wrong; then IC is limited to about (VCC - 0.2) / (RC + RE). Another mistake is using IE = IC + IB but then forgetting that RE carries IE, not IC. Students also mix up R1 and R2 in the divider formula. Finally, many forget to verify the beta x RE >= 10 x R2 rule before using the approximate method.

What exams ask: Draw and analyse fixed, emitter-stabilised and voltage-divider bias circuits, finding IB, IC and VCE. Draw the DC load line and mark the Q-point. Show what happens to the Q-point when beta doubles. Explain thermal runaway and how to prevent it. Define stability factor S and compare it for the different circuits. Design problems: choose R1, R2, RC and RE for a given ICQ and VCEQ.

Recap: Biasing parks the transistor at a Q-point on the DC load line VCE = VCC - IC x RC. Fixed bias is simple but depends on beta. Emitter-stabilised bias adds RE for negative feedback. Voltage-divider bias makes IC almost independent of beta and is the standard choice. RE fights thermal runaway. Next lesson, we push the transistor to the two ends of the load line and use it as a switch.
key_points: The Q-point (ICQ, VCEQ) is the resting DC point; for amplifiers keep it mid active region.
DC load line: VCE = VCC - IC x RC, from (VCC, 0) to (0, VCC / RC).
Fixed bias: IB = (VCC - 0.7) / RB; IC depends directly on beta, so unstable.
Emitter-stabilised: IB = (VCC - 0.7) / (RB + (beta + 1) RE); RE gives negative feedback.
Voltage-divider bias: VB = VCC R2 / (R1 + R2), IE = (VB - 0.7) / RE; nearly beta-independent if beta RE >= 10 R2.
Stability factor S: smaller is better; fixed bias S = beta + 1.
Thermal runaway: heat raises IC which raises heat; RE and heat sinks prevent it.
lessons.tip: After every bias numerical, write VCE on the side and ask: is it between 0.2 V and VCC? If not, the transistor is not in the active region and your answer must be redone with saturation or cut-off.
lessons.task: Using the voltage-divider example values (12 V, 22k, 4.7k, 2.2k, 1k), recalculate IC and VCE if RE is changed to 470 ohms. Then check whether the transistor is still in the active region.

quiz.q: In a fixed-bias circuit with VCC = 10 V, RB = 465 kilo-ohms, beta = 100, IC is about...
quiz.explain: IB = (10 - 0.7) / 465k = 20 microamps; IC = 100 x 20 microamps = 2 mA.

quiz.q: Which bias circuit makes IC almost independent of beta?
quiz.explain: With beta RE >= 10 R2, the divider sets VB and RE sets IE, so beta hardly matters.

quiz.q: For VCC = 12 V and RC = 3 kilo-ohms, the saturation end of the DC load line is at IC =
quiz.explain: IC(sat) = VCC / RC = 12 / 3k = 4 mA.

quiz.q: A voltage divider gives VB = 2.7 V and RE = 1 kilo-ohm. What is IE (approximate method)?
Thermal runaway is best prevented by...
options: an emitter resistor and a heat sink
quiz.explain: RE gives negative feedback and a heat sink removes heat, breaking the runaway loop.

lessons.title: The BJT as a Switch
lessons.content:
Think of the light switch on your bedroom wall. It has only two jobs: fully on or fully off. Nobody wants it half-on, because then it would get hot and the bulb would flicker. Now imagine a switch that you can flip a million times a second, with no moving parts, using a tiny current from a microcontroller pin. That is a transistor used as a switch. In the last two lessons we kept the transistor in the middle of the active region for amplifying. Here we do the opposite: we push it all the way to one end or the other.

Why this matters for CSE students: Every time you write digitalWrite(13, HIGH) on an Arduino or toggle a GPIO pin on a Raspberry Pi or ESP32, the pin can only supply a small current, typically a few milliamps up to about 20 mA, at 3.3 V or 5 V. But real things like relays, motors, buzzers, LED strips and solenoid door locks need more current or a higher voltage. A transistor switch is the bridge between your code and the physical world. And deep down, logic gates inside chips are just transistor switches arranged cleverly, which is how computing started.

What this lesson covers: The two switch states, cut-off and saturation, and why the in-between active region is avoided; how to design the base resistor so the transistor saturates with a safety margin (overdrive and forced beta); worked designs for driving an LED, a relay and a motor; why a flyback diode is needed for inductive loads; switching times and storage time; power loss in a switch; and the simple BJT logic inverter that started digital electronics.

The two states: When the input is low (0 V), the base-emitter junction is not forward biased, IB = 0, so IC is only a tiny leakage current. The transistor is in cut-off, acting like an open switch, and VCE is almost equal to VCC. When the input is high enough, we push so much base current that the transistor goes into saturation. Then VCE drops to VCE(sat), about 0.1 to 0.3 V, and the transistor acts like a closed switch. The load gets almost the full supply voltage.

Why avoid the active region in a switch: In the active region, both VCE and IC are large at the same time, so the power wasted in the transistor, P = VCE x IC, is large. Example: VCC = 12 V, load current 0.5 A. Fully off: IC is about 0, so P is about 0. Fully on: VCE(sat) = 0.2 V, so P = 0.2 x 0.5 = 0.1 W, small. Half way, VCE = 6 V and IC = 0.25 A, so P = 1.5 W, fifteen times more heat. A good switch spends as little time as possible in the middle.

The saturation condition: In the active region IC = beta x IB. But the outside circuit limits how big IC can be: the maximum is IC(sat) = (VCC - VCE(sat)) / RC. If beta x IB is larger than IC(sat), the transistor cannot give that much current, so it saturates. The condition for saturation is IB > IC(sat) / beta(min). We use the minimum beta from the datasheet, because the actual transistor might be a weak one.

Overdrive and forced beta: Designers do not just meet the condition, they exceed it, usually by a factor of 2 to 10, to be safe against low beta, temperature and part spread. This is called overdriving the base. When saturated, the ratio IC / IB is called the forced beta, and it is much smaller than the normal beta. A common rule of thumb is to design for a forced beta of about 10 to 20. Example: a load needs IC = 50 mA; take forced beta = 10, so IB = 5 mA.

Worked design 1, LED from a 3.3 V GPIO: You want to light a red LED (2 V) at 20 mA from a 5 V supply, controlled by a 3.3 V ESP32 pin, using a BC547 (minimum beta about 110, but let us use 100). Collector side: RC = (5 - 2 - 0.2) / 0.020 = 140 ohms, choose 150 ohms, giving about 18.7 mA. Base side: minimum IB = 18.7 / 100 = 0.19 mA; overdrive about 5 times to about 1 mA. RB = (3.3 - 0.7) / 1 mA = 2.6 kilo-ohms; choose 2.2 kilo-ohms, which gives IB = 1.18 mA. The GPIO only supplies about 1.2 mA but the LED gets about 19 mA. Forced beta is about 16.

Worked design 2, a relay: A 12 V relay coil has a resistance of 400 ohms, so it needs 12 / 400 = 30 mA (ignoring VCE(sat)). An Arduino Uno pin gives 5 V. Using a 2N2222 with minimum beta 100: minimum IB = 0.3 mA, overdrive to 1.5 mA. RB = (5 - 0.7) / 1.5 mA = 2.87 kilo-ohms; use 2.7 kilo-ohms. The relay contacts can then switch a 220 V fan or pump, completely separate from the low-voltage circuit. That is how a home automation project turns on the water pump of a Dhaka building's roof tank.

The flyback diode: A relay coil or motor is an inductor. An inductor hates sudden changes in current, V = L x di/dt. When the transistor switches off, the current tries to drop to zero in microseconds, so di/dt is huge and the coil generates a big voltage spike, often tens or even hundreds of volts, at the collector. This spike can destroy the transistor. The fix is a diode placed across the coil, reverse biased during normal operation (cathode to the positive supply). When the transistor turns off, the coil's current circulates through the diode and dies away safely. Every relay or motor driver needs one; a 1N4007 or 1N4148 is common.

Worked design 3, a small DC motor: A toy DC motor might draw 300 mA at 6 V, and up to around 1 A when starting. A small BC547 (100 mA maximum) is too weak. Options: a medium power transistor like the 2N2222 (600 mA) for small motors, or a Darlington like the TIP120, which is two transistors in one package with a total beta of 1000 or more, so a few milliamps from a GPIO can switch an amp or more. The catch: a Darlington's VCE(sat) is larger, around 1 V or more, so it wastes more heat. For bigger motors, MOSFETs (lesson 19) are usually better. Do not forget the flyback diode.

PWM, switching fast to control speed: Instead of a half-on transistor for half speed, we switch the motor fully on and fully off very quickly, say 1000 times a second. If it is on 30 percent of the time, the motor sees about 30 percent of the average voltage. This is pulse width modulation (PWM). Arduino's analogWrite() does exactly this. The transistor stays efficient because it is always either cut-off or saturated. Ceiling fan regulators and LED dimmers use the same trick with other devices.

Switching times: A real transistor does not switch instantly. When you apply the input pulse, there is a delay time td before IC starts rising, then a rise time tr while IC goes from 10 to 90 percent. When you remove the input, there is a storage time ts, then a fall time tf. Turn-on time is td + tr and turn-off time is ts + tf. For a small switching transistor these are tens to hundreds of nanoseconds. Storage time is usually the biggest piece.

Why storage time happens: In deep saturation, the base is flooded with extra minority carriers, more than needed to carry IC. When you switch off, these extra carriers must be removed first, and until then the transistor stays on. More overdrive means more stored charge and longer storage time. Tricks to speed it up: do not overdrive too much, add a small speed-up capacitor across RB, or put a Schottky diode between base and collector to stop the transistor from going deep into saturation. That last trick gave us the Schottky TTL logic family (74LS series).

The BJT logic inverter: Connect the input to the base through RB, and take the output from the collector with RC to VCC = 5 V. Input low (0 V): transistor cut-off, output close to 5 V, logic 1. Input high (5 V): transistor saturated, output about 0.2 V, logic 0. Output is the opposite of input: a NOT gate. This is resistor-transistor logic (RTL), used in early computers including the Apollo Guidance Computer, which flew to the Moon using thousands of RTL NOR gates. Put two transistors in parallel with the same RC, and either input high pulls the output low, giving a NOR gate.

Power in the switch: The heat in a saturated transistor is about VCE(sat) x IC + VBE x IB. For our LED example, 0.2 V x 18.7 mA = 3.7 mW plus 0.7 V x 1.18 mA = 0.8 mW, total under 5 mW, nothing at all. For a 2 A load with VCE(sat) = 0.5 V, it is 1 W, and you need a small heat sink. There is also switching loss every time it passes through the active region, which grows with switching frequency.

Real-life example 1, a smart switch board: Many Bangladeshi students build an ESP32 project to control home lights and the water pump from a phone app. The ESP32 pin gives 3.3 V and around 10 to 20 mA at most. The circuit uses a relay module: inside you will find an npn transistor with a base resistor, a flyback diode across the relay coil, and often an optocoupler (lesson 11) for isolation. When you tap the button on your phone, Wi-Fi delivers a message, your code sets the pin high, the transistor saturates, the relay clicks, and the pump starts filling the tank.

Real-life example 2, the electronic buzzer at a shop counter: Supershops and pharmacies use barcode scanners and cash drawers that beep and pop open. The buzzer and the drawer's solenoid are driven by transistor switches from a small controller. The solenoid is an inductor, so a flyback diode sits across it. Without it, the cash drawer circuit would fail within days because of the voltage spikes each time the drawer opens.

Common mistakes: Forgetting the base resistor and connecting the GPIO directly to the base, which can burn both the pin and the transistor because the base-emitter junction is a diode. Using the typical beta instead of the minimum beta. Forgetting the flyback diode on relays and motors. Thinking a saturated transistor has zero VCE; it is about 0.2 V. Expecting IC = beta x IB in saturation; it is not, the load sets IC.

What exams ask: Explain the transistor as a switch with the help of the output characteristics and load line, marking the cut-off and saturation points. Design RB to saturate a transistor for a given load. Define forced beta. Explain switching times and the cause of storage time. Draw an RTL inverter or NOR gate and explain its truth table. Explain the need for a freewheeling (flyback) diode.

Recap: A transistor switch lives at the two ends of the load line: cut-off (off, VCE about VCC) and saturation (on, VCE about 0.2 V). Saturate it by giving IB > IC(sat) / beta(min), overdriven by 2 to 10 times. Always use a base resistor and a flyback diode for inductive loads. PWM gives speed or brightness control while staying efficient. Storage time limits speed. The BJT inverter is the ancestor of all digital logic. Next, we go back to the active region and build small-signal amplifiers.
key_points: Switch states: cut-off (open, VCE about VCC) and saturation (closed, VCE(sat) about 0.1-0.3 V).
Saturation condition: IB > IC(sat) / beta(min), with IC(sat) = (VCC - VCE(sat)) / RC.
Overdrive 2-10 times; forced beta IC / IB in saturation is about 10-20 by design.
Always use a base resistor; never wire a GPIO pin directly to the base.
Inductive loads (relays, motors) need a flyback diode across them.
Darlington pairs give huge beta but higher VCE(sat).
Switching times: td, tr, ts, tf; storage time comes from excess base charge in saturation.
A single BJT with RB and RC makes a NOT gate (RTL); parallel transistors make NOR.
lessons.tip: For every switch design, write three lines: IC needed, IB needed with overdrive, RB value. Then add one more line: is the load inductive? If yes, draw the flyback diode right away.
lessons.task: Design a switch for a 5 V buzzer that needs 25 mA, driven by a 3.3 V pin, using beta(min) = 100 and an overdrive of 5. Find IB and RB, then pick the nearest standard resistor (1k, 1.2k, 1.5k, 1.8k, 2.2k, 2.7k, 3.3k).

quiz.q: A transistor used as a switch should spend most of its time in...
quiz.explain: Off (cut-off) or on (saturation) wastes the least power.

quiz.q: IC(sat) = 40 mA and beta(min) = 80. The minimum base current to saturate is...
quiz.explain: IB(min) = 40 mA / 80 = 0.5 mA; in practice overdrive above this.

quiz.q: Why is a diode placed across a relay coil?
options: To make the relay faster to switch on
To light up when the relay is on
To absorb the voltage spike when the transistor turns off
quiz.explain: The coil's inductance creates a big spike when current stops; the diode gives the current a safe path.

quiz.q: In a saturated BJT switch, IC / IB is called...
quiz.explain: In saturation IC is set by the load, so IC / IB is the forced beta, smaller than normal beta.

quiz.q: Which part of the turn-off time is caused by excess charge stored in the base?
quiz.explain: Extra minority carriers from deep saturation must be removed first: that is storage time ts.

lessons.title: BJT Small-Signal Amplifiers
lessons.content:
Imagine standing on a jetty at Cox's Bazar. The sea has a big, slow tide that sets the average water level, and on top of it small waves ripple up and down. If you only cared about the waves, you could measure from the tide level and ignore the rest. Transistor amplifiers work the same way. The DC bias from lesson 14 is the tide, a steady level. The music or sensor signal is the small wave riding on top. Small-signal analysis means looking only at the waves, assuming they are small enough that the transistor behaves almost like a straight line around its Q-point.

Why this matters: Microphones give a few millivolts, guitar pickups maybe 100 mV, antennas microvolts, and medical sensors like ECG electrodes about 1 mV. None of these can drive a speaker, an ADC or a long cable directly. A small-signal amplifier makes them bigger without changing their shape. Learning to calculate gain and impedance is the core skill of analog electronics, and these same models are used for MOSFETs (lesson 19), op-amp internals (lesson 23) and frequency response (lesson 21).

What this lesson covers: The idea of separating DC and AC analysis; the AC emitter resistance re = 26 mV / IE; the re model and the related hybrid-pi model with transconductance gm; the common-emitter amplifier with a bypassed emitter resistor, its voltage gain, input impedance and output impedance; what happens if RE is not bypassed; the effect of a load; and the job of coupling and bypass capacitors. We will use one worked circuit throughout, the voltage-divider circuit from lesson 14.

Splitting DC and AC: Every quantity in an amplifier is a DC value plus a small AC change, for example iC(total) = IC + ic. We analyse them separately and add the results (superposition, which works because we stay in a small, almost linear region). For DC analysis: capacitors are open circuits, and we find the Q-point exactly as in lesson 14. For AC analysis: capacitors are short circuits (they are chosen large enough), DC supplies are shorted to ground (an ideal supply has no AC voltage on it), and the transistor is replaced by its small-signal model.

The AC emitter resistance re: The base-emitter junction is a diode, and from lesson 6 a diode's small-signal resistance is rd = VT / I, where VT is the thermal voltage, about 26 mV at room temperature. For the transistor this is called re = 26 mV / IE. Example: IE = 1 mA gives re = 26 ohms; IE = 2 mA gives 13 ohms. Notice re is set by the DC bias: change the Q-point and the AC behaviour changes. This is the bridge between lesson 14 and this one.

The re model: For a common-emitter amplifier, the transistor looks like this from the AC point of view. Looking into the base, you see a resistance of beta x re (because base current is beta times smaller than emitter current, the emitter's re looks beta times bigger from the base). At the collector, there is a current source of value beta x ib (or about ic), pointing from collector to emitter. Optionally, there is a large output resistance ro = VA / IC in parallel with the source, from the Early effect of lesson 13.

The hybrid-pi model: Another way to say the same thing uses transconductance gm = IC / VT. It tells you how many milliamps of collector current change you get for each volt of base-emitter change. With IC = 1.41 mA, gm = 1.41 / 26 mV = 54 mA per volt (54 mS). The base input resistance is r-pi = beta / gm, here 100 / 0.054 = 1.85 kilo-ohms, which is the same as beta x re. The collector current source is gm x v-be. Both models give the same answers; textbooks like Boylestad prefer re, Sedra and Smith prefer hybrid-pi. Older books also use h-parameters, where hie is about beta x re and hfe is about beta.

Our worked CE circuit: VCC = 12 V, R1 = 22 kilo-ohms, R2 = 4.7 kilo-ohms, RC = 2.2 kilo-ohms, RE = 1 kilo-ohm, beta = 100. From lesson 14, IE is about 1.41 mA. Input signal comes in through a coupling capacitor C1 to the base. Output is taken from the collector through a coupling capacitor C2. RE has a bypass capacitor CE across it. First, re = 26 mV / 1.41 mA = 18.4 ohms.

Voltage gain with RE bypassed: For AC, the bypass capacitor shorts RE, so the emitter is at AC ground. The base AC voltage vi appears across re, so ie = vi / re. Nearly all of this current flows in the collector, through RC, making vo = -ic x RC. So Av = vo / vi = -RC / re. Here Av = -2200 / 18.4 = -120. The minus sign is the 180 degree phase inversion of the CE. A 10 mV input becomes a 1.2 V output, upside down. Using hybrid-pi: Av = -gm x RC = -0.054 x 2200 = -119, the same.

Input impedance: The signal source sees R1, R2 and the transistor's base resistance all in parallel (R1 and R2 go to ground for AC since VCC is AC ground). Zi = R1 parallel R2 parallel beta x re. R1 parallel R2 = 3.87 kilo-ohms. Beta x re = 100 x 18.4 = 1.84 kilo-ohms. So Zi = 3.87k parallel 1.84k = about 1.25 kilo-ohms. Medium input impedance, as lesson 13 promised for CE.

Output impedance: Looking back into the collector with the input source turned off, ib = 0, so the current source is zero and open. You see only RC (in parallel with ro, if included). So Zo is about RC = 2.2 kilo-ohms. If ro = 50 kilo-ohms were included, Zo = 2.2k parallel 50k = 2.1 kilo-ohms, so ignoring ro is fine when ro is at least about 10 times RC.

Adding a load: Connect a 10 kilo-ohm load RL through C2. Now the collector current flows into RC parallel RL = 2.2k parallel 10k = 1.80 kilo-ohms. The loaded gain becomes Av = -1800 / 18.4 = -98. The load stole some gain. Also, if the signal source has its own resistance Rs, only part of its voltage reaches the base: vi = vs x Zi / (Zi + Rs). With Rs = 600 ohms, vi = vs x 1250 / 1850 = 0.68 vs, so the overall gain from vs is about 0.68 x 98 = 66. This is why we care so much about impedances: they divide your signal at every connection.

Unbypassed RE, trading gain for stability: Remove the bypass capacitor. Now RE is in the AC emitter path, and Av = -RC / (re + RE) = -2200 / (18.4 + 1000) = -2.16. Much less gain! But look at the benefits. The gain now depends mostly on resistor values, not on re (which changes with temperature and bias), so it is stable and predictable. The input resistance looking into the base rises to beta x (re + RE), about 102 kilo-ohms. And distortion goes down. This is local negative feedback, and lesson 22 explains why it is so valuable. A common compromise is to split RE into two parts, say 100 ohms unbypassed and 900 ohms bypassed, giving Av about -2200 / 118 = -19.

Coupling capacitors: C1 and C2 let AC signal pass but block DC. Without C1, the signal source would be connected directly to the base and could upset the carefully set bias. Without C2, the DC collector voltage (about 7.5 V here) would be pushed into the load. Each coupling capacitor and the resistance it sees form a high-pass filter with cutoff f = 1 / (2 x pi x R x C). For C1 = 10 microfarads and Zi = 1.25 kilo-ohms, f = 1 / (2 x 3.14 x 1250 x 0.00001) = about 12.7 Hz, below the lowest note humans can hear, so fine for audio.

Bypass capacitor: CE must look like a short circuit compared to the small resistance seen at the emitter, which is roughly re plus (Rs parallel R1 parallel R2) / beta, only a few tens of ohms. That is why bypass capacitors are big, often 47 to 220 microfarads, and usually decide the low-frequency cutoff of the amplifier. Lesson 21 will turn these ideas into a proper frequency response.

Common-collector and common-base small-signal results: For completeness, the same re model gives the other two configurations quickly. Emitter follower: Av = RE / (RE + re), close to 1; Zi = beta x (re + RE), high; Zo about re, low (plus a small term from the source resistance). Common base: Av = RC / re, high and non-inverting; Zi about re, very low; Zo about RC. These match the comparison table of lesson 13, now with numbers.

Real-life example 1, a microphone preamp for a waz mahfil sound system: At a village event, the microphone produces maybe 5 mV. The mixer's first stage is a small-signal amplifier, often a CE stage like ours. With a gain of about 100, the 5 mV becomes 0.5 V, enough for the power amplifier that drives the horn speakers. Designers bias the stage carefully so that loud shouts do not clip, and they use coupling capacitors so the microphone's DC level does not matter. If the bypass capacitor dries out after years in the heat, the gain drops a lot and the technician complains that the mic sounds weak, a classic fault.

Real-life example 2, an FM radio front end: An FM signal at around 88 to 108 MHz arrives at the antenna as microvolts. The first transistor stage, a small-signal amplifier often in common-base or common-emitter, lifts it before the mixer. Here the capacitors are tiny, picofarads, because at 100 MHz even a small capacitor has low reactance. Same ideas, very different numbers: re, gm and impedances still decide the gain.

Common mistakes: Using RE instead of re in the gain formula when RE is bypassed, or forgetting to include RE when it is not bypassed. Forgetting the minus sign for CE. Calculating re from IC in the wrong units (26 mV divided by milliamps gives ohms). Forgetting R1 parallel R2 in Zi. Ignoring the load and source resistances, then wondering why measured gain is lower than calculated. And mixing DC and AC rules: capacitors are open for DC, short for AC.

What exams ask: Draw the AC equivalent circuit of a voltage-divider CE amplifier using the re model. Find re, Zi, Zo and Av, with and without the bypass capacitor and with a load. Explain the role of coupling and bypass capacitors. Derive Av = -RC / re. Compare re and hybrid-pi models and show gm x r-pi = beta. Explain why an unbypassed RE stabilises gain.

Recap: Separate DC (capacitors open) and AC (capacitors and supplies shorted). re = 26 mV / IE links the Q-point to AC behaviour. For a bypassed CE amplifier, Av = -RC / re, Zi = R1 parallel R2 parallel beta re, Zo about RC. Loads and source resistance reduce overall gain. An unbypassed RE cuts gain to about -RC / RE but makes it stable. Coupling capacitors block DC; bypass capacitors restore gain. Next, we meet the FET family, starting with the JFET.
key_points: Small-signal analysis: DC with capacitors open, AC with capacitors and DC supplies shorted.
re = 26 mV / IE; beta x re is the AC resistance looking into the base.
Hybrid-pi: gm = IC / VT, r-pi = beta / gm (same as beta x re).
Bypassed CE: Av = -RC / re (inverted); Zi = R1 || R2 || beta re; Zo about RC.
Load: replace RC with RC || RL; source resistance divides vs with Zi.
Unbypassed RE: Av about -RC / (re + RE); lower but stable gain, higher Zi.
Coupling capacitors block DC; bypass capacitor shorts RE for AC; each sets a low-frequency cutoff.
lessons.tip: Draw two separate pictures for every amplifier: the DC circuit (capacitors removed) and the AC circuit (capacitors and VCC replaced by wires to ground). Never solve both on one drawing; most mistakes start there.
lessons.task: Redo the worked CE example with IE = 2 mA instead of 1.41 mA (keep RC = 2.2k, beta = 100, R1 || R2 = 3.87k). Find re, Av with RE bypassed, and Zi.

quiz.q: At IE = 2.6 mA, re is about...
quiz.explain: re = 26 mV / 2.6 mA = 10 ohms.

quiz.q: A bypassed CE amplifier has RC = 3 kilo-ohms and re = 15 ohms. Av is about...
For AC analysis, coupling capacitors and the DC supply are treated as...
quiz.explain: Capacitors are chosen large so they are AC shorts; an ideal DC supply has no AC voltage, so it is AC ground.

quiz.q: Removing the emitter bypass capacitor in a CE amplifier...
options: lowers the gain but makes it more stable
quiz.explain: Gain becomes about -RC / (re + RE): smaller but set by resistors, with higher input resistance.

quiz.q: With beta = 100 and re = 20 ohms, the AC resistance looking into the base (RE bypassed) is...
quiz.explain: beta x re = 100 x 20 = 2000 ohms.

lessons.title: Field-Effect Transistors and the JFET
lessons.content:
Think of a garden hose. Water flows from the tap to the end. If you step on the hose, the pipe gets narrower and less water comes out. Step harder and the flow stops completely. You never touch the water itself; you just squeeze the path from outside. A field-effect transistor does exactly this to electric current. A voltage on a terminal called the gate squeezes a conducting channel from the side, using an electric field, and controls how much current flows through it. Almost no current goes into the gate, just as your foot does not add any water to the hose.

Why FETs matter: The BJT is current-controlled; it needs base current. A FET is voltage-controlled; its gate takes almost zero current. That one difference changed electronics. It means very high input impedance, easy to drive, and very low power when idle. The MOSFET, a member of the FET family, is the device inside every modern processor, memory chip and phone; a single phone chip today holds billions of them. Before we get to MOSFETs in the next lesson, the JFET is the simplest FET to understand, and its equations are the same shape as the MOSFET ones you will use later.

What this lesson covers: The FET family tree; the structure of n-channel and p-channel JFETs and their symbols; how the gate voltage and the drain voltage shape the channel, including pinch-off; the drain characteristics and transfer characteristic; Shockley's equation ID = IDSS (1 - VGS / VP) squared with worked numbers; self-bias of a JFET; transconductance gm; the JFET as a voltage-controlled resistor; and a clear FET versus BJT comparison.

The FET family tree: FETs split into two big branches. The JFET (junction FET) uses a reverse-biased PN junction to control the channel. The MOSFET (metal-oxide-semiconductor FET) uses a thin insulating oxide layer between gate and channel; it comes in depletion and enhancement types. Each type comes in n-channel and p-channel versions. All FETs are unipolar: current is carried by only one kind of carrier, electrons in n-channel and holes in p-channel. That is the opposite of the bipolar BJT.

JFET structure: Take a bar of n-type silicon. Connect one end to a terminal called the source (where carriers come from) and the other end to the drain (where they go). This bar is the channel. On both sides of the bar, diffuse heavily doped p-type regions, and connect them together to form the gate. Now there are PN junctions between gate and channel. In normal use these junctions are kept reverse biased, so the gate current is only a tiny leakage, often a nanoamp or less. For a p-channel JFET, everything is swapped: p-type channel, n-type gate.

The symbol: A JFET is drawn as a vertical line (the channel) with drain at top and source at bottom, and a gate line touching it from the side with an arrow. The arrow points from p to n, like a diode. In an n-channel JFET, the arrow points into the channel; in a p-channel JFET, it points out.

Effect of the gate voltage: For an n-channel JFET, we apply a negative VGS (gate more negative than source). This reverse biases the gate-channel junctions. A depletion region grows into the channel from both sides. Depletion regions have no free carriers, so the conducting part of the channel gets narrower, and its resistance rises. Make VGS more negative and the depletion regions grow until they meet in the middle. The channel is closed and ID becomes practically zero. The gate-source voltage at which this happens is called the pinch-off voltage VP, also written VGS(off). For a typical small JFET it might be -2 to -6 V.

Effect of the drain voltage, and pinch-off: Now set VGS = 0 and slowly raise VDS. At first the channel acts like a resistor, and ID rises in a straight line, this is the ohmic region. But the drain end of the channel is at a higher voltage than the source end, so the gate-channel junction is more reverse biased near the drain. The depletion regions are wider near the drain, making the channel wedge-shaped. When VDS reaches about |VP|, the channel almost closes at the drain end. This is pinch-off. Beyond it, extra VDS mostly drops across the tiny pinched region, and ID stays nearly constant. That constant current at VGS = 0 is called IDSS, the drain current with gate shorted to source, the maximum current the JFET normally carries.

Drain characteristics: Plot ID against VDS for several VGS values: 0, -1, -2, -3 V. You get a family of curves that looks a lot like the BJT's CE output curves. Each curve rises in the ohmic region and then flattens in the saturation (pinch-off) region. Higher curves are for VGS = 0, lower ones for more negative VGS. The boundary between ohmic and saturation is at VDS = VGS - VP. Example: VP = -4 V and VGS = -1 V gives a boundary at VDS = -1 - (-4) = 3 V. Far to the right, at large VDS, the junction breaks down; avoid that region. Careful with names: saturation in a FET means the flat part used for amplifying, the opposite of what saturation means in a BJT.

Shockley's equation: In the saturation region, the drain current depends on VGS by a square law: ID = IDSS x (1 - VGS / VP) squared. This is a parabola, called the transfer characteristic. Example: IDSS = 10 mA and VP = -4 V. At VGS = 0, ID = 10 mA. At VGS = -1 V, ID = 10 x (1 - 0.25) squared = 10 x 0.5625 = 5.6 mA. At VGS = -2 V, ID = 10 x 0.25 = 2.5 mA. At VGS = -3 V, ID = 10 x 0.0625 = 0.63 mA. At VGS = -4 V, ID = 0. A handy shortcut: at VGS = VP / 2, ID = IDSS / 4. Compare this with the BJT's exponential law; the JFET is gentler.

Biasing a JFET, self-bias: The simplest way to get a negative VGS without a negative supply is to put a resistor RS between source and ground and tie the gate to ground through a large resistor RG (say 1 mega-ohm). Since gate current is almost zero, VG = 0. The drain current flows through RS, so VS = ID x RS, and VGS = VG - VS = -ID x RS. The JFET biases itself. Then you solve this together with Shockley's equation.

Self-bias worked example: IDSS = 10 mA, VP = -4 V, RS = 1 kilo-ohm, VDD = 15 V, RD = 3 kilo-ohms. With ID in mA, VGS = -ID. Substitute: ID = 10 x (1 - ID / 4) squared. Expanding gives 0.625 ID squared - 6 ID + 10 = 0, so ID = (6 plus or minus square root of 11) / 1.25, giving 7.45 mA or 2.15 mA. The first would make VGS = -7.45 V, beyond pinch-off, which is impossible, so ID = 2.15 mA and VGS = -2.15 V. Then VDS = 15 - 2.15 x (3 + 1) = 6.4 V. Check saturation: VDS must be above VGS - VP = -2.15 + 4 = 1.85 V. Yes, 6.4 V is well above. You can also find this graphically: draw the parabola and the line VGS = -ID x RS, and the Q-point is where they cross.

Transconductance gm: For AC signals, the FET's gain is described by gm, the change in ID per volt change in VGS. Differentiating Shockley's equation gives gm = gm0 x (1 - VGS / VP), where gm0 = 2 x IDSS / |VP| is the value at VGS = 0. With IDSS = 10 mA and VP = -4 V, gm0 = 20 / 4 = 5 mS. At VGS = -2 V, gm = 5 x (1 - 0.5) = 2.5 mS. A common-source JFET amplifier with RD = 3 kilo-ohms then has a voltage gain of about -gm x RD = -2.5 mS x 3000 = -7.5. Typical BJT gm values at a few milliamps are tens of mS, so the BJT gives more gain for the same current, but the JFET wins on input impedance.

The JFET as a voltage-controlled resistor: In the ohmic region, at small VDS, the channel is just a resistor whose value depends on VGS. Near VGS = 0 it might be 100 ohms; near pinch-off, many kilo-ohms. This is useful in automatic gain control circuits, electronic volume controls and analog switches. The resistance rd is roughly r0 / (1 - VGS / VP) squared in a common approximation, where r0 is the resistance at VGS = 0.

Why the gate must stay reverse biased: If you make the gate of an n-channel JFET positive by more than about 0.5 V, the gate-channel junction becomes a forward-biased diode, gate current flows, and the high input impedance is lost. That is why n-channel JFETs work with VGS between VP and 0. This limit is one reason the MOSFET, whose gate is insulated by oxide, became more popular.

FET versus BJT: FET is voltage-controlled, BJT is current-controlled. FET input impedance is very high, often 10 to the power 9 ohms or more for a JFET and even higher for a MOSFET; a BJT's base is a few kilo-ohms. FET is unipolar; BJT is bipolar. FET follows a square law; BJT is exponential. BJTs usually give higher gain (higher gm) for the same current. FETs are usually quieter at high source impedances and have no thermal runaway in the same way, because at high currents their current falls as temperature rises. FETs are smaller and simpler to make in ICs, especially MOSFETs. BJTs are still strong in high-frequency analog and precision circuits.

Real-life example 1, the microphone in your earphones: The cheap electret microphones in many wired earphones, CCTV cameras and toys have a tiny JFET inside the capsule. The electret element produces a very small signal from a source with an extremely high impedance, which would be ruined by a normal amplifier input. The JFET, with its gate taking almost no current, acts as a buffer and converts this into a usable signal. That is why these microphones need a small bias voltage from the phone or laptop, often 2 to 5 V through a resistor. Next time you talk on a video call with cheap earphones, a JFET is helping your voice.

Real-life example 2, the multimeter and the guitar pedal: A good digital multimeter shows 10 mega-ohm input resistance on its voltage ranges so it does not disturb the circuit it measures. Many audio mixers and guitar effect pedals used at concerts in Dhaka use JFET-input op-amps like the TL072, prized for high input impedance and low noise with guitar pickups. Some classic distortion and boost pedals use discrete JFETs because their square-law behaviour gives a warm, tube-like sound.

Common mistakes: Forgetting that VGS for an n-channel JFET must be negative (between VP and 0). Choosing the wrong root of the quadratic in self-bias problems; always reject the one with |VGS| larger than |VP|. Mixing up FET saturation with BJT saturation. Forgetting to check VDS > VGS - VP before using Shockley's equation. And writing VP as positive for n-channel; it is negative for n-channel JFETs and positive for p-channel.

What exams ask: Draw and explain the structure and working of an n-channel JFET. Explain pinch-off with channel diagrams. Sketch drain and transfer characteristics. Use Shockley's equation to find ID for given VGS. Solve a self-bias problem by the quadratic or the graphical method. Derive gm and gm0. Compare FET and BJT in a table.

Recap: A FET controls current with an electric field from the gate, taking almost no gate current. In an n-channel JFET, a negative VGS widens the depletion regions and narrows the channel; at VGS = VP the channel is pinched off. In saturation, ID = IDSS (1 - VGS / VP) squared. Self-bias with RS gives VGS = -ID RS. gm = gm0 (1 - VGS / VP), with gm0 = 2 IDSS / |VP|. Next lesson, we meet the MOSFET, the FET that runs the digital world.
key_points: FETs are voltage-controlled, unipolar devices with very high input impedance.
JFET: channel between source and drain; reverse-biased gate junctions squeeze it.
Pinch-off voltage VP (VGS(off)): channel fully closed; IDSS is the current at VGS = 0.
Shockley: ID = IDSS (1 - VGS / VP)^2 in saturation; at VGS = VP/2, ID = IDSS/4.
Ohmic/saturation boundary at VDS = VGS - VP; FET saturation is the amplifying region.
Self-bias: VGS = -ID RS; reject the quadratic root beyond pinch-off.
gm = gm0 (1 - VGS / VP), gm0 = 2 IDSS / |VP|; CS gain about -gm RD.
lessons.tip: Memorise the shortcut points of the transfer curve: VGS = 0 gives IDSS, VGS = VP/2 gives IDSS/4, VGS = VP gives 0. With these three points you can sketch the parabola in seconds and check any calculation.
lessons.task: For a JFET with IDSS = 8 mA and VP = -4 V, calculate ID at VGS = 0, -1, -2, -3 and -4 V, and gm at VGS = -1 V. Plot ID against VGS on graph paper to see the parabola.

quiz.q: A JFET has IDSS = 12 mA and VP = -6 V. What is ID at VGS = -3 V?
For normal operation of an n-channel JFET, VGS is...
quiz.explain: The gate junction must stay reverse biased, so VGS is between VP (negative) and 0.

quiz.q: In a self-biased JFET, VGS equals...
quiz.explain: Gate is at 0 V and source at ID x RS, so VGS = -ID RS.

quiz.q: With IDSS = 10 mA and VP = -5 V, gm0 is...
quiz.explain: gm0 = 2 IDSS / |VP| = 20 mA / 5 V = 4 mS.

quiz.q: Which is a key advantage of a FET over a BJT?
options: Higher gain for the same current
quiz.explain: The gate draws almost no current, so input impedance is extremely high.

lessons.title: The MOSFET
lessons.content:
Picture a river with no bridge. People on one bank cannot cross. Now imagine a magic rope: when someone pulls it on the far side, a floating bridge of boats lines up across the river, and people stream over. Let go of the rope and the boats drift away. The rope never touches the people; it only makes the bridge appear. The MOSFET works like this. With no gate voltage, there is no path between source and drain. Apply enough voltage to the gate, and its electric field pulls electrons together into a thin bridge, called a channel, right under the gate. Current flows. Remove the voltage and the bridge disappears.

Why the MOSFET matters: It is the most manufactured device in human history. A modern phone processor has around 15 to 20 billion of them; your laptop's RAM has billions more. They also switch large currents in power supplies, electric vehicles, IPS inverters and motor drives. For a computer science student, the MOSFET is where software meets physics: every bit you store and every instruction your code runs is a pattern of MOSFETs turning on and off. Understanding its regions and equations prepares you for CMOS logic (lesson 20), computer architecture and VLSI design.

What this lesson covers: The MOS structure and why the gate is insulated; the enhancement-type n-channel MOSFET and how a channel is induced; threshold voltage; the three regions of operation, cut-off, triode (linear) and saturation, with their equations and worked numbers; channel-length modulation; the depletion-type MOSFET; p-channel MOSFETs; symbols; the body terminal; and handling precautions. Biasing and amplifiers come next lesson.

The MOS structure: MOS stands for metal-oxide-semiconductor, the three layers stacked at the gate. At the bottom is a lightly doped p-type silicon substrate, also called the body. On top is a very thin layer of insulating silicon dioxide, in old chips about 100 nanometres, in modern chips just a few nanometres or replaced by special high-k materials. On top of the oxide is the gate electrode, originally aluminium metal, later polysilicon, and in modern chips metal again. On either side of the gate, two heavily doped n+ regions form the source and the drain. Because the oxide is an insulator, the gate current is essentially zero at DC.

Inducing a channel: In an enhancement nMOS with VGS = 0, the source and drain are n+ islands in a p-type sea. Between them are two back-to-back PN junctions, so no current flows even if you apply VDS. Now apply a positive voltage on the gate. The gate and the substrate act like the two plates of a capacitor with the oxide in between. The positive gate pushes holes away from the surface, leaving a depletion region of negative ions. Increase VGS further and it starts to attract electrons, minority carriers in the p-type body, to the surface. When enough electrons gather, the surface right under the oxide behaves like n-type silicon. This thin layer is called the inversion layer, and it connects source to drain. A channel has been enhanced into existence, hence the name enhancement MOSFET.

Threshold voltage: The gate-source voltage at which a useful channel forms is called the threshold voltage Vt (or VTH). Below Vt the device is off; above it, more VGS means more electrons in the channel and more current. In modern logic transistors Vt is roughly 0.2 to 0.5 V. In discrete power MOSFETs it is higher; for example, the popular IRF540N has a VGS(th) of 2 to 4 V, which is why such MOSFETs may not turn fully on from a 3.3 V microcontroller pin, while logic-level MOSFETs are designed to. The excess VGS - Vt is called the overdrive voltage, often written VOV, and it appears in all the equations.

Region 1, cut-off: If VGS < Vt, there is no channel and ID is zero (apart from tiny leakage). The MOSFET is an open switch. Example: Vt = 1 V and VGS = 0.6 V gives ID about 0.

Region 2, triode (linear or ohmic): If VGS > Vt and VDS is small, specifically VDS < VGS - Vt, the channel stretches the whole way from source to drain and acts like a resistor controlled by VGS. The equation is ID = kn x [(VGS - Vt) x VDS - VDS squared / 2], where kn = k'n x (W / L) is the device parameter, k'n = mobility x oxide capacitance per area is set by the process, and W / L is the width-to-length ratio of the channel chosen by the designer. For very small VDS, the squared term is negligible and the MOSFET is a resistor rDS = 1 / (kn x (VGS - Vt)).

Triode worked example: Let kn = 2 mA per volt squared, Vt = 1 V, VGS = 3 V, so the overdrive is 2 V. For VDS = 0.5 V (less than 2 V, so triode): ID = 2 x [2 x 0.5 - 0.25 / 2] = 2 x [1 - 0.125] = 1.75 mA. For tiny VDS, rDS = 1 / (2 mA/V^2 x 2 V) = 250 ohms. Raise VGS to 5 V and rDS drops to 1 / (2 x 4) = 125 ohms. This is why, to switch a MOSFET fully on, we give the gate a generous voltage.

Region 3, saturation: As VDS rises, the voltage across the oxide near the drain is VGS - VDS. When this drops to Vt, the channel at the drain end vanishes; we say the channel is pinched off. This happens at VDS = VGS - Vt. Beyond this, extra VDS appears across the short pinched region, and ID stops increasing much. The equation becomes ID = (1/2) x kn x (VGS - Vt) squared. A square law again, just like the JFET.

Saturation worked example: Same device: kn = 2 mA/V^2, Vt = 1 V, VGS = 3 V. Saturation needs VDS >= 3 - 1 = 2 V. If VDS = 5 V, ID = 0.5 x 2 x (2) squared = 4 mA. If VGS rises to 4 V, ID = 0.5 x 2 x 9 = 9 mA. Notice the square law: overdrive went from 2 to 3 V (1.5 times), current went from 4 to 9 mA (2.25 times). At the boundary, the triode and saturation formulas give the same value; check: triode at VDS = 2 V gives 2 x [2 x 2 - 2] = 4 mA. They match.

The three-region test you will use always: First compare VGS with Vt: below means cut-off. If above, compare VDS with VGS - Vt: smaller means triode, equal or larger means saturation. In circuit problems you often assume saturation, solve, and then check this condition. If it fails, redo with the triode equation.

Channel-length modulation: In real MOSFETs, ID in saturation still rises slightly with VDS, because the pinch-off point moves toward the source, shortening the effective channel. We add a factor: ID = (1/2) kn (VGS - Vt) squared x (1 + lambda x VDS). Lambda is small, for example 0.02 per volt, and gets larger in very short-channel transistors. It plays the same role as the Early effect in BJTs and gives an output resistance ro, about 1 / (lambda x ID).

The depletion-type MOSFET: Here the manufacturer builds an n-type channel between source and drain during fabrication. So at VGS = 0, current already flows, the value is IDSS. A negative VGS repels electrons and shrinks the channel (depletion mode), until at VGS = VP the channel is gone. A positive VGS attracts more electrons and increases the current (enhancement mode), which a JFET cannot do safely, because the oxide blocks gate current. Its transfer curve follows the same Shockley equation as the JFET, extended to positive VGS. Depletion MOSFETs are less common today, used in some current sources and start-up circuits.

p-channel MOSFETs: Swap all the types: n-type body, p+ source and drain, and a channel made of holes. Everything flips: Vt is negative, for example -1 V, and the device turns on when VGS is more negative than Vt; current flows from source to drain. Holes have lower mobility than electrons, about two to three times lower in silicon, so a pMOS must be made wider to carry the same current as an nMOS. Remember this: it matters a lot when sizing CMOS gates in lesson 20.

Symbols and the body: A MOSFET symbol shows the gate as a separate line from the channel, a gap that represents the oxide. For an enhancement device, the channel line is drawn broken into three segments (no channel at rest); for a depletion device, it is solid. An arrow on the body terminal points in for n-channel and out for p-channel. MOSFETs actually have four terminals: gate, drain, source and body. In discrete parts the body is tied to the source. In ICs, all nMOS bodies share the p-substrate connected to the lowest voltage; when source and body are at different voltages, Vt shifts slightly, called the body effect.

Handle with care: The gate oxide is extremely thin, so a small static charge from your finger, often thousands of volts, can punch through it and destroy the MOSFET without any visible mark. That is why chips come in anti-static bags and labs ask you to touch grounded metal or wear a wrist strap. Modern ICs include protection diodes on their pins, but bare MOSFETs can still be damaged.

Real-life example 1, your phone's processor: Inside the chip in a mid-range phone sold in Bangladesh, there are billions of tiny enhancement MOSFETs, nMOS and pMOS, with channel lengths far smaller than a virus. When the chip runs your Facebook app, each MOSFET switches between cut-off and the triode region billions of times per second. The tiny gate capacitance must be charged and discharged each time, which is where most of the battery energy goes, a theme we return to in lesson 20. Process names like 5 nm or 3 nm are marketing labels for technology generations rather than one exact physical length, but the transistors really are only tens of atoms across in places.

Real-life example 2, the IPS during load shedding: When the grid goes off in the evening, the IPS in many homes and shops switches on. Inside, power MOSFETs like IRF3205 switch the 12 V battery current back and forth tens of thousands of times a second into a transformer to produce 220 V AC for fans and lights. When on, they sit in the triode region with very low resistance, just a few milliohms, so even at 50 amps the heat is manageable with a heat sink. Their gates take almost no DC current, so a small control chip can drive them, though fast switching needs gate drivers to charge the gate capacitance quickly.

Common mistakes: Mixing up the triode and saturation conditions; the boundary is VDS = VGS - Vt, not VDS = Vt. Forgetting the 1/2 factor in the saturation formula (some books define kn with the 1/2 inside; always check the definition your textbook uses). Thinking saturation means fully on as in BJTs; in MOSFETs, a fully-on switch is in triode. Forgetting that pMOS voltages are negative. And assuming a MOSFET with VGS(th) = 4 V will turn fully on from a 3.3 V pin; it will not.

What exams ask: Draw the structure of an enhancement nMOS and explain channel formation and threshold voltage. Explain pinch-off and the three regions. Write the ID equations for triode and saturation and solve numericals. Compare enhancement and depletion MOSFETs, and nMOS and pMOS. Sketch output and transfer characteristics. Explain channel-length modulation and body effect. Why is a MOSFET sensitive to static?

Recap: A MOSFET's insulated gate creates a channel using an electric field, with almost zero gate current. Enhancement nMOS: off below Vt; triode when VDS < VGS - Vt, ID = kn [(VGS - Vt) VDS - VDS^2 / 2]; saturation when VDS >= VGS - Vt, ID = (1/2) kn (VGS - Vt)^2. Depletion types conduct at VGS = 0. pMOS is the mirror image with slower holes. Next lesson, we bias MOSFETs and use them as amplifiers and switches.
key_points: MOSFET = metal (gate) + oxide (insulator) + semiconductor; gate current is about zero.
Enhancement nMOS: VGS > Vt induces an n-type inversion layer (channel).
Cut-off: VGS < Vt, ID = 0.
Triode: VDS < VGS - Vt, ID = kn[(VGS - Vt)VDS - VDS^2/2]; small VDS gives rDS = 1/(kn(VGS - Vt)).
Saturation: VDS >= VGS - Vt, ID = (1/2)kn(VGS - Vt)^2; with lambda, multiply by (1 + lambda VDS).
Depletion MOSFET conducts at VGS = 0 and works with VGS of either sign.
pMOS: negative Vt, holes, about 2-3 times lower mobility, so made wider.
Thin gate oxide is easily destroyed by static electricity.
lessons.tip: Write the region test as a tiny flowchart at the top of every MOSFET problem: VGS vs Vt, then VDS vs VGS - Vt. Assume, solve, then check. This one habit fixes most MOSFET mistakes.
lessons.task: For kn = 1 mA/V^2 and Vt = 0.8 V, find the region and ID for: (a) VGS = 0.5 V, VDS = 3 V; (b) VGS = 2.8 V, VDS = 0.4 V; (c) VGS = 2.8 V, VDS = 3 V.

quiz.q: An nMOS has Vt = 1 V, VGS = 4 V and VDS = 2 V. Which region is it in?
quiz.explain: VGS > Vt, and VDS = 2 V is less than VGS - Vt = 3 V, so triode.

quiz.q: With kn = 2 mA/V^2, Vt = 1 V, VGS = 2 V in saturation, ID is...
What forms the channel in an enhancement nMOS?
options: Holes pushed up from the drain
A built-in n-type layer made in the factory
Electrons attracted to the surface by a positive gate, forming an inversion layer
quiz.explain: A gate voltage above Vt attracts electrons and inverts the p-type surface.

quiz.q: Why is a pMOS usually made wider than an nMOS for the same current?
options: Holes have lower mobility than electrons
quiz.explain: Hole mobility is roughly 2-3 times lower, so more width is needed for equal current.

quiz.q: A depletion-type n-channel MOSFET at VGS = 0...
quiz.explain: Its channel is built in during manufacturing, so it conducts IDSS at VGS = 0.

lessons.title: MOSFET Biasing, Amplifiers and Switches
lessons.content:
Think of a pressure cooker on your mother's stove. The cooker can whistle softly, hiss steadily, or stay completely quiet, depending on how the flame is set. The same pot does different jobs depending on the setting. A MOSFET is just like that. Set it in the saturation region with a steady bias and it becomes an amplifier that makes small signals bigger. Drive its gate hard between zero and a high voltage and it becomes a near-perfect switch. This lesson is about setting the flame: biasing, then the two big uses.

Why this matters: Almost every analog block inside a chip, the amplifiers in your phone's microphone path, the sense amplifiers in RAM, the radio receiver in Wi-Fi, is built from MOSFET amplifiers. And almost every modern power circuit, from laptop chargers to e-bike controllers and the motor driver in a robotics project, uses MOSFET switches. If you do embedded systems, IoT or hardware projects, you will choose MOSFETs for switching loads more often than BJTs.

What this lesson covers: Biasing the enhancement MOSFET with a voltage divider and a source resistor, with a full worked example; the drain-feedback bias; transconductance gm and the small-signal model; the common-source amplifier, its gain, input and output impedances, with and without the source bypass capacitor; a quick look at the source follower and common gate; and the MOSFET as a switch, including RDS(on), logic-level gates, gate resistors, pull-downs, body diodes and low-side versus high-side switching. We use ID = (1/2) kn (VGS - Vt) squared from lesson 18.

Why we need bias: The gate takes no DC current, so biasing a MOSFET is in some ways easier than a BJT: there is no base current to worry about. But the square law means ID is very sensitive to VGS, and Vt and kn vary between devices and with temperature. So, just as with BJTs, we use a source resistor RS to add negative feedback and make the Q-point stable.

Voltage-divider bias: Two resistors RG1 (top) and RG2 (bottom) set the gate voltage VG = VDD x RG2 / (RG1 + RG2). Because no gate current flows, this is exact, no approximation needed. Since the gate current is zero, the resistors can be very large, mega-ohms, which keeps the amplifier's input impedance high. The source goes to ground through RS, and the drain to VDD through RD. Then VGS = VG - ID x RS. Combine with the square law and solve.

Worked bias example: VDD = 12 V, RG1 = 2 mega-ohms, RG2 = 1 mega-ohm, RS = 1 kilo-ohm, RD = 3 kilo-ohms, kn = 2 mA/V^2, Vt = 1 V. VG = 12 x 1 / 3 = 4 V. With ID in mA: VGS = 4 - ID, and ID = 0.5 x 2 x (VGS - 1) squared = (VGS - 1) squared. Let u = VGS - 1, then u + 1 = 4 - u squared, so u squared + u - 3 = 0, giving u = (-1 + square root of 13) / 2 = 1.30 V (the negative root is rejected because it would mean VGS < Vt). So VGS = 2.30 V and ID = 1.30 squared = 1.70 mA. Then VS = 1.70 V, VD = 12 - 1.70 x 3 = 6.91 V, VDS = 5.21 V.

Check the region: Saturation needs VDS >= VGS - Vt = 1.30 V. We have 5.21 V, so yes. Always do this check. If instead VDS came out smaller than the overdrive, the MOSFET would be in triode and we would redo the calculation with the triode equation.

Stability with RS: Suppose a replacement MOSFET has Vt = 1.5 V instead of 1 V. Without RS, with VGS fixed at 2.3 V, ID would drop from 1.70 mA to 0.5 x 2 x 0.8 squared = 0.64 mA, a big change. With RS, when ID falls, VS falls, VGS rises and partly restores ID. Solving again gives about 1.34 mA, a much smaller change. The source resistor is the hero again, exactly like RE for the BJT.

Drain-feedback bias: For an enhancement MOSFET, another simple circuit connects a large resistor RG from drain to gate. Since no current flows in RG, VG = VD, so VGS = VDS. That guarantees VDS > VGS - Vt, so the device is always in saturation. If ID rises, VD falls, VGS falls, and ID is pulled back down. It uses only two resistors besides the MOSFET.

Transconductance: The small-signal gain of a MOSFET is gm, the change in ID per change in VGS. From the square law, gm = kn x (VGS - Vt) = 2 x ID / (VGS - Vt) = square root of (2 x kn x ID). For our example: gm = 2 x 1.30 = 2.61 mS. Using the second form: 2 x 1.70 / 1.30 = 2.61 mS. Same. Notice gm grows only as the square root of ID for a MOSFET, while for a BJT gm = IC / 0.026 grows linearly. At 1.7 mA a BJT would have gm about 65 mS, much more. That is one reason BJTs still win in some high-gain analog circuits.

The small-signal model: For AC, the MOSFET becomes an open circuit between gate and source (no gate current) and a current source gm x vgs from drain to source, with an optional output resistance ro = 1 / (lambda x ID) in parallel. With lambda = 0.02 per volt and ID = 1.7 mA, ro is about 29 kilo-ohms. The same AC rules apply as lesson 16: capacitors and DC supplies become shorts.

Common-source amplifier: Input to the gate through a coupling capacitor, output from the drain through another, and RS bypassed by a capacitor. Voltage gain Av = -gm x (RD parallel ro), or about -gm x RD if ro is large. Here Av = -2.61 mS x 3 kilo-ohms = -7.8, inverted like the BJT CE. Including ro = 29 kilo-ohms: RD parallel ro = 2.72 kilo-ohms, so Av = -7.1. With a 10 kilo-ohm load, the effective drain resistance drops to about 2.3 kilo-ohms and the gain to about -6.

Input and output impedance: Zi = RG1 parallel RG2 = 2M parallel 1M = 667 kilo-ohms. Huge compared with the 1.25 kilo-ohms of our BJT amplifier in lesson 16, and it can be made even bigger with larger resistors. Zo = RD parallel ro, about RD = 3 kilo-ohms. So the MOSFET amplifier hardly loads the source at all, which is great for sensors with high internal resistance.

Unbypassed RS: Remove the bypass capacitor. The gain becomes Av = -gm x RD / (1 + gm x RS) = -7.8 / (1 + 2.61) = -2.2. Lower, but more stable and more linear, the same trade-off as in BJT amplifiers.

Source follower and common gate in one line each: The source follower (common drain) takes the output from the source: Av = gm RS / (1 + gm RS), a bit less than 1, with very high input impedance and output impedance about 1 / gm, here roughly 380 ohms. The common-gate stage feeds the input at the source: gain about +gm RD, non-inverting, with a low input impedance of about 1 / gm, useful at high frequency, just like the BJT common base.

The MOSFET as a switch: To switch a load, we use an enhancement nMOS with the load between the supply and the drain and the source to ground. This is called low-side switching. Gate at 0 V: cut-off, open switch. Gate well above Vt: the MOSFET goes deep into the triode region and behaves like a tiny resistor, RDS(on). Unlike a BJT, there is no VCE(sat) of 0.2 V; the voltage drop is just I x RDS(on), and the gate needs no steady current.

Switch worked example: A 12 V LED strip draws 5 A. A logic-level MOSFET with RDS(on) of about 25 milliohms at VGS = 5 V drops 5 x 0.025 = 0.125 V and wastes I squared R = 25 x 0.025 = 0.63 W, fine with a small heat sink or a large copper area. A BJT with VCE(sat) = 0.3 V would waste 1.5 W and would need about 50 to 250 mA of base current. That is why MOSFETs dominate power switching.

Practical gate details: Use a logic-level MOSFET, rated for full RDS(on) at 4.5 V or lower, when driving from a 3.3 V or 5 V microcontroller.
