Add a small gate resistor, about 100 ohms, to limit the current spike that charges the gate capacitance and to reduce ringing. Add a pull-down resistor, about 10 to 100 kilo-ohms, from gate to source so the MOSFET stays off while the microcontroller is booting and its pin is floating. Power MOSFETs have a built-in body diode from source to drain, which conducts if the drain goes below the source; it is useful in motor bridges but must be remembered. Inductive loads still need a flyback diode. For high-side switching, where the load goes to ground and the switch sits between the supply and the load, a pMOS is often used, with its gate pulled below its source to turn it on.

Real-life example 1, the soil-moisture pump project: A student in Bogura builds an automatic plant watering system. A capacitive soil sensor feeds a small amplifier to the ESP32's ADC; the high input impedance of a MOSFET-based op-amp stage hardly loads the sensor. When the soil is dry, the code sets a pin high, which drives a logic-level nMOS through a 100 ohm gate resistor, with a 10 kilo-ohm pull-down. The MOSFET switches a 12 V pump drawing 2 A, dropping only about 0.05 V. A flyback diode across the pump protects it. Total heat in the MOSFET: about 0.1 W, no heat sink needed.

Real-life example 2, the battery-powered sensor node: In a smart meter or a weather station running on batteries, the microcontroller sleeps most of the time. A pMOS high-side switch cuts power to sensors and the radio when they are not needed, because even a few milliamps of idle current would empty the battery in weeks. When it is time to measure, the pMOS turns on for a second, the reading is sent, and everything turns off again. Zero gate current is exactly what makes this possible.

Common mistakes: Forgetting to reject the root with VGS < Vt in bias problems. Not checking VDS >= VGS - Vt. Using the BJT formula gm = I / 26 mV for a MOSFET; the MOSFET formula is gm = 2 ID / VOV. Driving a standard MOSFET (Vt up to 4 V) from a 3.3 V pin and wondering why it gets hot; it is only partly on, in a high-resistance state. Forgetting the gate pull-down, so the load turns on randomly at power-up.

What exams ask: Solve voltage-divider and drain-feedback bias problems for enhancement MOSFETs, finding ID, VGS and VDS and verifying saturation. Derive gm in its three forms. Draw the small-signal model of a CS amplifier and find Av, Zi and Zo, with and without RS bypassed. Compare MOSFET and BJT amplifiers. Explain the MOSFET as a switch and calculate power loss from RDS(on).

Recap: Bias a MOSFET with a gate divider plus RS (or drain feedback), solve the square law, reject the root below Vt, and check saturation. gm = kn VOV = 2 ID / VOV. CS amplifier: Av = -gm RD, Zi = RG1 || RG2 (very high), Zo about RD. As a switch, drive the gate well above Vt into triode; loss is I^2 RDS(on). Use logic-level parts, gate resistor, pull-down and flyback diode. Next lesson: CMOS, where nMOS and pMOS switches team up to build logic gates.
key_points: Gate current is zero, so VG from a divider is exact: VG = VDD RG2 / (RG1 + RG2).
Bias: VGS = VG - ID RS with ID = (1/2) kn (VGS - Vt)^2; reject root with VGS < Vt.
Always check saturation: VDS >= VGS - Vt.
gm = kn (VGS - Vt) = 2 ID / VOV = sqrt(2 kn ID).
Common source: Av about -gm (RD || ro); Zi = RG1 || RG2 (very high); Zo about RD.
Unbypassed RS: Av = -gm RD / (1 + gm RS).
Switch: drive deep into triode; loss = I^2 RDS(on); use logic-level MOSFETs for 3.3/5 V drive.
Add a gate resistor, a gate pull-down and, for inductive loads, a flyback diode.
lessons.tip: For every MOSFET amplifier, write gm first, before anything else. Once you have gm, gain, follower output impedance and every other small-signal answer is one line away.
lessons.task: Repeat the worked bias example with RS = 2 kilo-ohms (everything else the same). Find ID, VGS, VDS, check saturation, then find gm and the bypassed common-source gain with RD = 3 kilo-ohms.

quiz.q: A MOSFET has kn = 2 mA/V^2 and VGS - Vt = 1.5 V. gm is...
quiz.explain: gm = kn (VGS - Vt) = 2 x 1.5 = 3 mS.

quiz.q: Why can the gate divider resistors of a MOSFET amplifier be mega-ohms?
options: The gate draws essentially no DC current
quiz.explain: With zero gate current, large resistors do not change VG and keep input impedance high.

quiz.q: A bypassed CS amplifier has gm = 4 mS and RD = 5 kilo-ohms. Av (ignoring ro) is...
quiz.explain: Av = -gm RD = -4 mS x 5 kilo-ohms = -20.

quiz.q: A MOSFET switch with RDS(on) = 0.05 ohm carries 4 A. Power lost in it is...
What is the gate pull-down resistor for in a MOSFET switch?
options: To keep the MOSFET off when the driving pin is floating
To act as a flyback diode
quiz.explain: During boot or disconnection the pin floats; the pull-down holds the gate at 0 V so the load stays off.

lessons.title: CMOS Circuits: Inverter, NAND, NOR and Moore's Law
lessons.content:
Imagine a water tank with two taps: one at the top connected to the overhead supply, one at the bottom connected to the drain. If you open the top tap and close the bottom one, the tank fills up. Open the bottom and close the top, and it empties. The rule is: never open both at once, or water just runs straight through and gets wasted. A CMOS logic gate is exactly this. A pMOS transistor is the top tap, connecting the output to the supply. An nMOS transistor is the bottom tap, connecting the output to ground. One is always on and the other is always off, so the output is either full or empty, 1 or 0, and almost no current is wasted when nothing is changing.

Why CMOS matters: CMOS stands for complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor, complementary because it pairs nMOS and pMOS. It is the technology inside nearly every digital chip made today: processors, memory controllers, microcontrollers, phone SoCs, GPUs and image sensors. In Digital Logic Design you learned that gates are boxes that compute AND, OR and NOT. In this lesson you look inside those boxes and see the transistors. This is the bridge from electronics to computer architecture and VLSI design.

What this lesson covers: The CMOS inverter, how it works and its voltage transfer characteristic; switching threshold and noise margins; sizing nMOS and pMOS; how to build NAND and NOR gates using series and parallel transistors, and any function using pull-up and pull-down networks; power consumption, dynamic power and leakage; propagation delay and fan-out; why CMOS won over other technologies; Moore's law and its slowdown; and a short word on latch-up and transmission gates.

The CMOS inverter: Connect the gates of a pMOS and an nMOS together as the input. Connect their drains together as the output. The pMOS source goes to VDD and the nMOS source goes to ground. Input low (0 V): the nMOS has VGS = 0, below its threshold, so it is off. The pMOS has VGS = -VDD, well beyond its negative threshold, so it is on. The output is connected to VDD: output high. Input high (VDD): the nMOS turns on and the pMOS turns off, so the output is pulled to ground: output low. That is a NOT gate made of just two transistors.

Full rail-to-rail swing: Because the off transistor is truly off, the output reaches all the way to VDD or all the way to 0 V. There is no resistor divider and no 0.2 V saturation drop as in the BJT inverter of lesson 15. This clean, full swing makes CMOS very robust against noise.

The voltage transfer characteristic: Plot output voltage against input voltage as the input slowly rises from 0 to VDD. At first the output stays at VDD. Near the middle, both transistors are briefly on together, and the output drops very steeply. Then it stays at 0. The curve looks like a reversed letter Z with a nearly vertical middle section. The input voltage at which output equals input is called the switching threshold VM. For a symmetric inverter, VM is VDD / 2, for example 0.5 V for a 1 V supply.

Sizing for symmetry: Holes are about two to three times slower than electrons (lesson 18). If the pMOS and nMOS had the same size, the pMOS would be weaker, VM would shift below VDD / 2, and the output would rise more slowly than it falls. Designers fix this by making the pMOS about two to three times wider than the nMOS. A typical textbook rule: W/L of pMOS is about 2 to 2.5 times W/L of nMOS for equal rise and fall.

Noise margins: A logic gate must understand slightly noisy inputs correctly. VIL is the highest input voltage still read as 0, and VIH is the lowest input voltage still read as 1. VOL and VOH are the output levels for 0 and 1. The noise margins are NML = VIL - VOL and NMH = VOH - VIH. Because CMOS outputs go all the way to 0 and VDD and the transfer curve is steep, CMOS noise margins are large, often close to 0.4 x VDD each. Example with VDD = 5 V: VIL might be about 2.1 V and VIH about 2.9 V, giving noise margins of about 2.1 V on each side.

Static power is almost zero: In either stable state, one transistor is off, so there is no direct path from VDD to ground. Only tiny leakage current flows. In older processes this leakage was so small that a CMOS chip doing nothing used almost no power. That is the single biggest reason CMOS won. In modern nanometre processes, leakage is no longer negligible and is a major design concern, but it is still far smaller than in older logic families.

Dynamic power: Power is used when the output switches. Each output drives a load capacitance C, made of wires and the gates of the next stages. Charging it from 0 to VDD draws energy C x VDD squared from the supply; half is stored in the capacitor, half is lost as heat in the pMOS. Discharging dumps the stored half as heat in the nMOS. So the average dynamic power is P = alpha x C x VDD squared x f, where f is the clock frequency and alpha is the activity factor, the fraction of clock cycles in which the node switches. Example: C = 10 fF, VDD = 1 V, f = 2 GHz, alpha = 0.1 gives 10e-15 x 1 x 2e9 x 0.1 = 2 microwatts for one node. Multiply by hundreds of millions of nodes and you see why phones get warm.

The power of voltage: Since P depends on VDD squared, lowering the supply voltage is the strongest power-saving tool. Cutting VDD from 1.2 V to 0.8 V reduces dynamic power to (0.8 / 1.2) squared, about 44 percent of before. But lower VDD also makes transistors slower, so the chip must run at a lower frequency. Phones constantly trade speed for battery by changing voltage and frequency together, called dynamic voltage and frequency scaling (DVFS). There is also a small short-circuit power during each transition, when both transistors are partly on for a moment.

Propagation delay: The time for a change at the input to show at the output is the propagation delay, tp. It is roughly proportional to C x VDD / I, where I is the current the on-transistor can supply. Wider transistors give more current and less delay but also present more capacitance to the previous stage. Each extra gate input connected to an output, called fan-out, adds capacitance and slows the gate. Typical delays in modern chips are a few picoseconds to tens of picoseconds per gate.

The NAND gate: Two inputs, A and B. Pull-down network: two nMOS in series between output and ground; the output goes low only if both A and B are high. Pull-up network: two pMOS in parallel between VDD and output; the output goes high if either A or B is low. Truth table: 00 gives 1, 01 gives 1, 10 gives 1, 11 gives 0. That is NAND, using four transistors.

The NOR gate: Pull-down network: two nMOS in parallel; the output goes low if either input is high. Pull-up network: two pMOS in series; the output goes high only if both inputs are low. Truth table: 00 gives 1, everything else gives 0. That is NOR, also four transistors.

The pattern, and why NAND is preferred: Notice the duality. Series in the pull-down means parallel in the pull-up, and vice versa. Any logic function of the form NOT(something) can be built this way: write the pull-down network from the function using series for AND and parallel for OR, then build the pull-up as its dual with pMOS. For example, Y = NOT(A x B + C) needs A and B nMOS in series, together in parallel with C, and the dual pMOS network. Series transistors are slower, because their resistances add. In NAND, the series stack is in the nMOS side, which is fast anyway; in NOR, the series stack is the slow pMOS side. So for the same speed, NAND gates are smaller, and designers prefer NAND-based logic. Note that CMOS naturally makes inverting gates: an AND gate is a NAND followed by an inverter, six transistors.

Why CMOS rules chips: Near-zero static power; full rail-to-rail output; large noise margins; very high input impedance, so one output can drive many inputs; and it scales beautifully, because the same structure works as transistors shrink. Older families such as TTL (built from BJTs, lesson 25) drew steady current and could not be packed as densely. By the 1980s and 1990s, CMOS had taken over almost all digital logic.

Moore's law: In 1965, Gordon Moore, who later co-founded Intel, observed that the number of components on a chip was doubling about every year; in 1975 he revised it to about every two years. This observation, Moore's law, held remarkably well for decades. Intel's first microprocessor, the 4004 of 1971, had about 2,300 transistors; today's large chips have tens of billions. For a long time, shrinking transistors also let voltage and power per transistor drop in step, called Dennard scaling. Around the mid-2000s, that broke down because leakage and heat stopped voltages from falling further. Clock speeds stopped climbing at a few gigahertz, and the industry switched to multi-core processors. Today transistor counts still grow, using 3D transistors like FinFETs and gate-all-around devices and stacking chiplets, but more slowly and at great cost.

Latch-up and transmission gates: Inside a CMOS chip, the n and p regions accidentally form a pair of parasitic BJTs that can, if triggered by a voltage spike, latch into a short circuit between VDD and ground and burn the chip. Layout rules and guard rings prevent this latch-up. A transmission gate is an nMOS and a pMOS in parallel, controlled by opposite signals, that acts as a good on-off switch for any voltage between 0 and VDD; it is used in multiplexers and flip-flops.

Real-life example 1, your phone battery: Why does a phone last a day on a small battery while running a processor with billions of transistors? CMOS. When the screen is off and the phone is idle, most transistors are not switching, so dynamic power is tiny, and parts of the chip are power-gated to cut leakage. When you start a heavy game like PUBG Mobile, the processor raises its voltage and clock, activity factor shoots up, power jumps by watts, and the phone gets warm in your hand. When it gets too hot, it throttles, lowering frequency and voltage to protect itself. Every one of these behaviours follows P = alpha C V^2 f.

Real-life example 2, the CMOS battery on a motherboard: Open an old desktop computer in a Bangladeshi cyber cafe or a university lab and you will find a coin cell battery on the motherboard. It is commonly called the CMOS battery because it powers a small block of CMOS memory and a real-time clock that store BIOS settings and the date and time while the computer is unplugged. Because CMOS uses so little static power, that tiny coin cell can last several years. When it finally dies, the PC forgets the date at every start, a common sign technicians recognise.

Common mistakes: Putting nMOS in the pull-up and pMOS in the pull-down; it is the reverse, pMOS pulls up, nMOS pulls down. Making NAND pull-down parallel instead of series. Thinking CMOS uses no power at all; it uses dynamic power whenever it switches, plus leakage. Forgetting that power scales with V squared, not V. And stating Moore's law as speed doubling; it is about transistor count.

What exams ask: Draw a CMOS inverter, explain its operation and sketch its transfer characteristic. Define noise margins. Draw CMOS NAND and NOR gates with truth tables, or design a CMOS circuit for a given Boolean function. Derive or use P = alpha C V^2 f. Explain why NAND is preferred over NOR. Explain why CMOS is the dominant technology. State Moore's law and discuss its limits.

Recap: A CMOS gate is a pMOS pull-up network plus an nMOS pull-down network, one on and the other off in each steady state. The inverter needs two transistors; NAND and NOR need four. Series in one network means parallel in the other. Static power is near zero; dynamic power is alpha C V^2 f. pMOS is made wider to match the nMOS. CMOS's low power and scalability made Moore's law possible. Next, we study how amplifiers behave with frequency and how stages are cascaded.
key_points: CMOS inverter: pMOS from VDD to output, nMOS from output to ground, gates tied together.
In steady state one transistor is off, so static power is nearly zero; output swings rail to rail.
Switching threshold VM = VDD/2 when pMOS is sized about 2-3 times wider than nMOS.
NAND: nMOS in series, pMOS in parallel; NOR: nMOS in parallel, pMOS in series.
Dynamic power P = alpha C VDD^2 f; lowering VDD is the strongest power saver.
NAND is preferred over NOR because its series stack uses faster nMOS.
Moore's law: transistor count roughly doubles about every two years (1975 revision); Dennard scaling ended around the mid-2000s.
lessons.tip: Learn one sentence: pMOS pulls up, nMOS pulls down, and the two networks are duals. With it you can draw any CMOS gate from its Boolean expression in under a minute.
lessons.task: Draw the CMOS transistor circuit for Y = NOT(A x B + C). Count the transistors, then fill a truth table for all 8 input combinations and check it against the expression.

quiz.explain: Input high turns the nMOS on and the pMOS off, pulling the output to ground.

chip price doubles every two years

lessons.title: Frequency Response and Multistage Amplifiers
lessons.content:
Think of a group of friends singing at a picnic. Some voices are deep, some are high. If one friend has a sore throat, he can only manage the middle notes; very low and very high notes come out weak. Amplifiers are like that. They amplify middle frequencies well, but at very low and very high frequencies their gain falls. How gain changes with frequency is called the frequency response. And when one amplifier is not enough, we chain several together, like passing a message along a line of people, which is a multistage amplifier.

Why this matters: An audio amplifier must handle bass at 20 Hz and cymbals at 20 kHz equally. A Wi-Fi receiver must work at 2.4 or 5 GHz. A data link must pass fast digital edges without smearing them. If you do not understand frequency response, your bass disappears, your radio picks up nothing, or your digital signal turns to mush. These ideas also appear in signals and systems, communication engineering, control systems and computer networks.

What this lesson covers: Decibels and why engineers use them; the shape of an amplifier's frequency response, midband, lower and upper cutoff frequencies and bandwidth; Bode plots with their 20 dB per decade slopes; what causes the low-frequency roll-off (coupling and bypass capacitors) and the high-frequency roll-off (internal transistor capacitances and the Miller effect); the gain-bandwidth trade-off; and multistage amplifiers, including coupling methods, overall gain with loading, and how bandwidth shrinks when stages are cascaded.

Decibels: Gains can be huge numbers, and multiplying them is clumsy. Decibels turn multiplication into addition. For voltage gain, gain in dB = 20 x log10(Av). For power gain, gain in dB = 10 x log10(Ap). Useful values: a gain of 10 is 20 dB, 100 is 40 dB, 1000 is 60 dB, 2 is about 6 dB, 1 is 0 dB, and 0.707 is about -3 dB. A gain below 1, a loss, gives negative dB. Example: an amplifier with Av = 316 has 20 x log10(316) = 20 x 2.5 = 50 dB.

Why -3 dB is special: When the voltage gain falls to 0.707 (that is 1 / square root of 2) of its midband value, the output power falls to half, because power goes as voltage squared. In dB that is a drop of 3 dB. The frequencies where this happens are called the cutoff frequencies or half-power points, and they define the edges of the useful band.

The shape of the response: Plot gain in dB against frequency on a logarithmic axis. A typical RC-coupled amplifier shows three regions. At low frequencies the gain rises. In the middle, the midband, the gain is flat; this is the value we calculated in lessons 16 and 19. At high frequencies the gain falls again. The lower cutoff frequency fL and the upper cutoff frequency fH are the -3 dB points. Bandwidth is BW = fH - fL, and since fH is usually much bigger than fL, BW is about fH. Example: fL = 50 Hz and fH = 200 kHz gives BW of about 200 kHz.

Bode plots: A single RC network gives a simple shape. Below its cutoff (for a high-pass) the gain falls at 20 dB per decade, meaning every time frequency drops by a factor of 10, the gain falls by 20 dB (equivalently 6 dB per octave, a factor of 2). At the cutoff frequency, the true curve is 3 dB below the straight-line approximation, and the phase shift is 45 degrees. Engineers sketch frequency responses quickly using these straight-line pieces, called asymptotic Bode plots.

Low-frequency roll-off: At low frequencies, capacitors have high reactance, Xc = 1 / (2 x pi x f x C). The coupling capacitors at input and output, and the emitter or source bypass capacitor, stop behaving like short circuits. Each forms a high-pass RC filter with the resistance it sees, giving a cutoff f = 1 / (2 x pi x R x C). Recall lesson 16: C1 = 10 microfarads and Zi = 1.25 kilo-ohms gave 12.7 Hz. The bypass capacitor sees only a small resistance, tens of ohms, so it usually produces the highest of these cutoffs and dominates fL. Bigger capacitors push fL lower. A direct-coupled amplifier, with no coupling capacitors, has no lower cutoff at all and amplifies down to DC, which op-amps (lesson 23) do.

High-frequency roll-off: At high frequencies, the capacitors we added are perfect shorts, but tiny capacitances inside the transistor start to matter: the base-emitter capacitance and the base-collector capacitance in a BJT (gate-source and gate-drain in a MOSFET), plus wiring capacitance. They are only a few picofarads, but at megahertz frequencies their reactance becomes small enough to short the signal to ground. They form low-pass filters and set fH.

The Miller effect: In an inverting amplifier with gain -Av, a small capacitance Cf connected between input and output behaves, seen from the input, like a much larger capacitance: C_in(Miller) = Cf x (1 + |Av|). Why? When the input rises by 1 mV, the output falls by Av mV, so the voltage across Cf changes by (1 + Av) mV, and it draws that much more current. Example: base-collector capacitance 2 pF in a CE stage with gain 100 looks like 2 x 101 = 202 pF at the input. If the source and bias resistance seen there is 500 ohms, fH = 1 / (2 x pi x 500 x 202 pF), about 1.6 MHz. Without the Miller effect it would be about 160 MHz from that capacitance alone. That is why CE stages are limited at high frequency and why the common-base stage, with no Miller multiplication at the input, is used in RF.

Gain-bandwidth trade-off: For many amplifiers, especially those with one dominant high-frequency pole, gain times bandwidth stays roughly constant. Increase gain and the bandwidth shrinks; reduce gain and the bandwidth grows. This product is called the gain-bandwidth product (GBW). An op-amp with GBW = 1 MHz has a bandwidth of about 100 kHz at a gain of 10, and about 10 kHz at a gain of 100. You will use this rule a lot in lesson 23.

Why use several stages: One stage rarely does everything. A CE stage gives good voltage gain but has medium output impedance and cannot drive a speaker. A single stage's gain is also limited. So we cascade stages: the output of one feeds the input of the next. A classic arrangement is CE (gain) followed by CE (more gain) followed by CC (low output impedance to drive the load).

Coupling between stages: RC coupling uses a coupling capacitor between stages, so each stage can be biased independently. It is cheap and simple but cannot pass DC and needs large capacitors for low frequencies. Direct coupling connects stages without capacitors; it passes DC and very low frequencies and is used inside ICs, where large capacitors are impossible, but bias drift in one stage is amplified by the next. Transformer coupling uses a transformer, giving impedance matching and isolation, used in some RF and older audio power stages but bulky and frequency-limited.

Overall gain with loading: The total voltage gain is the product of the individual loaded gains: Av(total) = Av1 x Av2 x ... In dB, just add. But careful: each stage's gain must be calculated with the next stage's input impedance as its load. Example: two identical stages from lesson 16, each with RC = 2.2 kilo-ohms, re = 18.4 ohms and Zi = 1.25 kilo-ohms, and a final 10 kilo-ohm load. Stage 1 sees RC parallel Zi2 = 2.2k parallel 1.25k = 797 ohms, so Av1 = -797 / 18.4 = -43. Stage 2 sees RC parallel RL = 1.8 kilo-ohms, so Av2 = -98. Total = 43 x 98 = 4,214, positive because two inversions cancel. In dB: 20 x log10(4214) = about 72.5 dB. Notice stage 1 lost almost two-thirds of its unloaded gain of 120 because of loading.

Bandwidth shrinks when you cascade: If each of n identical stages has upper cutoff fH, the overall response falls faster, and the overall upper cutoff becomes fH(n) = fH x square root of (2 to the power 1/n minus 1). For two stages the factor is 0.64; for three, 0.51. So two stages each with fH = 100 kHz give an overall fH of about 64 kHz. Similarly the lower cutoff rises: fL(n) = fL / square root of (2 to the power 1/n minus 1). More gain, less bandwidth again.

Special multistage combinations: The Darlington pair, two BJTs where the first's emitter drives the second's base, acts like one transistor with beta of about beta1 x beta2, used in high-current drivers and followers. The cascode, a common-emitter (or common-source) stage feeding a common-base (or common-gate) stage, gets high gain while avoiding the Miller effect because the first stage sees a low load, giving much wider bandwidth; it is common in RF and in IC op-amps. Differential pairs, the input stage of op-amps, are covered in lesson 23.

Measuring frequency response in the lab: Feed a sine wave from a signal generator at a fixed small amplitude, say 10 mV, and measure the output with an oscilloscope while stepping the frequency: 10 Hz, 20 Hz, 50 Hz, 100 Hz and so on up to a few megahertz. Calculate gain in dB at each point and plot on semi-log graph paper. Mark where it drops 3 dB from midband to find fL and fH. This is a standard lab experiment in EDC courses.

Real-life example 1, the rooftop TV antenna booster: Many houses in Bangladeshi towns still have a rooftop antenna with a small box called a booster for watching BTV and other terrestrial channels. The booster is a multistage RF amplifier tuned to the TV bands. Its designers use transistors and stages, like cascode or common-base, that keep good gain at hundreds of megahertz despite the Miller effect. A cheap booster with too narrow a bandwidth might boost one channel and lose another, which is a frequency-response problem in real life.

Real-life example 2, the wedding sound system: At a holud night, the sound system plays deep bass and crisp vocals. The mixer, equaliser and power amplifier are a chain of stages, each designed so that the overall response is flat from about 20 Hz to 20 kHz. If a coupling capacitor in one stage has dried out and lost capacitance, fL rises and the bass vanishes, and guests complain the music sounds thin. The equaliser knobs on the mixer are deliberately shaped frequency responses, boosting or cutting bands in dB.

Common mistakes: Using 10 log instead of 20 log for voltage gain. Forgetting that -3 dB means 0.707 of voltage but half of power. Calculating multistage gain by multiplying unloaded gains, which ignores loading and gives far too large an answer. Thinking that adding stages increases bandwidth; it reduces it. Forgetting that the Miller capacitance uses (1 + |Av|), not Av alone. And mixing up which capacitors set fL (large external ones) and which set fH (small internal ones).

What exams ask: Convert gains to and from dB. Define cutoff frequencies and bandwidth, sketch a frequency response and a Bode plot. Find the low-frequency cutoffs due to coupling and bypass capacitors. Explain the Miller effect and calculate the Miller input capacitance. Find the overall gain of a two-stage amplifier with loading. Compare RC, direct and transformer coupling. Calculate the bandwidth of n cascaded identical stages.

Recap: Gain in dB is 20 log Av; -3 dB points give fL and fH, and BW = fH - fL. Coupling and bypass capacitors set fL; internal capacitances, magnified by the Miller factor (1 + |Av|), set fH. Gain times bandwidth is roughly constant. Multistage gain is the product of loaded stage gains (sum in dB), but cascading shrinks bandwidth. Next lesson: feedback, the trick that trades a little gain for a lot of stability, and oscillators, where feedback creates signals out of nothing.
key_points: Voltage gain in dB = 20 log10(Av); power gain in dB = 10 log10(Ap); 0.707 is -3 dB.
fL and fH are the -3 dB points; bandwidth BW = fH - fL.
Single RC roll-off is 20 dB per decade (6 dB per octave), with 45 degrees phase at cutoff.
Coupling and bypass capacitors set fL; internal transistor capacitances set fH.
Miller effect: feedback capacitance looks like Cf (1 + |Av|) at the input of an inverting stage.
Gain-bandwidth product is roughly constant for single-pole amplifiers.
Multistage gain = product of loaded gains (sum in dB); n identical stages shrink fH by sqrt(2^(1/n) - 1).
lessons.tip: Learn the dB ladder by heart: x2 = 6 dB, x10 = 20 dB, x100 = 40 dB, x1000 = 60 dB, x0.707 = -3 dB. With it you can do most dB conversions in your head, which saves time in every exam question about gain.
lessons.task: Two stages have loaded gains of -25 and -40. Find the overall gain as a number and in dB. Then, if each stage alone has fH = 500 kHz, estimate the overall fH.

lessons.title: Feedback and Oscillators
lessons.content:
Picture a teacher reading a student's essay. If the student wrote it too long, the teacher says cut it down; too short, add more. The correction always pushes the essay back towards what is wanted. That is negative feedback. Now picture a microphone held too close to the speaker at a school function. A tiny sound comes out of the speaker, goes back into the mic, gets amplified, comes out louder, goes back in again, and within a second the whole hall hears a horrible screech. That is positive feedback. Both ideas, the calm one and the wild one, are the heart of this lesson.

Why this matters: Almost every serious amplifier you will meet uses negative feedback to make its gain exact, stable and clean. And every clock in every computer, phone, watch and microcontroller comes from an oscillator, which is just positive feedback tamed so it makes a steady wave instead of a screech. The CPU in your laptop ticks billions of times a second because some oscillator is ticking. Control systems, communication, embedded systems and computer architecture courses all build on these ideas.

What this lesson covers: The basic feedback loop and the gain formula Af = A / (1 + A beta); the benefits of negative feedback (stable gain, wider bandwidth, less distortion, controlled impedances); positive feedback and the Barkhausen criterion for oscillation; the RC phase-shift oscillator and the Wien bridge oscillator; LC oscillators in one look; crystal oscillators and why your watch uses 32.768 kHz; and finally the famous 555 timer chip in astable and monostable modes.

The feedback loop: Take an amplifier with gain A (called the open-loop gain). Take a sample of the output, multiply it by a fraction beta (the feedback factor, often set by two resistors), and bring it back to the input. In negative feedback this sample is subtracted from the input signal. Some algebra: the amplifier sees Vin - beta x Vout, so Vout = A x (Vin - beta x Vout). Rearranging gives the closed-loop gain Af = Vout / Vin = A / (1 + A beta). The quantity A beta is called the loop gain.

A worked example: Let A = 100,000 and beta = 0.01. Then A beta = 1000 and Af = 100,000 / 1001 = 99.9. Notice that this is almost exactly 1 / beta = 100. When the loop gain is large, Af is approximately 1 / beta. That is the magic: the overall gain no longer depends on the messy, temperature-sensitive transistor gain A, only on beta, which is set by two cheap, accurate resistors.

Benefit 1, gain stability (desensitivity): Suppose heat or ageing halves A to 50,000. New Af = 50,000 / 501 = 99.8. The amplifier's own gain dropped by 50 percent, but the closed-loop gain dropped by only about 0.1 percent. The factor (1 + A beta) is called the desensitivity factor; changes in A are divided by it. This is exactly the same idea as the emitter resistor stabilising the Q-point in lesson 14; RE was negative feedback all along.

Benefit 2, wider bandwidth: For many amplifiers, gain times bandwidth stays roughly constant. If feedback reduces the gain by the factor (1 + A beta), the bandwidth grows by about the same factor. Example: an amplifier with gain 100,000 and bandwidth 10 Hz, with feedback giving gain 100, will have bandwidth around 10 kHz. You trade gain, which you had too much of, for bandwidth, which you needed.

Benefit 3 and 4, less distortion and noise, controlled impedance: Distortion produced inside the amplifier is also reduced by about (1 + A beta), so music sounds cleaner. Feedback also changes input and output impedances in useful ways. The four feedback topologies, voltage-series, voltage-shunt, current-series and current-shunt, decide whether the input impedance goes up or down and whether the output behaves more like a voltage source or a current source. For example, voltage-series feedback raises the input impedance and lowers the output impedance by about (1 + A beta), which is what a good voltage amplifier wants. The price of all these benefits is lower gain, but gain is cheap; you can add another stage.

Positive feedback: Now flip the sign so the sample is added to the input. The formula becomes Af = A / (1 - A beta). If A beta is close to 1, the denominator approaches zero and the gain shoots towards infinity. In practice this means the circuit produces an output even with no input at all. Any tiny noise gets fed back in phase, grows, and becomes a sustained signal. Uncontrolled, this is the mic screech. Controlled at one frequency, it is an oscillator.

The Barkhausen criterion: For a circuit to oscillate steadily at a frequency f, two conditions must hold at that frequency. First, the magnitude of the loop gain must be 1: |A beta| = 1. Second, the total phase shift around the loop must be 0 degrees, or a multiple of 360 degrees. If |A beta| is less than 1, the oscillation dies out. If it is a bit more than 1, the oscillation grows until the amplifier starts to clip, which naturally pulls the effective gain back to 1. Real oscillators are designed with loop gain slightly above 1 so they start reliably from noise.

The RC phase-shift oscillator: Use an inverting amplifier, which gives 180 degrees of phase shift. Add three RC sections in a chain in the feedback path; together, at one particular frequency, they add another 180 degrees, giving 360 in total. With three equal sections of R and C, that frequency is f = 1 / (2 pi x sqrt(6) x R x C), and at that frequency the network attenuates the signal by a factor of 29, so the amplifier needs a gain of at least 29. Example: R = 10 kilo-ohms and C = 10 nF gives RC = 0.1 ms, so f = 1 / (2 x 3.14 x 2.45 x 0.0001), about 650 Hz. It is simple and good for audio frequencies.

The Wien bridge oscillator: Another favourite for audio. It uses a series RC and a parallel RC in the positive-feedback path of a non-inverting amplifier. At f = 1 / (2 pi R C) the network has zero phase shift and passes one third of the signal, so the amplifier needs a gain of exactly 3. With R = 10 kilo-ohms and C = 10 nF, f is about 1.59 kHz. Because a gain of exactly 3 is hard to hold, real designs add a lamp, thermistor or diodes to gently adjust the gain, giving a very clean sine wave. Hewlett-Packard's first product in 1939 was a Wien bridge audio oscillator.

LC oscillators: For radio frequencies, from hundreds of kilohertz to hundreds of megahertz, we use an inductor and a capacitor as the frequency-setting tank. They resonate at f = 1 / (2 pi x sqrt(L x C)). Example: L = 10 microhenry and C = 100 pF gives about 5 MHz. The Colpitts oscillator taps the tank with two capacitors, the Hartley with two inductors (or a tapped coil). FM radios and old transmitters used these.

Crystal oscillators: A quartz crystal is a thin slice of quartz with metal electrodes. Quartz is piezoelectric: squeeze it and it makes a voltage, apply a voltage and it bends. So a crystal vibrates mechanically at a very precise natural frequency set by its size and cut, and electrically it behaves like an LC circuit with an extremely high quality factor, often 10,000 to over 100,000. That makes the frequency stable to around tens of parts per million, far better than RC or ordinary LC circuits. Microcontrollers use crystals like 8 MHz or 16 MHz (the Arduino Uno uses 16 MHz), and computers use crystal-based clocks multiplied up to GHz inside the chip.

Why 32.768 kHz: Look inside a cheap quartz wall clock or a wristwatch and you will find a tiny crystal running at 32,768 Hz. That number is 2 to the power 15. A chain of 15 divide-by-two flip-flops turns it into exactly 1 pulse per second, which drives the second hand. A beautiful link between electronics and the binary arithmetic you learn in digital logic.

The 555 timer: Introduced in 1971 by Signetics, the 555 is one of the most popular ICs ever made, with billions sold. Inside it has a voltage divider of three equal resistors that sets reference levels at one third and two thirds of VCC, two comparators, a flip-flop, an output stage and a discharge transistor. With a few external resistors and one capacitor it becomes a timer or an oscillator. It works from roughly 4.5 V to 15 V and its output can drive around 200 mA, enough for LEDs, buzzers and small relays.

555 astable mode (free-running oscillator): The capacitor charges through R1 + R2 until it reaches two thirds VCC, then discharges through R2 alone until it falls to one third VCC, again and again. The high time is 0.693 x (R1 + R2) x C, the low time is 0.693 x R2 x C, and the frequency is f = 1.44 / ((R1 + 2 R2) x C). Example: R1 = 10 kilo-ohms, R2 = 47 kilo-ohms, C = 10 microfarads. High time = 0.693 x 57k x 10 microfarads = 0.395 s. Low time = 0.693 x 47k x 10 microfarads = 0.326 s. Period is about 0.72 s, so f is about 1.39 Hz: an LED blinking a bit faster than once a second.

555 monostable mode (one-shot timer): Here the output is normally low. A short trigger pulse makes the output go high for a fixed time T = 1.1 x R x C, then it returns low by itself. Example: R = 100 kilo-ohms and C = 10 microfarads gives T = 1.1 s. Uses: a staircase light that stays on for a minute after you press the switch, debouncing a push button, or a delay before a relay switches.

Real-life example 1, Eid and wedding fairy lights: The chasing and blinking strings of lights that decorate houses for weddings and Eid in Bangladesh often use a simple oscillator, sometimes a 555 or a small microcontroller with a crystal or RC clock, feeding switching transistors or triacs. Change the capacitor in a 555 circuit from 10 to 4.7 microfarads and the blink speed roughly doubles. Many electronics hobbyists in Dhaka's Patuatuli and Stadium market areas have built their first 555 blinker exactly this way.

Real-life example 2, the IPS inverter during load shedding: When power goes, a home IPS converts 12 V battery DC into 220 V AC at 50 Hz. Inside, an oscillator, usually in a control IC or microcontroller with a crystal, generates the 50 Hz timing. Negative feedback then watches the output voltage and adjusts the switching so that your fan and lights get a steady voltage whether one bulb or the whole house is on. Positive feedback makes the rhythm, negative feedback keeps it under control.

Common mistakes: Writing Af = A / (1 - A beta) for negative feedback; the minus sign belongs to positive feedback. Thinking negative feedback increases gain; it reduces gain but improves everything else. Forgetting that Barkhausen needs both magnitude 1 and phase 0 or 360 degrees. Using f = 1 / (2 pi R C) for the RC phase-shift oscillator; that formula is for the Wien bridge, while the phase-shift oscillator has sqrt(6) in it. Mixing up the 555 high and low time formulas; R1 only appears in the high time.

What exams ask: Derive Af = A / (1 + A beta) and list the advantages of negative feedback. Calculate the closed-loop gain and its percentage change when A changes. State and explain the Barkhausen criterion. Draw an RC phase-shift or Wien bridge oscillator and find its frequency and required gain. Explain why crystal oscillators are stable. Draw the 555 internal block diagram and design an astable circuit for a given frequency and duty cycle.

Recap: Negative feedback trades gain for stability, bandwidth, low distortion and good impedances, and with large loop gain Af is about 1 / beta. Positive feedback with |A beta| = 1 and 0 degrees loop phase gives an oscillator. RC phase-shift (gain 29, sqrt(6) formula) and Wien bridge (gain 3) make audio sine waves; LC tanks make radio frequencies; crystals give precise clocks; the 555 makes square waves and timed pulses easily. Next, we meet the op-amp, the amplifier designed to be used with feedback.
key_points: Negative feedback: Af = A / (1 + A beta); if A beta is large, Af is about 1 / beta.
Negative feedback stabilises gain, widens bandwidth, cuts distortion and sets impedances, at the cost of gain.
Positive feedback adds the sample in phase; it is used for oscillators.
Barkhausen criterion: |A beta| = 1 and loop phase 0 or 360 degrees.
RC phase-shift: f = 1 / (2 pi sqrt(6) RC), needs gain at least 29; Wien bridge: f = 1 / (2 pi RC), gain 3.
Crystals are piezoelectric with very high Q; 32.768 kHz = 2^15 gives 1 Hz after 15 divide-by-2 stages.
555 astable: f = 1.44 / ((R1 + 2R2)C); monostable: T = 1.1 RC.
lessons.tip: Keep one sheet with only formulas from this lesson: Af, Barkhausen, the two oscillator frequencies with their gains, and the 555 formulas. Before the exam, cover the right side and recite them; they are short but easy to mix up.
lessons.task: Design a 555 astable that blinks an LED about 2 times per second using C = 10 microfarads and R1 = 10 kilo-ohms. Find R2 from f = 1.44 / ((R1 + 2R2)C), then pick the nearest standard resistor.

quiz.q: An amplifier has A = 10,000 and beta = 0.1 in negative feedback. The closed-loop gain is about...
Which is NOT a benefit of negative feedback?
quiz.explain: Negative feedback reduces gain; that is the price paid for the other benefits.

quiz.q: The Barkhausen criterion for sustained oscillation requires...
options: loop gain magnitude 1 and loop phase 0 or 360 degrees
quiz.explain: Both magnitude 1 and total phase shift 0 (or multiples of 360) degrees are needed.

quiz.q: Why does a wristwatch crystal run at 32,768 Hz?
options: It is the resonant frequency of all quartz
It equals 2^15, so 15 divide-by-2 stages give 1 Hz
It is the mains frequency times 655
It is the fastest a crystal can vibrate
quiz.explain: 32,768 = 2^15; halving it 15 times gives exactly one pulse per second.

quiz.q: A 555 monostable has R = 100 kilo-ohms and C = 10 microfarads. The pulse width is about...
quiz.explain: T = 1.1 x 100k x 10 microfarads = 1.1 s.

lessons.title: The Operational Amplifier
lessons.content:
Imagine a super-sensitive see-saw in a playground. Put one gram more on the left seat than on the right, and the see-saw slams all the way down to the left. It does not care how heavy the children are in total, only about the tiny difference between the two sides, and it reacts to that difference enormously. An operational amplifier, or op-amp, is exactly this see-saw made of transistors. It has two inputs, it looks only at the difference between them, and it multiplies that difference by a huge number, often a hundred thousand or more.

Why op-amps matter: Before op-amps, every amplifier had to be designed transistor by transistor with all the biasing work of lessons 14 and 16. The op-amp packs a carefully designed multi-stage amplifier into one small chip, so you can build amplifiers, filters, sensors, oscillators and even analog computers with a few resistors. The name comes from the 1940s and 1950s, when such amplifiers performed mathematical operations like adding and integrating in analog computers. Today op-amps are in ECG machines, weighing scales, audio mixers, phone microphones, battery chargers and the sensor boards CSE students use with microcontrollers.

What this lesson covers: The op-amp symbol and pins; the ideal op-amp and its five golden properties; open-loop gain and why an op-amp alone saturates; what is inside, starting with the differential amplifier; differential-mode and common-mode signals and the CMRR; the two golden rules with negative feedback, including the virtual short; and the main real-world limits: offset voltage, bias current, gain-bandwidth product and slew rate. The useful circuits built from these ideas are the topic of lesson 24.

The symbol and pins: An op-amp is drawn as a triangle pointing right. On the left are two inputs: the non-inverting input marked + and the inverting input marked -. On the right tip is the output. Power pins, usually +VCC and -VEE such as +15 V and -15 V, are often left out of drawings but are always there. The classic 741 op-amp in an 8-pin package has pin 2 as the inverting input, pin 3 as the non-inverting input, pin 6 as the output, pin 7 as +V, pin 4 as -V, and pins 1 and 5 for offset null.

The basic equation: The output is Vout = A x (V+ - V-), where A is the open-loop gain, meaning the gain with no feedback. If V+ is larger, the output goes positive; if V- is larger, the output goes negative. That is why the - input is called inverting: a signal applied there appears upside down at the output.

The ideal op-amp: To make design simple, we first imagine a perfect op-amp with five properties. Infinite open-loop gain. Infinite input resistance, so no current flows into either input. Zero output resistance, so the output voltage does not sag whatever load you connect. Infinite bandwidth, so it works the same at every frequency. And zero offset, so the output is exactly zero when the two inputs are equal. No real op-amp is ideal, but good ones come close enough that ideal analysis gives answers within a percent or so.

Real numbers for the 741: Typical open-loop gain is about 200,000 (around 106 dB). Input resistance is about 2 mega-ohms. Output resistance is about 75 ohms. The gain-bandwidth product is about 1 MHz. Modern op-amps with FET inputs have input resistances of a million mega-ohms or more. So the ideal assumptions are not crazy at all for most circuits.

Open loop means saturation: Suppose a 741 runs on plus and minus 15 V, and the output can swing to roughly plus or minus 13 V. With A = 200,000, the input difference needed to reach 13 V is only 13 / 200,000 = 65 microvolts. Any bigger difference, even a millivolt, slams the output into saturation at the positive or negative limit. So an op-amp used alone, with no feedback, is not a linear amplifier; it is a comparator that tells you which input is larger. To get a useful, controlled gain we must add negative feedback, exactly as lesson 22 promised: with feedback, gain becomes about 1 / beta, set by resistors.

Inside the op-amp: A typical op-amp has three main stages. The input stage is a differential amplifier, which gives the op-amp its two inputs and rejects signals common to both. The middle stage is a high-gain voltage amplifier, often a common-emitter stage, which provides most of the gain and contains a small compensation capacitor to keep the whole thing stable with feedback. The output stage is a push-pull emitter follower pair, an npn and a pnp, which gives low output resistance and can source or sink current. The 741 has about twenty transistors inside.

The differential amplifier: Take two matched transistors, Q1 and Q2, with their emitters joined and connected to a constant current source, called the tail; this is the long-tailed pair. Each collector has a resistor to the supply. If both bases get the same voltage, the tail current splits equally and nothing changes at the output. If base 1 goes slightly up and base 2 slightly down, more current flows through Q1 and less through Q2, and the collector voltages move in opposite directions. The output, taken between the two collectors, depends on the difference V1 - V2. The tail current source is what makes the pair ignore common changes.

Differential and common-mode signals: Any two input voltages V1 and V2 can be split into two parts. The differential signal Vd = V1 - V2, which we want to amplify. The common-mode signal Vcm = (V1 + V2) / 2, the average both inputs share, which we usually want to ignore. The output is Vout = Ad x Vd + Acm x Vcm, where Ad is the differential gain and Acm the common-mode gain. A perfect amplifier would have Acm = 0.

CMRR: The common-mode rejection ratio measures how well an amplifier ignores common signals: CMRR = Ad / Acm, usually given in decibels as 20 log10 (Ad / Acm). The 741 has a typical CMRR around 90 dB, which means Ad is about 30,000 times larger than Acm. Worked example: Ad = 1000 and Acm = 0.01, so CMRR = 100,000, which is 100 dB. Inputs V1 = 2.001 V and V2 = 2.000 V give Vd = 1 mV and Vcm = 2.0005 V. Output = 1000 x 0.001 + 0.01 x 2.0005 = 1 V + 0.02 V = 1.02 V. The wanted part is 1 V and the error is only 20 mV; with a poor CMRR the error would swamp the signal.

The two golden rules with negative feedback: When an op-amp has negative feedback and is not saturated, two simple rules let you analyse almost any circuit. Rule 1: no current flows into either input (because input resistance is huge). Rule 2: the output does whatever it takes to make V+ equal to V- (because with huge gain, a tiny difference is enough). Rule 2 is called the virtual short: the two inputs sit at the same voltage, as if shorted, yet no current flows between them. If V+ is grounded, V- is also at 0 V, which we call a virtual ground.

A quick taste of the virtual short: Ground the + input, connect the input signal through 10 kilo-ohms to the - input, and connect 100 kilo-ohms from the output back to the - input. By the virtual short, the - input is at 0 V. A 1 V input pushes 1 V / 10k = 0.1 mA through the input resistor. Since no current enters the op-amp, the same 0.1 mA must flow through the 100k resistor, so the output must be 0 - 0.1 mA x 100k = -10 V. Gain = -10, set purely by two resistors. That is the inverting amplifier, and lesson 24 is full of such circuits.

Offset voltage and bias current: Real op-amps have small errors. Input offset voltage is the small DC voltage you would need between the inputs to make the output zero; for the 741 it is typically about 1 mV and at most about 5 mV. A circuit with a gain of 100 turns 1 mV of offset into 0.1 V of error at the output. Input bias current is the small DC current the input transistors actually need, around 80 nA typically for the 741, and only picoamps for FET-input op-amps. Flowing through large resistors, bias currents create extra offset. The 741's offset null pins and careful resistor choices reduce these errors.

Gain-bandwidth product: An op-amp's open-loop gain is huge only at very low frequencies. For the 741 it starts falling at around 5 to 10 Hz and keeps falling until it reaches 1 at about 1 MHz. For such internally compensated op-amps, closed-loop gain times bandwidth is roughly constant and equal to this unity-gain frequency, the GBW. So a 741 amplifier with gain 10 has a bandwidth around 100 kHz, and with gain 100 only about 10 kHz. If you need gain 100 at 100 kHz, you need an op-amp with a GBW of at least 10 MHz, or two stages.

Slew rate: There is also a limit on how fast the output voltage can change, called the slew rate, measured in volts per microsecond. For the 741 it is about 0.5 V per microsecond. A sine wave of peak Vp and frequency f changes fastest at its zero crossing, at a rate of 2 pi f Vp. So the largest undistorted frequency at full swing, the full-power bandwidth, is f = SR / (2 pi Vp). For a 741 with a 10 V peak output, f = 500,000 / (2 x 3.14 x 10), about 8 kHz. Above that, sine waves turn into triangles. Faster op-amps have slew rates of tens or hundreds of volts per microsecond.

Real-life example 1, the ECG machine in a hospital: An ECG measures the heart's electrical signal, only about 1 mV, picked up by electrodes on the chest and arms. But the patient's body also picks up 50 Hz hum from the mains wiring in the walls, often far larger than the heart signal, and it appears almost equally on both electrodes. It is a common-mode signal. The ECG front end uses an instrumentation amplifier built from op-amps with a very high CMRR, often over 100 dB, so it amplifies the difference (the heartbeat) and throws away the common hum. In a clinic in Sylhet or Dhaka, that clean wavy line on the monitor exists because of CMRR.

Real-life example 2, the digital scale at the mudi shop: The digital weighing scale at your local grocery shop uses a load cell, a metal block with strain gauges arranged as a Wheatstone bridge. Putting 1 kg of rice on it changes the bridge output by only a few millivolts, riding on a common-mode voltage of about half the supply. An op-amp based differential or instrumentation amplifier picks out the tiny difference, rejects the common part, and amplifies it hundreds of times so an ADC (lesson 25) can read it. The shopkeeper just sees 1.000 kg.

Common mistakes: Applying the virtual short to an op-amp with no negative feedback, such as a comparator; there the inputs are not equal and the output saturates. Thinking that no current into the inputs means no current anywhere; current flows freely through the feedback and input resistors and into the output pin. Forgetting the power supply limits: an op-amp powered from plus and minus 12 V cannot output 20 V. Confusing GBW (small-signal limit) with slew rate (large-signal limit).

What exams ask: List the characteristics of an ideal op-amp. Draw the block diagram of an op-amp and explain the differential amplifier input stage. Define CMRR and calculate the output for given V1, V2, Ad and Acm. Explain the virtual short and virtual ground. Define slew rate and find the maximum frequency for a given output swing. Define input offset voltage, bias current and gain-bandwidth product.

Recap: An op-amp amplifies V+ - V- by a huge open-loop gain, so alone it saturates. Inside it has a differential input stage, a gain stage and a push-pull output. CMRR = Ad / Acm measures how well common signals are rejected. With negative feedback: no input current and V+ = V- (virtual short), so gain is set by resistors. Real limits are offset, bias current, GBW and slew rate. Next lesson, we use these rules to build a whole toolbox of op-amp circuits.
key_points: Op-amp: Vout = A(V+ - V-); open-loop gain A is huge (about 200,000 for the 741).
Ideal op-amp: infinite gain, infinite input resistance, zero output resistance, infinite bandwidth, zero offset.
Without negative feedback, a tiny input difference saturates the output.
Input stage is a differential amplifier (long-tailed pair) that amplifies V1 - V2.
CMRR = Ad / Acm, in dB 20 log(Ad / Acm); the 741 is about 90 dB.
With negative feedback: no input current, and V+ = V- (virtual short / virtual ground).
GBW: gain x bandwidth is about constant (about 1 MHz for the 741).
Slew rate limits large signals: f(max) = SR / (2 pi Vp); 741 SR is about 0.5 V/microsecond.
lessons.tip: Before solving any op-amp circuit, ask one question: is there negative feedback from the output to the - input? If yes, use the two golden rules. If no, it is a comparator and the output sits at a supply limit.
lessons.task: A 741 (slew rate 0.5 V per microsecond) must output a 5 V peak sine wave. Find the highest frequency it can deliver without distortion. Then repeat for 1 V peak and compare.

quiz.q: Which is a property of the ideal op-amp?
quiz.explain: The ideal op-amp draws no input current: infinite input resistance.

quiz.q: A 741 with A = 200,000 has output limits of plus or minus 13 V. With no feedback and 1 mV input difference, the output is...
quiz.explain: 1 mV x 200,000 = 200 V is impossible, so the output saturates at the supply limit.

quiz.q: Ad = 2000 and Acm = 0.02. CMRR in dB is...
In an op-amp with negative feedback and the + input grounded, the - input is at about 0 V. This is called...
quiz.explain: The virtual short makes V- equal V+ = 0 V: a virtual ground.

quiz.q: An op-amp has GBW = 1 MHz and is used at a closed-loop gain of 20. Its bandwidth is about...
quiz.explain: Bandwidth is about GBW / gain = 1 MHz / 20 = 50 kHz.

lessons.title: Op-Amp Circuits
lessons.content:
Think of a LEGO box. The bricks are all simple, but with the same bricks you can build a car, a house or a spaceship, depending on how you arrange them. An op-amp is the brick, and a few resistors and capacitors are the connectors. Arrange them one way and you get an amplifier with a gain of exactly 10. Another way and it adds numbers. Another way and it does calculus. Another way and it makes a clean on-off decision from a noisy sensor. This lesson opens the toolbox.

Why these circuits matter: Most analog circuits on real boards, from the audio jack in your laptop to a temperature sensor feeding an Arduino, are combinations of the dozen circuits in this lesson. Interview questions for embedded and hardware jobs often ask you to find the output of an op-amp circuit in a minute. And in exams, op-amp circuits are some of the most predictable marks you can earn, because two rules solve them all.

What this lesson covers: Using the golden rules from lesson 23 (no input current, V+ = V- with negative feedback), we will analyse the inverting amplifier, the non-inverting amplifier, the voltage follower, the summing amplifier, the difference amplifier and a word on the instrumentation amplifier, the integrator and the differentiator, and a first-order active filter. Then we switch to circuits without negative feedback: the comparator and the Schmitt trigger with hysteresis. All op-amps here are treated as ideal unless we say otherwise.

The inverting amplifier: The + input is grounded. The input signal goes through Rin to the - input, and Rf connects the output back to the - input. Virtual ground puts the - input at 0 V, so the input current is Vin / Rin. That current cannot enter the op-amp, so it all flows through Rf, giving Vout = -(Rf / Rin) x Vin. Gain = -Rf / Rin. Example: Rin = 10 kilo-ohms, Rf = 100 kilo-ohms, gain = -10; Vin = 0.5 V gives Vout = -5 V. The input resistance seen by the source is just Rin, because the other end of Rin is at virtual ground.

The non-inverting amplifier: Now the signal goes directly to the + input. Rf goes from output to the - input, and R1 goes from the - input to ground. The virtual short makes V- = Vin. The output divides through Rf and R1, so V- = Vout x R1 / (R1 + Rf). Setting this equal to Vin gives Vout = (1 + Rf / R1) x Vin. Example: R1 = 10 kilo-ohms, Rf = 90 kilo-ohms, gain = 10; Vin = 0.3 V gives Vout = 3 V, not inverted. The big bonus: the signal source sees the op-amp's input directly, so the input resistance is extremely high. Note the gain can never be less than 1.

The voltage follower: Make Rf = 0 (a wire from output to - input) and remove R1. The non-inverting formula gives gain = 1 + 0 = 1. The output simply copies the input. Why bother? Because the input resistance is enormous and the output resistance is tiny. It is a perfect buffer, like the emitter follower of lesson 13 but without the 0.7 V drop. Example: a sensor with 100 kilo-ohm internal resistance cannot drive a 1 kilo-ohm load directly; most of its voltage would be lost inside it. Put a follower in between and the load gets the full sensor voltage.

The summing amplifier: Take the inverting amplifier and add more input resistors to the same - input. Each input pushes its own current Vk / Rk into the virtual ground, and all those currents add up and flow through Rf. So Vout = -Rf x (V1 / R1 + V2 / R2 + V3 / R3). With all resistors equal to 10 kilo-ohms and inputs 1 V, 2 V and -0.5 V, Vout = -(1 + 2 - 0.5) = -2.5 V. Choose different input resistors and you get weighted sums; choose Rf = R / 3 with three inputs and you get the average. This is the heart of an audio mixer and of the weighted-resistor DAC you will meet in lesson 25.

The difference amplifier: Use one op-amp and four resistors. V1 goes through R1 to the - input, with R2 from output to - input. V2 goes through R3 to the + input, with R4 from + input to ground. If R1 = R3 and R2 = R4, then Vout = (R2 / R1) x (V2 - V1). Example: R1 = R3 = 10 kilo-ohms, R2 = R4 = 100 kilo-ohms, V2 = 1.2 V and V1 = 1.0 V gives Vout = 10 x 0.2 = 2 V. The common 1 V shared by both inputs disappears. The resistors must match closely, because mismatch lets common-mode signals leak through and lowers the CMRR.

The instrumentation amplifier, in one look: The simple difference amplifier has a problem: its input resistance is only about R1, which loads a weak sensor. The fix is to put a voltage follower-like stage in front of each input. The classic three-op-amp instrumentation amplifier has two input op-amps and one difference amplifier, and its gain is set by a single resistor Rg: with all other resistors equal to R, the gain is 1 + 2R / Rg. It has very high input resistance and very high CMRR, which is why it sits inside ECG machines and weighing scales, as you saw in lesson 23. Ready-made chips like the AD620 and INA128 package it all.

The integrator: Replace Rf in the inverting amplifier with a capacitor C. The input current Vin / R flows into the capacitor and charges it. The capacitor voltage is the running total of that current over time, so Vout = -(1 / RC) x integral of Vin dt. Example: R = 10 kilo-ohms, C = 1 microfarad, RC = 10 ms. A steady 1 V input makes the output fall at 1 V / 10 ms = 100 V per second, so after 50 ms the output is -5 V, and it keeps falling until it saturates. Feed a square wave and you get a triangle wave. In practice, a large resistor is placed across C so that tiny DC offsets do not slowly push the output into saturation.

The differentiator: Swap the positions: capacitor at the input, resistor in the feedback. The capacitor current is C x dVin/dt, which flows through R, so Vout = -RC x dVin/dt. Example: R = 1 kilo-ohm, C = 1 microfarad, RC = 1 ms. An input ramp rising at 2 V per ms gives Vout = -1 ms x 2 V/ms = -2 V, constant while the ramp lasts. Feed a triangle wave and you get a square wave. The catch: the gain rises with frequency, so high-frequency noise gets amplified a lot. Practical differentiators add a small resistor in series with C to limit high-frequency gain.

Active filters: Put a capacitor Cf in parallel with Rf in the inverting amplifier. At low frequencies the capacitor is nearly open and the gain is -Rf / Rin. At high frequencies the capacitor shorts Rf and the gain falls. The cutoff frequency is f = 1 / (2 pi Rf Cf). Example: Rf = 10 kilo-ohms, Cf = 16 nF gives about 1 kHz. This is a first-order active low-pass filter: it gives gain, filtering and a low output resistance in one stage. Higher-order filters like Sallen-Key and Butterworth designs are covered in signals or analog electronics courses.

The comparator: Remove all feedback. Now the op-amp compares its two inputs and the output slams to the positive limit if V+ > V-, or the negative limit if V+ < V-. Put a reference voltage, say 2.5 V, on one input and a sensor signal on the other, and the output tells you whether the sensor is above or below 2.5 V. With the reference at 0 V it becomes a zero-crossing detector that turns a sine wave into a square wave. Dedicated comparator chips like the LM393 and LM339 switch faster than general op-amps and have outputs designed to connect directly to logic.

The trouble with simple comparators: Real signals are noisy. If a slowly rising sensor voltage hovers near the reference, a little noise makes it cross back and forth many times, and the output chatters on and off rapidly. A pump or a light controlled by such a comparator would flicker or click repeatedly, which is bad for relays and annoying for people.

The Schmitt trigger: The cure is a little positive feedback. In the inverting Schmitt trigger, the input goes to the - input, and a voltage divider from the output feeds the + input: R2 from output to + input and R1 from + input to ground. Now the threshold depends on the output itself. When the output is high at +Vsat, the threshold is the upper trip point UTP = +Vsat x R1 / (R1 + R2). When the output is low, the threshold is LTP = -Vsat x R1 / (R1 + R2). Example: Vsat = 12 V, R1 = 10 kilo-ohms, R2 = 50 kilo-ohms gives UTP = +2 V and LTP = -2 V. The gap between them, 4 V, is the hysteresis. Noise smaller than 4 V cannot cause chattering, because once the output switches, the threshold jumps away.

Reading the Schmitt trigger: Start with a low input and output at +12 V. The threshold is +2 V. As the input rises past +2 V, the output snaps to -12 V and the threshold drops to -2 V. Now the input must fall all the way below -2 V before the output snaps back to +12 V. Plot Vout against Vin and you see a rectangle-shaped loop, the hysteresis loop. Digital chips like the 74HC14 contain Schmitt trigger inputs for cleaning up slow or noisy signals.

Real-life example 1, automatic street light and water tank: Many Bangladeshi towns now have street lights that turn on by themselves at dusk. A light-dependent resistor in a voltage divider gives a voltage that changes with daylight. A Schmitt trigger compares it with a reference, so the light turns on when it gets dark but does not flicker during cloudy twilight or when a car's headlights sweep past. The same idea controls the water pump of a roof tank: start the pump when the level is low, stop only when the tank is full, with the gap between the two levels acting as hysteresis so the pump does not start and stop every few seconds.

Real-life example 2, the sound mixer at a gaye holud: At a wedding or a university cultural night, the DJ's mixer takes several microphones and music channels and combines them. Each channel has a preamp, often a non-inverting op-amp stage, to lift the tiny microphone signal. Volume knobs set the weights, and a summing amplifier adds the channels together. Tone controls are active filters. A follower or similar buffer then drives the long cable to the power amplifier and speakers. Almost every block in that mixer is a circuit from this lesson.

Common mistakes: Forgetting the minus sign in the inverting gain. Writing the non-inverting gain as Rf / R1 instead of 1 + Rf / R1. Applying the virtual short to comparators and Schmitt triggers, which do not have negative feedback. Forgetting that outputs saturate near the supply rails, so a gain-of-100 amplifier with a 0.2 V input and plus-minus 12 V supplies cannot give 20 V. In integrator problems, forgetting the 1 / RC factor or the minus sign.

What exams ask: Derive the gain of the inverting and non-inverting amplifiers. Find the output of a summing or difference amplifier with given values. Derive the integrator and differentiator output equations and sketch the output for a square or triangle input. Explain why the practical integrator and differentiator need extra resistors. Design a Schmitt trigger for given trip points and draw its hysteresis loop. Compare comparator and Schmitt trigger.

Recap: Inverting: -Rf / Rin. Non-inverting: 1 + Rf / R1. Follower: 1, a buffer. Summing: adds weighted inputs. Difference: (R2 / R1)(V2 - V1). Integrator: -(1 / RC) integral; differentiator: -RC d/dt. Low-pass active filter: f = 1 / (2 pi Rf Cf). Comparator: no feedback, output at a rail. Schmitt trigger: positive feedback gives two thresholds and clean switching. Next and final lesson, we zoom out from single devices to whole chips, logic families and the bridge between analog and digital.
key_points: Inverting amplifier: Vout = -(Rf / Rin) Vin; input resistance is Rin.
Non-inverting amplifier: Vout = (1 + Rf / R1) Vin; very high input resistance.
Voltage follower: gain 1, high input and low output resistance, a buffer.
Summing amplifier: Vout = -Rf (V1/R1 + V2/R2 + ...); difference amplifier: (R2/R1)(V2 - V1) with matched resistors.
Integrator: Vout = -(1/RC) integral of Vin dt; differentiator: Vout = -RC dVin/dt.
Comparator: no feedback, output saturates depending on which input is larger.
Schmitt trigger: positive feedback, UTP and LTP = plus or minus Vsat R1/(R1 + R2), hysteresis stops chatter.
lessons.tip: For every op-amp circuit write the same three lines: V- = V+ (if negative feedback), current into the input resistor, same current through the feedback element. Those three lines solve almost every circuit in this lesson.
lessons.task: Design a non-inverting amplifier with a gain of 11 using standard resistors, then design an inverting summer that gives Vout = -(2V1 + V2) with Rf = 20 kilo-ohms. Write the resistor values.
