A non-inverting amplifier with R1 = 10 kilo-ohms and Rf = 40 kilo-ohms has a gain of...
An integrator has R = 10 kilo-ohms and C = 1 microfarad. A constant +2 V input makes the output change at...
quiz.explain: Rate = -Vin / RC = -2 / 0.01 = -200 V per second.

quiz.q: A difference amplifier with R2/R1 = 5 gets V2 = 3.1 V and V1 = 3.0 V. Vout is...
What does hysteresis in a Schmitt trigger prevent?
options: Output chattering from a noisy input near the threshold
quiz.explain: Two separate thresholds mean small noise cannot flip the output back and forth.

lessons.title: From Devices to Chips: ICs, Logic Families, ADC and DAC
lessons.content:
Think of the journey of a cup of tea at a roadside tong. Tea leaves grew in a garden in Sreemangal, were picked, dried, packed, trucked to Dhaka, sold in the bazar, and finally boiled with milk and sugar into the cup in your hand. You just sip it, but a long chain of steps made it possible. A chip in your phone is the same. Everything you learned in this course, PN junctions, BJTs, MOSFETs, CMOS gates and op-amps, is packed by the billions onto a tiny piece of silicon through a long, careful process. In this final lesson we follow that journey, see how different chip families talk to each other, and learn how the analog world of voltages becomes the digital world of numbers and back.

Why this matters: As a CSE graduate you might write software, design hardware, work on embedded systems or join a chip design team. In every case it helps to know where chips come from, why a 3.3 V board and a 5 V board sometimes refuse to talk, and how a temperature sensor's voltage becomes a number your program can print. ADCs and DACs are the doors between physics and code, and every microcontroller you will program has them.

What this lesson covers: A short history of the integrated circuit; how chips are made, from sand to wafer to packaged IC; process nodes and Moore's law in practice; logic families, especially TTL and CMOS, with their voltage levels, noise margins, fan-out, speed and power; interfacing between families; the ADC with resolution, step size, sampling and the main ADC types; the DAC with the weighted-resistor and R-2R ladder designs; and finally a recap of the whole course.

The integrated circuit: Before 1958, circuits were built from separate transistors, resistors and capacitors soldered together. In 1958 Jack Kilby at Texas Instruments built the first integrated circuit, putting several components on one piece of germanium. In 1959 Robert Noyce at Fairchild made a silicon version using the planar process, which could be mass-produced. The idea of making all the parts and their connections at once on one chip is what allowed computers to shrink from room-sized machines to the phone in your pocket.

From sand to wafer: Silicon comes from silica, the main part of sand and quartz. It is purified to electronic grade, about 99.9999999 percent pure, which means fewer than one foreign atom per billion. Then a single huge crystal is grown by the Czochralski method: a small seed crystal is dipped into molten silicon and slowly pulled up while rotating, and a cylindrical ingot forms. The ingot is sliced into thin discs called wafers, today usually 300 mm across, and polished to a mirror finish. One wafer will hold hundreds of chips.

Making the chip, step by step: Chip fabrication repeats a few basic steps many times, building layers. Oxidation grows a thin insulating layer of silicon dioxide on the surface. Photolithography coats the wafer with a light-sensitive photoresist, shines light through a mask carrying the circuit pattern, and develops it, so the pattern is printed on the wafer much like an old photo negative. Etching removes material where the resist is open. Doping adds impurities into chosen regions, by diffusion at high temperature or more precisely by ion implantation, which fires dopant ions into the silicon; this makes the n and p regions of lesson 3. Deposition adds new layers such as polysilicon gates or more oxide. Metallization lays down metal wires, copper in modern chips, in many stacked layers to connect the transistors.

Finishing the chip: After hundreds of steps, each chip on the wafer is tested with tiny probes. The wafer is cut (diced) into individual dies, the good ones are mounted in packages, connected with fine bond wires or solder bumps, sealed, and tested again. The fraction of good chips is called the yield. All of this happens in cleanrooms, where the air has far fewer dust particles than a hospital operating theatre, because one speck of dust is bigger than many transistors and can ruin a chip. Workers wear full-body suits for this reason.

Process nodes and Moore's law: In 1965 Gordon Moore observed that the number of transistors on a chip was doubling regularly; the version usually quoted is roughly every two years. Shrinking transistors made chips faster, cheaper per transistor and more power-efficient. Today, phone and laptop processors hold tens of billions of transistors. Modern factories use extreme ultraviolet light with a wavelength of 13.5 nm to print the smallest patterns. Names like 7 nm, 5 nm and 3 nm are generation labels; they no longer equal any single physical gate length, so do not take them literally. Shrinking is getting harder and more expensive, which is why chip makers also stack chips in 3D and package several dies together.

Logic families: A logic family is a set of digital chips built with the same circuit technology, so they share voltage levels, speed and power. The two you must know are TTL (transistor-transistor logic), built from BJTs, and CMOS, built from nMOS and pMOS pairs as in lesson 20. The famous 7400 series started as TTL; its part numbers live on in CMOS versions like the 74HC00, which is still four NAND gates. Other families like ECL (emitter-coupled logic) use non-saturating BJTs for very high speed at the cost of high power.

Voltage levels and noise margin: Every family defines four numbers. VOH(min): the lowest voltage a gate guarantees for a logic 1 output. VOL(max): the highest voltage for a logic 0 output. VIH(min): the lowest input voltage guaranteed to be read as 1. VIL(max): the highest input voltage guaranteed to be read as 0. The noise margins are NMH = VOH(min) - VIH(min) and NML = VIL(max) - VOL(max). They tell you how much noise can be added to a wire before a 1 or 0 is misread. Bigger noise margins mean a more robust system.

Standard TTL numbers: TTL runs on 5 V. VOH(min) = 2.4 V, VOL(max) = 0.4 V, VIH(min) = 2.0 V, VIL(max) = 0.8 V. So NMH = 2.4 - 2.0 = 0.4 V and NML = 0.8 - 0.4 = 0.4 V. Standard TTL has a propagation delay of about 10 ns per gate and uses around 10 mW per gate even when idle, because its transistors draw current in both states. Fan-out, the number of inputs one output can drive, is 10 for standard TTL. An unconnected TTL input usually behaves like a 1, but good practice is never to leave inputs floating.

CMOS numbers: A 74HC CMOS gate at 5 V has input thresholds that scale with the supply: VIH(min) is about 3.5 V and VIL(max) about 1.5 V. Its outputs swing almost rail to rail, about 4.9 V and 0.1 V with light loads. So its noise margins are about 1.4 V, much better than TTL. Static power is nearly zero, because in either steady state one transistor of each pair is off. Power is used mainly when switching: P is about C x V squared x f, as you saw in lesson 20. CMOS inputs draw almost no current, so fan-out is limited mainly by speed rather than DC current. One rule: never leave a CMOS input floating, because it can drift between levels and make both transistors half-on.

Interfacing between families: Problems appear when chips from different families or voltages are connected. A TTL output may give only 2.4 V for a logic 1, but a 74HC input at 5 V wants at least 3.5 V, so it may not be read reliably. The fix is the 74HCT family, CMOS chips with TTL-compatible input thresholds, or a pull-up resistor. A very common modern case: an ESP32 or Raspberry Pi works at 3.3 V, while some sensors and an Arduino Uno work at 5 V. A 5 V output can damage a 3.3 V input, so you use a level shifter or a simple resistor divider. Checking these four voltage numbers in datasheets is the most practical skill in this lesson.

The ADC: The world is analog. Temperature, sound and light are continuous. Computers work with numbers. An analog-to-digital converter (ADC) measures a voltage and outputs a binary number. Its resolution n is the number of bits, giving 2 to the power n levels. The step size, also called 1 LSB, is Vref / 2^n. Example: the Arduino Uno has a 10-bit ADC with a 5 V reference, so it has 1024 levels and a step of 5 / 1024 = 4.88 mV. A reading of 512 means about 2.5 V. Because the input is rounded to the nearest level, there is always a quantisation error of up to half a step.

ADC worked example: An LM35 temperature sensor gives 10 mV per degree Celsius. At 30 degrees C its output is 0.300 V. The Arduino reads 0.300 / 0.00488 = 61.4, which becomes 61. Your code converts back: 61 x 4.88 mV = 297.7 mV, which is 29.8 degrees C. The 0.2 degree difference is quantisation error. Want finer readings? Use a lower reference voltage, such as 1.1 V, or an ADC with more bits.

Sampling and ADC types: An ADC takes samples at a fixed rate. The sampling theorem (Nyquist) says the sampling rate must be more than twice the highest frequency in the signal, or the signal gets corrupted (aliasing). Music CDs sample at 44.1 kHz to capture sound up to about 20 kHz. Main ADC types: the flash ADC uses 2^n - 1 comparators at once, for example 255 comparators for 8 bits, so it is extremely fast but large and power-hungry, used in oscilloscopes. The successive-approximation (SAR) ADC tries one bit at a time like a binary search, finishing in n steps; it is the common microcontroller ADC. The sigma-delta ADC oversamples and filters to get high resolution, used in audio and precision scales. The dual-slope ADC integrates the input with an op-amp integrator (lesson 24), slow but accurate and noise-rejecting, used in digital multimeters.

The DAC: A digital-to-analog converter goes the other way: number in, voltage out. For an n-bit DAC, Vout = Vref x D / 2^n, where D is the input number. Example: an 8-bit DAC with Vref = 5 V and D = 128 gives 5 x 128 / 256 = 2.5 V; D = 255 gives about 4.98 V. The binary-weighted resistor DAC is simply the summing amplifier of lesson 24 with input resistors R, 2R, 4R, 8R and so on, so each bit adds twice the weight of the next. Its problem is that for many bits you need a huge range of accurate resistor values. The R-2R ladder DAC solves this with only two resistor values, R and 2R, repeated, which is easy to make accurately on a chip. Many microcontrollers fake a DAC using PWM plus a low-pass filter.

Real-life example 1, a voice call to your nani in the village: When you speak into your phone, the microphone makes a tiny analog voltage. An op-amp preamp boosts it, a filter removes frequencies above what the system needs, and an ADC samples it into numbers; for classic telephone voice, 8000 samples per second covers speech up to about 3.4 kHz. The numbers are compressed and sent as radio signals to the tower and across the network to your nani's phone in Barishal. There a DAC turns the numbers back into a voltage, an amplifier drives the tiny speaker, and she hears you. Almost every lesson of this course is inside that one call, all on CMOS chips made in cleanrooms.

Real-life example 2, a smart poultry farm: Poultry farmers in Bangladesh lose birds when sheds get too hot. A student project uses an ESP32 at 3.3 V with a temperature sensor read by its ADC. The code checks the temperature; above 32 degrees C it switches on fans through a transistor or MOSFET driver and a relay, and sends a phone alert. The designer must check that the sensor output stays within the ADC range, that 5 V modules are level-shifted to 3.3 V, and that the relay has a flyback diode. Device knowledge and coding work together. Bangladesh also now has companies in Dhaka doing chip design and verification for global semiconductor firms, so these skills can lead to real careers.

Common mistakes: Mixing up VIH and VOH, or calculating noise margin the wrong way around. Assuming any 1 from one chip is a valid 1 for another. Leaving CMOS inputs floating. Forgetting that ADC step size is Vref / 2^n, not Vref / (2^n - 1) in most textbook problems (some books use 2^n - 1; follow your course's convention). Thinking a 10-bit ADC is accurate to 10 bits; noise and reference errors reduce real accuracy. Taking 3 nm as a real measured size.

What exams ask: Outline the steps of IC fabrication. Define noise margin and calculate it for TTL and CMOS. Compare TTL and CMOS in a table (supply, speed, power, noise margin, fan-out). Explain why a TTL output may not drive a CMOS input and how to fix it. Find the step size and digital output of an ADC for a given input. Compare flash and successive-approximation ADCs. Find the output of an n-bit DAC, and explain the R-2R ladder.

Course recap: We started with voltage, current and Ohm's law, then met semiconductors, electrons and holes, and doping. The PN junction gave us diodes, and diodes gave us rectifiers, filters, clippers, clampers, Zener regulators and the special diodes that make and catch light. The BJT taught us amplification and switching, biasing and small-signal gain. FETs and MOSFETs led to CMOS, the technology behind every modern processor. Frequency response, feedback and oscillators showed how real amplifiers behave and how clocks are born. Op-amps gave us a ready-made amplifier block for precision circuits. And today we saw how all of it is fabricated into chips and how analog and digital meet. Next steps: digital logic design, computer architecture, microprocessors and embedded systems, and VLSI design if chips excite you.

Recap of this lesson: ICs are built on purified silicon wafers using oxidation, photolithography, etching, doping, deposition and metallization, in cleanrooms. TTL: 5 V, 0.4 V noise margins, fan-out 10. CMOS: almost zero static power, rail-to-rail outputs, larger noise margins. Check VOH, VOL, VIH and VIL when connecting chips. ADC step = Vref / 2^n; sample faster than twice the highest frequency. DAC output = Vref x D / 2^n; the R-2R ladder needs only two resistor values. Well done on finishing Electronic Devices and Circuits.
key_points: First ICs: Kilby (1958, TI) and Noyce (1959, Fairchild, planar silicon).
Fabrication: purified silicon, Czochralski ingot, wafers; oxidation, photolithography, etching, doping, deposition, metallization, all in cleanrooms.
Noise margins: NMH = VOH(min) - VIH(min), NML = VIL(max) - VOL(max).
Standard TTL: 5 V, VOH 2.4, VOL 0.4, VIH 2.0, VIL 0.8, so 0.4 V margins; fan-out 10.
CMOS: near-zero static power, rail-to-rail outputs, bigger noise margins; never leave inputs floating.
ADC: step = Vref / 2^n (10-bit, 5 V gives 4.88 mV); sample faster than 2 x fmax.
ADC types: flash (fastest), SAR (common), sigma-delta (high resolution), dual-slope (multimeters).
DAC: Vout = Vref x D / 2^n; R-2R ladder uses only R and 2R.
lessons.tip: Make a single page with the four TTL voltages and the four CMOS voltages drawn as two vertical bars side by side. Seeing them as a picture makes noise margin and interfacing questions almost automatic.
